1.spine: A State is an organisation, and power centralises in a strong personality: Babur's guns founded a Mughal State, Akbar built its machinery (Mansabdari and land revenue), and the machine ran on personal loyalty, so when the King could not deliver, it began to hollow out.
beats:
A State is an organisation.
Power centralises in a strong personality, and when that personality weakens power leaves either vertically downwards (decentralisation) or sideways to another personality (horizontal displacement, as Kodak gave way to smartphones). A State is the organisation that rules a territory (the country) and its people (the nation), by making laws, implementing them and settling disputes (L, E, J). Sovereignty adds a symbolic head of State.
→ Now watch one such organisation arrive in India.

The Mughal ledger.
There are fifteen Mughal monarchs, from Babur 26-30 to Bahadur Shah Zafar 37-57, and the reign codes pass the baton from one to the next. Humayun 30-40 is the only one with two reign periods. The teacher writes the Mughal State as 1526-1858 with an intermission 1540-55.
→ It all starts with a prince who has lost his home.

A prince without a home.
Babur 26-30 was born in 1483 in Fergana, a Timurid descendant (the Mughals are 'Mongol' in Persian, but they took pride in Timur, who captured Delhi in 1398). He lost Fergana by 1512, and Kabul (1504) was economically poor. India was rich but politically fragile under the Lodis, and with Ottoman gunners he began attacking from 1519.
→ So he comes down through the Khyber Pass.

Panipat, 1526.
Babur 26-30 had about 12,000 men but small bronze cannons, and Ibrahim Lodi was killed. The Delhi Sultanate (1206-1526) ended and the Mughal Kingdom was born, a kingdom and not yet an empire. Panipat saw battles in 1526, 1556 and 1761 because it lay near the Khyber Pass, in the corridor between the Thar Desert and the Himalayan foothills, with the Yamuna as a choke-point.
→ But a kingdom is easier to win than to keep.

The son loses it.
Humayun 30-40 was defeated by Sher Shah 40-45 Suri 40-45 at Chausa (1539) and Kanauj (1540), and the Suri dynasty (1540-55) pushed the Mughals out. Sher Shah's three reforms outlasted him: the Patta and Qabuliyat revenue system, the silver Rupiya, and the Grand Trunk Road from Peshawar to Sonargaon.
→ Humayun now needs an ally.

Persia's price.
The Safavids of Iran helped, at a price: Shia forms, Kandahar ceded, Persian culture promoted. With 14,000 Iranian troops Humayun 30-40 won at Sirhind (1555), but in January 1556 he fell from the stairs of his library and died. Hemu seized Delhi and declared himself Samrat, and Bairam Khan, guardian of the 13-year-old Akbar 56-05, defeated him at the Second Panipat (1556).
→ Now a boy emperor must build the machine.

Akbar's machine: the Mansabdar.
Every Mansabdar held a mansab (a post), with a military and civil role, and two ranks: Zat (personal) plus Sawar (horsemen to maintain). Lineage mattered more than merit, with Birbal the exception. Pay came in cash (Naqdi) or by Jagir, and Mughal land was Jagir, Khalisa, Inam or Mashrut; four-fifths of LR came from Jagirs. A Tankha Jagir was transferable, capped and confiscated on death, while a Watan Jagir was hereditary with 10% Peshkash.
→ Someone has to fill the treasury that pays them.

Land revenue: who gets what.
Four stakeholders hold rights in land: owner, tenant, collector and State. The State assessed through the Patwari, Qanungo, Amil and Amalguzar, settled with a Patta and a Qabuliyat, and collected through the Zamindar (about 10% as Nankar / Malikana) and the village Muqaddam. LR was a share of gross produce, and the Khudkasht had occupancy rights while the Pahikasht had none.
→ But a machine run on personal loyalty has a flaw.

The flaw.
Mansabdari was a patron-client bond: the King gave rank and Jagir, the Mansabdar gave loyalty and an army. The loyalty was personal, not institutional. After 1707, if the King could not deliver the desired Mansab and Jagir, loyalty dissolved, and the end state was an army of 2 lakh on paper and 1 lakh in reality.
→ A short-of-cash State then reaches for the auction.

The auction door.
Ijaradari (revenue farming) arises from need (war, bad harvest, a short treasury) or greed. The Ijaradar paid in advance, worked for profit on a contract of 3 to 5 years, and gave the peasant no Patta. It began as the Muqatai of the Delhi Sultanate, was practically abolished by Akbar 56-05 and then revived by weaker rulers (Jahangir, Shahjahan, Aurangzeb, Jahandar Shah, Farukhsiyar) until Warren Hastings 73-85 formalised it as the Farming System in 1772. When the Zamindar (leader) and the ryots (followers) are both unhappy, a strong revolt follows, as with Churaman 95-21 Jat about 1695.
→ Meanwhile Akbar tried to hold his diverse realm by faith.

Akbar's faith ladder.
Akbar 56-05 built the Ibadat Khana at Fatehpur Sikri (1575), issued the Mahzar (1579) making the Emperor the final word on faith, and set up the Din-i-Ilahi (1582), a religio-political experiment rather than a movement. Behind them all stood Sulh-i-Kul, universal peace through equal respect for every faith. Jizya, by contrast, was first imposed in Sindh by Muhammad bin Qasim and institutionalised by Qutb-ud-din Aibak 06-10 and his successors.

2.spine: Peak, then rot, then collapse: Aurangzeb 58-07 reaches the peak in 1707 but his wars, religious policy and the Jagirdari crisis empty the treasury and the people's goodwill; weak emperors cannot keep the Mansabdari bargain, so factions and corruption rot the court and army; the Marathas and Nadir Shah then expose the rot and the emperor ends up under Maratha protection.
beats:
The peak that hid the rot (1707).
By 1707 the Mughal State has its greatest extent under Aurangzeb 58-07, yet the teacher says its economic power and social power have not peaked. State power is Political + Economic + Military + Social + Technological, and the decline will weaken all five at once. Aurangzeb laid the foundation of decline; the weak emperors after him could not revive the State or added to the decline.
→ So what exactly did Aurangzeb do?

The emperor who never stopped fighting.
Aurangzeb 58-07 comes to power in 1658 after killing his elder brother Dara Shikoh, and wants all India, above all the Deccan. He annexes Bijapur in 1686 (Adil Shahi, 1489-1686) and Golconda in 1687 (Qutb Shahi, 1518-1687), but the Marathas never accept Mughal authority. About 40 years of war drain the treasury and cripple the Mansabdars, who must maintain armies; by 1705 the Marathas are winning.
→ But war was not his only mistake: he also lost the people.

The people turn away.
Aurangzeb 58-07 follows an orthodox Islam in his governance. He re-introduces Jizya in 1679 (Akbar 56-05 had abolished it in 1564) and demolishes the Kashi Vishwanath temple in 1669 (his court record, the Maasir-i-Alamgiri, documents it). He executes Guru Tegh Bahadur in 1675 and Sambhaji 80-89 in 1689; both refuse to convert and become martyrs, hardening Sikh and Maratha feeling.
→ Meanwhile the nobles who run his army are being squeezed too.

The bargain breaks.
The Mansabdari system runs on personal loyalty to the emperor and a give-and-take: Mansabs and Jagirs for military service. A strong emperor keeps even an unhappy Mansabdar quiet through faith in fairness or through fear. A weak emperor cannot, so the Mansabdar acts on his disloyalty: lobbying, backbiting, a takhtapalat to bring his favourite to the throne.
→ Nobles busy in court politics are not busy with the army.

A paper army.
Europeans win with smaller numbers using file firing, grapeshot and the bayonet on the Brown Bess musket; Haider Ali 61-82 reforms on a European model, but the Mughals, paralysed by factionalism, reform nothing. Commanders are chosen by court politics, not merit, and Mansabdars keep far fewer cavalry than their Sawar rank requires.
→ And the money problem explains why they cheat.

Too many Mansabdars, too little land.
The Jagirdari crisis is like a water crisis: the number of Mansabdars goes up and the land goes down. After 1686 and 1687 Aurangzeb 58-07 makes most Bijapur and Golconda land Khalisa yet absorbs the Deccani nobles; later Mughals over-recruit to buy loyalty; land shrinks as the Marathas win. Then 5% of Mansabdars control 61% of Jagir revenue, and luxury inflation hurts the rest. The teacher calls its impact the most important in the decline.
→ Insecure tenure turns the Jagirdars into looters.

Kal ho na ho Jagir.
Jagirs are shuffled to satisfy disgruntled Naqdi Mansabdars, so no Jagirdar knows how long he holds his land. He extracts the maximum in the minimum time, Ijaradari spreads, and Zamindar-led revolts follow: the Jat Kingdom grows from the 1695 revolt of Churaman 95-21 Jat. Military corruption brings victories to rebel states (Sikh, Marathas, Afghans) and to an outsider like Nadir Shah.
→ At court, the factions now fight for the throne itself.

Five factions, three rounds.
The court splits into Irani, Turani, Hindustani, Hindu and Deccani groups. Bahadur Shah 07-12 fights his brothers; Jahandar Shah 12-13 rules with Zulfiqar Khan and is executed by Farukhsiyar 13-19, who rises with the Sayyid Brothers. He refuses to be their puppet, so the Sayyids ally with the Marathas (15,000 cavalry in Delhi, 1719), kill him and install Muhammad Shah 19-48. Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48 beats the Sayyids with the Irani group, then takes Hyderabad in 1724.
→ The Marathas watch Delhi's weakness.

The Marathas test Delhi.
From 1705 the Marathas defeat Mughal forces; by the mid-18th century they recover Aurangzeb 58-07's gains and take Akbar 56-05's Gujarat, and only Hyderabad holds out. In 1737 Peshwa Bajirao 20-40 plunders Delhi and briefly holds Md Shah prisoner. In 1738 they beat the army led by Nizam, and the Treaty of Bhopal gives them the Chambal-Narmada lands and Malwa.
→ Then a bigger predator arrives from Iran.

Nadir Shah, the lowest point (1739).
Nadir Shah wants plunder, not annexation. At Karnal the Mughal army is routed and Sadat Khan 22-39 is captured; Nizam, now Mir Bakshi, buys peace for Rs 50 lakh. But Sadat Khan, passed over for that post, goads Nadir Shah to attack Delhi: he rules for 60 days, about 2 lakh civilians die, about 100 crore is looted, including the Peacock Throne with the Kohinoor. The Marathas, home in the South after Bhopal, simply wait.
→ After this blow, the emperor needs a protector.

Protector and puppet (1752-54).
Nadir Shah's victory encourages Abdali's first invasion of 1748. In 1752 the emperor comes under Maratha protection for fear of Afghan invasions, and in 1754 the Marathas install Alamgir II 54-59 as their puppet. By the mid-18th century there are many States, not one: successors (Bengal, Awadh, Hyderabad), rebels (Jats, Marathas, Rohilkhand, Farukhabad) and the already autonomous (Mysore, Rajputs, Travancore), with the Marathas as No. 1 power. The emperor keeps symbolic sovereignty until 1858.
→ Now: how will the exam ask this?

How the exam asks it.
Prelims 2003: Shah Alam II 60-06 stayed away from Delhi in his early years for fear of his Wazir Imad-ul-Mulk, not a frontier invasion; read A and R separately, then think. Mains 2017 asked about a fragmented polity: find the protagonist and weight 30% Mughal decline and 70% regional powers, and flip the weights if the Mughal Empire itself is the subject.

3.spine: The emperor's own governors took his Sword, Purse and Eyes into one hand through a five-step recipe, yet kept his name on top, so Bengal, Awadh and Hyderabad became real States on paper still Mughal. That gap between paper and power is what the EIC stepped into.
beats:
Control is not rule.
The teacher opens with a warning: control can exist without rule (absentee colonialism, like Angola and Mozambique, where raw materials leave and few people live on the ground). Rule means doing L, E, J, making and implementing laws, plus governance of health, education and infrastructure. For the EIC in Bengal, Plassey 1757 was control and Buxar 1764 was rule.
→ But what kind of India was the EIC stepping into?

A patchwork.
By the mid-18th century the Mughal State no longer worked as one unified polity. Power decentralised from 1707 to 1800 into three classes of State: Successor, Rebel and Already Autonomous. The teacher lists the later emperors as proof of decline, circling FS 13-19 and Md Shah 19-48 as the reigns in which the Successor States arose.
→ Now to the first class: the governors who stabbed the emperor in the back.

Three founders, three years.
Bengal was set up by Murshid Quli Khan (MQK 17-27) in 1717, Awadh by Sadat Khan 22-39 in 1722, Hyderabad by Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48 in 1724. Each ruled de facto as sovereign, yet none declared independence. Four reasons: symbolic legitimacy, ambitions at Delhi (Nizam was Wazir 1722-24 and Mir Bakshi 1739-40), military assistance and trade barriers.
→ So how did a mere governor get so much power?

Sword, Purse, Eyes.
Akbar 56-05's system split a province in three. The Subahdar (Nizamat) held the Sword and reported to the Emperor; the Diwan (Diwani) held the Purse and reported to the Imperial Diwan; the Bakshi held military audit and intelligence and reported to the Mir Bakshi. The Diwan and the Bakshi both bypassed the Nazim: checks and balances.
→ But every founder had to break exactly this design.

The recipe.
Extract the Subahdari, end the checks and balances with personal loyalists, build revenue strength (field survey, efficient LR system), co-opt the men of money (merchants, bankers and Ijaradars given Mansabs) and convert Tankha Jagirs into Vatan Jagirs. The result is a diffused autonomous polity: a Nawab on top of a network of powerful actors, with the Mughal link kept as a symbol.
→ Bengal shows the recipe at its clearest.

Bengal: two hats and fifteen friends.
In 1717 MQK 17-27 became Nazim while already Diwan, ending Akbar 56-05's checks. His field surveys and intermediary Zamindars paid off: by 1727 just fifteen collected 50% of Bengal Suba's LR. The Jagat Seths, a hereditary title of a banking family, funded it all. Proof of diffusion: in 1740 Alivardi Khan 40-56 toppled Sarfaraz Khan with a Jagat Seth's backing and bought the emperor's approval with a promised crore.
→ Then an outside shock deepened the break.

Bengal breaks away.
From 1745 to 1751 Raghuji Bhonsle of Nagpur raided Bengal and Alivardi could not beat him. The 1751 settlement gave Bhonsle the Chauth (one-fourth of revenues) of Bengal and Bihar plus direct control of Orissa. Alivardi stopped sending revenue to Delhi and stopped seeking approval for appointments. After him came Siraj 56-57, Mir Jafar 57-60, Mir Qasim 60-63, Mir Jafar again, and in 1765 the Diwani passed to the EIC.
→ Awadh followed its own road to the same place.

Awadh: Sadat, Safdar, Shuja.
Sadat Khan 22-39 became Subahdar in 1722 as a reward for crushing revolts and kept ambitions at the centre. Passed over for Mir Bakshi, he convinced Nadir Shah to invade Delhi in 1739, and died by suicide. Safdar Jung 39-54, Wazir in 1748, annexed Farukhabad and was forced to resign in 1753: Awadh's virtual break. Shuja 54-75 fought at Panipat (1761) and lost at Buxar (1764); Awadh was annexed in 1856.
→ In the south, the Nizam had gone home for good.

Hyderabad: the Nizam goes home.
Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48 (Chin Qulich Khan, Asaf Jah I) led the Turani group, helped remove the Sayyid Brothers in 1720, and took Hyderabad in 1724 after beating Mubariz Khan. The Marathas beat him in 1728 and 1738. After serving as Mir Bakshi (1739-40) he gave up on the centre. Hyderabad kept the emperor's name on coins and the Khutba, tolerated its Hindu majority, and converted Tankha to Vatan Jagirs most aggressively.
→ And inside Hyderabad lay a smaller State of its own.

The Carnatic: a tenant downstairs.
The Hyderabad Subah had two parts: Hyderabad north of the Krishna, and the Carnatic (Hyderabad-Karnatic), twelve districts south with capital Gingee and its own Nawab who reported to the Nizam. Saadatullah Khan (1710-32) moved the capital to Arcot and made the post hereditary; Dost Ali Khan (1732-40) was killed by the Marathas; Anwar-ud-din Khan (from 1744) was the Nizam's pick but became autonomous too. This is the Prelims 2021 trap.
→ Put the three States side by side and the pattern shows.

The gap the EIC stepped into.
Across all three, a powerful Mansabdar concentrated power, none declared independence, the Carnatic was a successor State inside a successor State, and the emperor became a constitutional monarch with no executive power. Legitimacy and real power had come apart, which made the subcontinent vulnerable to outside penetration.

4.spine: One strong man builds Svarajya with guerrilla war, a navy and forts; after him a weak centre lets the Sardars build Samrajya and live on Chauth. The Peshwa takes the real power (Sangola 1750), factions grow, and Abdali beats a divided Maratha camp at Panipat (1761); the vacuum is filled by the EIC.
beats:
A boy from the Maval.
Shivaji 74-80 Bhonsle is born on 19 February 1630 to Shahji (Jagirdar of Poona, a General and Mansabdar in Bijapur) and Jijabai. Guided by Dadaji Kondadev, he takes his first fort at 16, in 1646, working from the hilly, forested Maval region with local warriors and peasants.
→ But a boy with a few forts must beat much bigger armies, so he needs a method.

Guerrilla war and the Purandhar squeeze.
From 1657 he attacks oppressive Bijapur, and in 1659 he kills Afzal Khan with the concealed Bagh Nakh and a Bichhwa. In 1663 he defeats Shaista Khan 64-88 and sacks Surat, so Aurangzeb 58-07 sends Jai Singh 99-43, who cuts off supplies and in 1665 besieges Purandhar. To spare his soldiers and people Shivaji 74-80 signs the Treaty of Purandhar: 23 of 35 forts go, Sambhaji 80-89 becomes a Mansabdar of 5,000, and he backs the Mughals against Bijapur.
→ Now a man who has survived the squeeze must turn a raiding band into a State.

Crown, army and navy.
In 1666 he and Sambhaji 80-89 are insulted and imprisoned at Agra, and escape disguised as Sadhus. In 1674 he is crowned at Raigarh as Chhatrapati, declaring himself independent of the Mughals, and Svarajya covers the Marathi-speaking region. His army of 30,000 to 40,000 light cavalry holds 240 forts; his navy grows from 20 ships in 1657 to 200 by 1664 (peak 700), guarded by Jaladurg sea-forts, and he pays officials in cash, never in Jagirs.
→ But a State also needs ministers, officers and courts.

How the Chhatrapati ruled.
He governs with the Ashtapradhan, eight ministers headed by the Peshwa as Prime Minister, like a British monarch with a Privy Council. Under the Peshwa sit the Darakhdars, and in 1774 twelve of them form the Barbhai Mandal under Nana Fadnavis. Provinces (Sarkars) have Governors whose office is auctioned, cross-checked by the Deshmukhi, while villages run under a Patil and justice climbs from the Panch to the Peshwa.
→ Yet the whole machine hung on one strong man, and he died in 1680.

A troubled succession.
Sambhaji 80-89 is captured by Aurangzeb 58-07 and killed in 1689 after weeks of torture, and Rajaram 89-00 dies of tuberculosis in 1700, aged 30. His widow Tarabai rules as regent for the infant Shivaji II until 1707, when the Mughals release Shahu 19-49, the elder son of Sambhaji 80-89. The release triggers a civil war that lasts until 1719, while Sardars and Deshmukhs keep switching sides, which the Mughals encourage.
→ So the question is who wins, and which side has the better minister.

Shahu wins, the Sardars rise.
The sixth Peshwa, Balaji Vishwanath 13-20, wins Brahmin banking families and the new Sardars for Shahu 19-49 and persuades Admiral Kanhoji Angre to switch in 1714. The Treaty of Warna (1731) splits the house into Satara and Kolhapur. Four Sardars become kingmakers, Gaikwad at Baroda, Holkar at Indore, Scindia at Gwalior and Bhonsle at Nagpur, so Svarajya (inside Maharashtra) is ruled by the Peshwa and Samrajya (outside, from 1719) by the Sardars.
→ Now the Sardars rule far from home, so how do they pay for it?

Chauth and Sardeshmukhi.
Chauth is 25% of the revenue of a protected state, paid for military protection; the annual drain weakens that state until it cannot pay and is annexed after a short war, which beats a long, costly war of direct annexation. Sardeshmukhi is an extra 10%, collected both inside and outside. When Sardars collect Chauth abroad they keep 66% (Mokasa), send 25% (Babti) to the Chhatrapati, give 6% (Sahotra) to the Pant Sachiv and 3% (Nadgaunda) to the Chhatrapati's discretion.
→ Chauth feeds the empire, and the Peshwa now bargains with the Mughal kingmakers.

The bargain of 1719 and the decade of growth.
In 1719 Balaji Vishwanath 13-20 allies with the Sayyid Brothers, who remove Farrukhsiyar 13-19 and install Muhammad Shah 19-48 as a puppet. The Marathas win autonomy in Maharashtra, the Chauth of Malwa and Gujarat, and Chauth plus Sardeshmukhi of six Deccan provinces, but the Nizam beats the Sayyids in 1720 and stops paying in 1724. A decade of expansion follows (1727-39): Gujarat at 60%, Malwa in 1729, Delhi plundered in 1737 by Baji Rao 20-40, the Treaty of Bhopal in 1738 and Bassein in 1739, then Odisha, Khandesh, Ahmedabad and Alamgir II 54-59 as a puppet in 1754.
→ But as the Marathas grow, power slides from the Chhatrapati down to the Peshwa.

Sangola 1750.
Balaji Vishwanath 13-20, then Baji Rao 20-40, then Nana Saheb (1740-61) hold the Peshwa's chair, so after three generations it is hereditary in effect, and Shahu 19-49 keeps delegating to him. When Tarabai says Shahu's adopted son Ramraja is not her grandson, Nana Saheb backs Ramraja but makes him sign the Treaty of Sangola in February 1750, and all real power passes to the Peshwa. The teacher's family table shows the eldest brother taking the father's seat.
→ Now a house with a weaker centre meets a united enemy from the north-west.

Panipat, 1761.
From 1756 Abdali invaded, took Lahore and Kashmir and made his son Timur Shah Governor, but in March 1758 Raghunath Rao 73-74 expelled Timur from Lahore, the peak of Maratha power and Abdali's immediate reason to return. Abdali (60,000) joins the Rohillas under Najib-ud-Daula 57-70, the Bangash Pathans under Ahmad Khan (1750-82) and Awadh under Shuja-ud-Daula 54-75, while the Marathas (50,000) under Sadasiv Rao Bhau face them with the Sikhs, Rajputs and Jats neutral and their supply route from Delhi cut at Panipat. Swivel guns pierce their armour, Raghuji Bhonsle refuses to fight, and about 50,000 Marathas die.
→ Neither side rules India afterwards, so the Marathas fight on in decline.

Decline, and why no all-India rule.
Young and weak Peshwas follow (Madhav Rao 61-72, Narayan Rao 72-73, the infant Madhav Rao II 74-95), though the Marathas win the First Anglo-Maratha War (1775-82) and Mahadji Scindia 68-94 retakes Delhi in 1771 and builds the Campoo army in 1784. The EIC takes Delhi in 1803 and annexes Svarajya in 1817-19. The Marathas never ruled all India because they took tribute instead of ruling, and their centre was weak: they had control but not rule.

5.spine: Delhi's weakness offers rebels a deal (the middle path), so Jats, Bangash Pathans and Rohillas turn local force into rule; but each stands on an outside prop (Abdali, Maratha backing) and falls when the prop is removed, and Abdali's own reason for coming was a family quarrel over Lahore.
beats:
Two bad options and a middle path.
When rebels establish their rule in an area, the emperor can fight on and end the rebellion, or lose the territory and let the rebel set up an independent kingdom. The middle path: the rebel accepts Mansabdar status, the Mughal as emperor, tribute to Delhi and a duty to maintain an army and help the emperor militarily. The emperor accepts dynastic governorship, the territory as the rebel's Watan Jagir, and non-interference. Both core interests are met; only the Sikhs, who never accepted Mughal symbolic sovereignty (except once, in 1707), stand outside.
→ So who actually took this path?

Three more Rebel States.
Apart from the Marathas, the 18th century saw three more: the Jat Kingdom of Bharatpur in East Rajasthan, Farrukhabad (est. 1714, Bangash Pathans) and Rohilkhand (process began 1721, completed 1737-40, Rohilla Afghans). All three turned local military power into territorial rule as the Mughal Empire weakened, yet none built a large, sustainable empire.
→ First, the farmers who fought back.

The Jats rise from the soil.
The Jats were an agrarian community, hostile to the Mughals since Jahangir 05-27, when harsh land revenue and the drive to subordinate local autonomy pushed their Zamindars into organised resistance, mainly by guerrilla warfare. The chain runs Gokla (first revolt, 1669), Rajaram 89-00, Churaman 95-21, who formally founds the Jat Kingdom of Bharatpur in 1695, and Badan Singh (1722-55), who consolidates it.
→ Then one ruler takes it to the peak.

Surajmal's peak, and the fall.
Surajmal 56-63 builds a strong, centralised State and forces the Mughal emperor to recognise him as autonomous. He recruits European soldiers, introduces a Mughal-style revenue system and removes relatives from court posts; the State stretches from Delhi to Agra and from the Chambal to the Ganga, with the Iron Fort Lohagarh as his pride. At Panipat 1761 he wanted guerrilla warfare, Sadasiv Rao Bhau did not, yet the Jats still sent supplies. After he dies in 1763 the State collapses: it was no peasant utopia, since land revenue stayed high and power stayed with Zamindars.
→ But the Afghans have a story that began much earlier.

The Afghan who ruled Delhi.
Afghans had been migrating into North India since the 15th century, driven by poor economy and instability at home, and worked as wandering warlords in its military labour markets. Farid Khan, born around 1486 at Sasaram in Bihar to the Sur clan, rises through ability, serves the Mughals after 1526 and studies their administration. By 1540, as Sher Shah 40-45, he defeats Humayun 30-40 at Kanauj and seizes Delhi.
→ And what does he do with five years?

Five years that mattered (1540-45).
Sher Shah 40-45 builds the Suba-Sarkar-Pargana hierarchy (Akbar 56-05 later adopts it), upgrades the Uttarapath into the Grand Trunk Road, sets up the Dak Chowki relay post, issues the standard silver Rupiya and fixes a fair land revenue directly with the peasant, recorded in a Patta and a Qubuliat. After he dies in 1545 the Afghans fragment; the Suri Interregnum (1540-55) ends when Humayun 30-40 retakes Delhi after Sirhind in 1555.
→ In the 18th century a new Afghan surge arrives.

Farrukhabad: a warlord and a flattering name.
Md Khan Bangash, a Pathan warlord, backs Farrukhsiyar 13-19 with 12,000 troops and is rewarded with the rank of Nawab and revenue near the Ganga; he founds Farrukhabad in 1714, after first naming a town Mohammadabad after himself, which annoyed the emperor. His son Qaim Khan is killed in 1749 through the scheme of Safdar Jung 39-54, and Farrukhabad is annexed to Awadh and plundered.
→ Then Ahmad Khan comes back.

Ahmad Khan's see-saw.
Ahmad Khan Bangash 50-71 retakes Farrukhabad in 1750, is driven out in 1751-52 by Marathas (Holkar and Scindia) and Jats at Awadh's request, and returns by a treaty that hands half of Farrukhabad to Holkar and Scindia. In 1761 he fights beside Abdali 47-72 at Third Panipat and recovers his full dominions. The EIC annexes Farrukhabad in 1802.
→ Rohilkhand rises another way, from the ground.

Rohilkhand: hired guns become rulers.
Zamindars of Katehr (around Bareilly and Moradabad) hire Afghan mercenaries, the Rohillas, who grow dominant under Daud Khan. When he dies in 1721 his adopted son Ali Md Khan takes over and spends two decades absorbing lands. In 1739 Nadir Shah paralyses Delhi, so Ali stops paying taxes; in 1740 Md Shah 19-48 co-opts him with the Subadar title and Katehr is renamed Rohilkhand.
→ Like Farrukhabad, it ends with the Abdali prop gone.

The end of Rohilkhand.
Najib-ud-Daula 57-70 backs Abdali at Panipat in 1761 and Delhi is under Rohilla influence until 1771, when Mahadji Scindia 68-94 retakes it. Najib dies in 1770; in 1774 Awadh, with EIC help (allies since the Treaty of Allahabad 1765), annexes most of Rohilkhand. A small remainder becomes the State of Rampur, under the EIC from 1801.
→ Why did Abdali come in the first place?

Why Abdali came (Prelims 2010).
In March 1758 Raghunath Rao 73-74 crossed into Punjab and drove away Timur Shah, Abdali's son and Governor of Punjab and Kashmir. The Marathas made Adina Beg Khan Governor of Punjab for Rs 75 lakh a year, and later Sabaji Scindia held Attock and Peshawar on the Afghan border. The immediate reason for Third Panipat was to avenge Timur Shah.
→ Now step back: one pattern fits all three.

One pattern, one prop.
The Jats rose from an agrarian base upward, Farrukhabad from court politics downward, Rohilkhand from the ground up over two decades. The common rule: each needed external support to peak (Abdali for the Afghan kingdoms, Maratha tactical backing for Surajmal 56-63) and each collapsed once that support was removed: Abdali left in 1761 and Surajmal died in 1763.

6.spine: Territory turns a faith into a power: the Mughals kill two Gurus, so the Sikhs arm themselves (Khalsa) and demand a State at Anandpur. Banda Bahadur 08-15 builds one State and loses it; the Misl confederacy keeps the idea alive as a weak centre; Ranjit Singh 01-39 centralises it, then balances it, and signs treaties with the EIC.
beats:
A peaceful faith.
Guru Nanak Dev (1469-1539), a contemporary of Babur 26-30, teaches four things: one formless God, direct access without rituals or priests, no caste, honest living and selfless service. He makes four Udasis over 30 years (about 30,000 km), then settles at Kartarpur and starts the Langar, a free kitchen for equality.
→ But a faith meets a State the moment territory enters the picture.

Territory, and the first blow (1606).
The teacher says a State is an organisation with a territory motive, and until the Sikhs wanted territory there was no dispute. They begin demanding a Sikh State in and around Anandpur (west of Shimla, south of Chamba), land held by Shivalik hill chiefs who are Mughal allies. In 1606 Jahangir 05-27 executes the 5th Guru, Arjan Dev, and a peaceful movement starts turning martial.
→ A second Guru is killed, and the answer is an army.

The Khalsa (1675-1699).
In 1675 Aurangzeb 58-07 has the 9th Guru, Teg Bahadur, executed in Delhi. In 1699 the 10th Guru, Gobind Singh 76-08, founds the Khalsa at Anandpur: a Sikh military organisation, something like an NSG or STF, to defend the Panth and struggle for a Sikh State. Its identity is the five Ks.
→ But Anandpur never comes, and the Guru's family pays.

The Sahibzadas and a broken promise (1704-1707).
In December 1704 the two elder sons, Ajit Singh (18) and Jujhar Singh (14), die at Chamkaur. The same month the two younger, Zorawar Singh (9) and Fateh Singh (6), are buried alive in a wall on the orders of Wazir Khan, Faujdar of Sirhind. In 1707 Bahadur Shah 07-12, on a pacifist policy, gives the Guru a high Mansab and promises Anandpur, but never keeps it.
→ And the promise is followed by a plot.

Nanded and the Book (1708).
On 7 October 1708 Wazir Khan's assassins strike the Guru at Abchal Nagar Sahib in Nanded; he kills them but dies of his injuries at 42, and Wazir Khan is not punished. A few days before, he had declared the Guru Granth Sahib the final Guru, to stop Jat versus Khatri tension: Jats dominated the Khalsa and all ten Gurus were Khatri traders. The Book was installed at the Akal Takht.
→ Now someone must carry the struggle and take revenge.

Banda Bahadur 08-15's State.
From 1708 Banda Bahadur 08-15 carries on. On 10 May 1710 at Chappar Chiri he kills Wazir Khan and takes Sirhind. His State between the Ravi and the Jamuna has its own coins, officials and seal, which the teacher reads as full independence. Farrukhsiyar 13-19 sends Abdus Samad Khan as Governor of Lahore to crush it.
→ But a State needs its own people behind it.

Why it fell (1715-1716).
The Khatri traders, hurt by constant war, turned away. Jahandar Shah 12-13 brought Ijaradari to Punjab to co-opt them, and he and Farrukhsiyar 13-19 offered them Mansabs. Hindu Jat zamindars switched too: Churaman 95-21 went over when the Mughals recognised his Jat Kingdom. Banda Bahadur 08-15 was also not a Guru. He was defeated in 1715 and executed in 1716.
→ Yet the Sikh State does not die.

The Misl confederacy.
The Mughals are too weak to take Punjab back, so power spreads to Misl chiefs: kinship clans that unite in wars, especially against Afghan invasions, and otherwise act alone. Conquered land is shared by contribution. By 1770 there are 12 major Misls with the Dal Khalsa at the centre; at Manupur 1748 it prepares a joint defence and Abdali is defeated. This is a weak centre, a fragmented polity, like the Maratha Confederacy.
→ But power tends to gather in a strong personality.

Ranjit Singh 01-39 centralises.
Zaman Shah's invasions are a crisis that becomes an opportunity for Ranjit Singh 01-39 of the Sukerchakia Misl, who takes Lahore from the Bhangi Misl and is crowned Maharaja in 1801. The other Misl chiefs become tribute-paying vassals holding Jagirs, not Watan. The handout dates Lahore to 1801, the slides to 1799.
→ Now he must settle accounts with the EIC across the Sutlej.

Treaties and conquests (1809-1838).
In 1809 Charles Metcalfe, the EIC's Resident at Delhi, signs the Treaty of Amritsar: Ranjit Singh 01-39 is recognised as sovereign, there is a military alliance, the Sutlej is the border, and he is free to expand on his side. He then takes Multan (1818), Kashmir (1819) and Peshawar (1834, Hari Singh Nalwa). The 1838 Tripartite Treaty with Shah Shuja makes Afghanistan and Punjab a buffer against feared Russian invasion.
→ So what kind of State held all this together?

A balanced, secular State.
Ranjit Singh 01-39 built power by coercion, diplomacy and balance between Misl chiefs, the Khalsa army, Khatri traders and non-Sikh nobles such as the Dogras. Only 40% of land was Jagirdari; the rest paid the King directly, collected by Kardars (collector, magistrate, police chief, customs officer). Village autonomy was respected, Fakir Azizuddin was Foreign Minister, Dewan Dina Nath Finance Minister, and Sahajdhari Sikhs were included.

7.spine: None of these three was ruled by the Mughals in the middle path, and each built State capacity in its own way: the Rajputs by bargaining, Travancore by trade, Mysore by a war machine; each ended up under EIC pressure.
beats:
Outside the middle path.
These are the third class of regional States from Chapter 3: Already Autonomous States, where even when the Mughal was powerful he did not rule. The Rajputs were brought into the Mughal system but kept their homes, Travancore was never part of the Mughal Empire, and Mysore grew out of the Vijayanagar world.
→ Start in the north, with Akbar's deal.

Akbar's Rajput bargain.
Rajputana had no single centre, only roughly 20 major clans (a multi-polar world). Defeating them all would be expensive and uncertain, so Akbar 56-05 co-opted the powerful chiefs as Mansabdars with Vatan Jagirs, and in return they accepted the Emperor, paid tribute and sent troops. They formed a Hindu bloc of about 15% of the Mansabdars, and Akbar helped them subdue smaller chiefs: a partial consolidation.
→ That held for most of the 17th century, until Aurangzeb.

1680.
Mewar under Raj Singh began expanding aggressively, and Aurangzeb 58-07 grew uneasy at one Rajput power dominating Rajputana. In 1680 a child came to the throne of Marwar, which lay astride the trade route from Delhi and Agra to Ahmedabad, and Aurangzeb interfered. Marwar and Mewar revolted, but the other chiefs refused to join for fear of Mewar, and the revolt collapsed.
→ After 1707 the Rajputs went their own way.

Own terms, then new masters.
After Aurangzeb's death in 1707 the Rajputs increasingly acted on their own terms, most prominently Sawai Jai Singh 99-43 of Amber. From 1751 the Marathas began regular raids for tribute but never fully conquered the region. After the Second Anglo-Maratha War (1803-05) the EIC replaced them and signed Subordinate Alliances: the ruler keeps his throne but surrenders foreign policy and defence.
→ One Rajput of that age deserves a close look.

Four hats.
Sawai means 1.25 times more able than any contemporary ruler, a title from Aurangzeb 58-07. Jai Singh was a Mughal Mansabdar, state-builder, astronomer and town planner, Subedar of Malwa (1729-37) and Agra. His Hurda conference of 1734 collapsed, and the Treaty of Bhopal (1738) gave Malwa to the Marathas. He founded Jaipur in 1727 (Vidyadhar Bhattacharya, Vastu Shastra, grid, the first planned city of modern India), and was the last Indian ruler to perform the Ashvamedha and Vajapeya Yajnas.
→ His other passion was the sky.

Stone and sky.
Five Jantar Mantars stand at Delhi (1724), Jaipur (1734), Ujjain, Mathura and Varanasi; Jaipur's is the largest, a UNESCO site (2010), and its Samrat Yantra measures time to 2 seconds. The old tables (Zij-i-Ulugh Begi, Siddhantic) had accumulated errors, so fresh observations gave the Zij-i-Muhammad Shahi (1733), dedicated to Muhammad Shah 19-48, and a delegation went to Portugal (1730). The Samrat, Jai Prakash and Ram Yantras were stone, not brass, for accuracy.
→ Now go south, where the Mughals never reached.

Travancore builds on trade.
Marthanda Varma 29-58 subjugated local chiefs, built a centralised State and a European-style military, and held a State monopoly over the trade of the Malabar coast. The revenues went into the military, irrigation works and transport. In 1741 his army crushed the Dutch East India Company at Colachel, leaving them as mere merchants in Cochin; Bedara (1759) and the 1795 expulsion finished the Dutch.
→ But his successor chose art over arms.

Malabar slips, the Company arrives.
Under Rama Varma 58-98 Travancore became a centre of art and scholarship but its military declined. In 1766 Haider Ali 61-82 annexed Malabar and Calicut, the heart of the spice trade. After 1798 British influence grew; in 1805 the Nair troops mutinied over unpaid salaries and Travancore signed a Subsidiary Alliance. In 1809 Velu Thampi Dalawa issued the Kundara Proclamation, and when it was suppressed he took his own life.
→ The man who took Malabar came from Mysore.

From Vijayanagar to Haider Ali.
Mysore was part of the Vijayanagar Empire (1336-1646), which Deccan Sultanates shattered at Talikota in 1565. The Wodeyars then made Mysore autonomous, and Chikka Devaraja 72-04 Wodeyar made it militarily powerful. By 1761 a corrupt Prime Minister, NanjRaj, had made the Wodeyars figureheads, and Haider Ali 61-82, a junior officer, overthrew him and kept the Wodeyar as nominal head.
→ He needed an army and the money to pay it.

The machine and the money.
With French help Haider Ali 61-82 built Risalas on a European model and spent roughly twenty years subjugating the Poligars and Deshmukhs. To pay for it Mysore practised Military Fiscalism: Khalisa land expanded, Jagirdari minimised, Deshmukhs removed so State officials collected directly, field surveys, canals, cash crops and sericulture.
→ His son took the machine abroad.

Tipu looks abroad.
Tipu 82-99 ran a government-owned trading company with 30 centres including Muscat, and used indigenous iron-cased rockets (range 2 km) that inspired Congreve's. In 1785 he declared independence and asked the Khalifa for a sanad; he set up embassies in France, Turkey and Egypt (Prelims 2001). He also planted a Tree of Liberty and joined the Jacobin Club, but the French alliance gave no military support.
→ Ambition then met a bill it could not pay.

Why Mysore lost.
Mysore wanted to dominate all of South India and its trade (Vijayanagar 2.0), but constant war drained the State faster than Military Fiscalism could refill it. The 1766 annexation of Malabar and Calicut triggered the First Anglo-Mysore War (1767-69), and four wars (1767-69, 1780-84, 1790-92, 1799) ended with Tipu 82-99's death at Seringapatam.

8.spine: Europe wanted Asia's goods, the Ottomans closed the land road, and the Portuguese opened the sea road as a State enterprise. The Dutch and English companies, backed by capital and Charters, took the sea from them, and the EIC's 1661 powers started the shift from trader to ruler.
beats:
Why Asia?
Asia was the economic power of the world: Indonesia gave spices, India textiles, China silk and tea. Arabs and the merchants of Genoa and Venice carried them to a Europe that was not wealthy, and each handoff made huge profit. Da Gama's 1498 cargo sold at 800% profit, and in the 1600s a kilogram of clove cost the equivalent of a kilogram of gold.
→ But in 1453 the road was cut.

The road closes.
In 1453 the Ottoman Empire captured Constantinople and (the teacher corrects it to 'effectively') blockaded the land routes between Europe and Asia. Necessity drove the Age of Discovery, led first by Portugal and Spain. The era gave the astrolabe, the magnetic compass, latitudes and longitudes, geography as a discipline and the caravel, a ship that could sail at an angle against the wind.
→ Two rivals now claimed one ocean, and someone had to draw a line.

The line.
Pope Alexander VI mediated the Treaty of Tordesillas in 1494. An imaginary line in the Atlantic, about 1,185 miles west of the Cape Verde Islands, gave lands to the east to Portugal and lands to the west to Spain. Brazil's eastern tip fell on the Portuguese side, so Brazil became the only Portuguese colony in the Americas.
→ Armed with the line, Portugal sent Da Gama round Africa.

Calicut and Cochin.
Da Gama reached Calicut in 1498 and got permission to trade from the Zamorin, but faced Arab opposition and left without a factory. In 1500 Cabral set up the first factory at Calicut, which Arab merchants destroyed, and then the first permanent factory at Cochin under the Raja of Cochin's protection. In 1502 Da Gama bombarded Calicut, and in 1503 Albuquerque built Fort Manuel at Cochin, the first European fort in India.
→ Now Portugal needed a way to hold the sea.

Blue water, then Goa.
Almeida 05-09, the first Governor, chose naval supremacy over territory (the Blue Water Policy) and forced every non-Portuguese ship to buy a Cartaz. In 1509 he beat a coalition of Gujarat, Mamluk Egypt and the Zamorin at Diu. Albuquerque 09-15 took Goa from the Sultan of Bijapur in 1510, a rare land conquest, and Nuno da Cunha 29-38 moved the HQ to Goa in 1530 and acquired Bassein (1534) and Diu (1535).
→ But a State trading empire built on force carried the seeds of its own fall.

The fall of the Portuguese.
The Goa Inquisition (1560-1812) and forced conversions bred resistance. St Francis Xavier, who spearheaded conversions, died on Shangchuan Island in 1552, not Goa. The causes of decline were political (the Marathas), religious backlash, corruption and personal trade, the English and Dutch, and overextension with Brazil as the priority.
→ Those English and Dutch were already at the gates.

The companies arrive.
After the English beat the Spanish Armada in 1588, British and Dutch ships could sail to Asia. The VOC was founded in 1602 by merging six companies and was the first joint-stock company with tradable shares. It reached Masulipatnam in 1605 and took Cochin in 1663. It was beaten at Colachel in 1741 by Marthanda Varma 29-58 and at Bedara in 1759, lost its posts through the Kew Letters of 1795 and was dissolved in 1799.
→ The English company had its own Charter ladder to climb.

A licence that became power.
The English EIC began on 31 December 1600 under a Royal Charter of Elizabeth I 58-03, a 15-year monopoly pooled from 215 London merchants. James I 03-25 made it perpetual in 1609 and Cromwell 51-60 made it a permanent joint-stock company in 1657. The 1661 Charter of Charles II 60-85 gave it forts, troops, war and peace and civil and criminal jurisdiction, so it became a quasi-State.
→ With those powers it needed a base on the west coast.

Surat, Swally and Roe.
In 1608 Hawkins went to Jahangir 05-27's court for a Surat factory but was expelled under Portuguese pressure. The lesson was to defeat Portugal first, and in 1612 Thomas Best won the Battle of Swally. Jahangir then issued a Royal Farman in 1613 for a permanent factory at Surat, and Thomas Roe (1615-19) won the Farman of 1618 for liberal trading rights across the Mughal Empire.
→ One more royal wedding moved the base to Bombay.

Presidencies.
In 1661 Catherine of Braganza's dowry gave England Bombay and Tangier and 500,000 pounds, and in 1668 the Crown gave Bombay to the EIC for 10 pounds a year. The EIC's first Presidency was Surat (1618), then Madras (1652/1653), Bombay (1687) and Calcutta (1699/1700), each named after its fort. Each began as a trade HQ and grew into a province of British India.
→ Two smaller rivals were left in the field.

Danes, French and the order.
The Danes (company 1616, Tranquebar 1620, Serampore 1755) sold their mainland posts to Britain by 1845. The French company (1664) opened at Surat in 1668 and acquired Pondicherry in 1674, which Francois Martin 01-06 made the capital in 1701. Pondicherry's occupiers ran Portuguese, Danes, French, Dutch, English, then India in 1954, so the order of arrival is a favourite Prelims test.

9.spine: A profit-making company discovers that Indian quarrels can buy territory: Dupleix 42-54 proves it at Adyar 1746 and in the 2nd Carnatic War (back a claimant, station an army, take land, sit in court). The EIC reacts at Arcot, wins the 3rd war with royal armies, a navy and deeper pockets, and the Treaty of Paris 1763 leaves it the trade and the road to Plassey.
beats:
A shop that became a State.
Companies exist for profit, and the EIC was no different, yet by 1857 it ruled 63% of India's territory and 78% of its population. The 1661 Charter had given it forts, troops, war and peace and courts, and 1676 its own mint. Its wars were for trade (defensive, like the Carnatic Wars) or for territory, when a Governor was personally ambitious or the EIC Army pushed for war.
→ But first the Company met an Indian power, and lost.

Child's War (1686-90).
Aurangzeb 58-07's wars and quarrels over bribes and customs in Bengal pushed the EIC to seize Hugli and attack Mughal ships. Aurangzeb 58-07 crushed it in Bombay and Bengal, the Company surrendered by 1690, and in February 1690 he pardoned it for Rs 1.5 lakh. The 1691 Farman, technically a Parwana, gave duty-free trade in Bengal for Rs 3,000 a year, because the EIC brought forex and gold and fed bankers, merchants, artisans and ryots.
→ So the Company learns patience, and a rival arrives from France.

Enter Dupleix.
Joseph Francois Dupleix 42-54 is Governor-General of the French EIC from 1742 to 1754, with personal ambitions of empire and of dominating South India's trade; by 1740 French trade is about half of the British. The three Carnatic Wars are 1746-48, 1749-54 and 1756-63: the 1st and 3rd are global wars spilling into India, and the 2nd is factionalism, R versus R.
→ The first war begins in Europe, but Dupleix fights it in India.

Adyar, 1746.
The War of the Austrian Succession (1740-48) reaches India, and Dupleix 42-54 captures the EIC's Fort St George at Madras. Anwaruddin 44-49, Nawab of Carnatic, expected the fort and, when Dupleix 42-54 refused, sent 10,000 cavalry; at Adyar about 700 French-trained sepoys and 300 French soldiers destroyed them with light cannon, infantry squares and regular pay. It was a turning point: Indian kings now wanted European help to modernise their armies.
→ But Madras is traded away in Europe, and Dupleix 42-54 'aches'.

Aix-La-Chapelle, 1748.
The treaty ended the Austrian war and returned possessions in America and India, so Madras went back to the EIC. The French had won in India but the British in the Americas, and Britain's main interest was India while France's was the Americas. Nothing changed in territory, European infantry stayed far greater than Indian cavalry, and Dupleix 42-54 was left empty-handed.
→ But India offers new quarrels at once.

Two quarrels, four claimants.
In Carnatic, Md Ali 52-95 (son of Anwaruddin 44-49) faces Chanda Sahib 49-52 (son-in-law of Dost Ali Khan 32-40). In Hyderabad, after Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48 dies in 1748, his son Nasir Jung 48-50 faces his grandson Muzaffar Jung 50-51. The French move first for Chanda Sahib 49-52 and Muzaffar Jung 50-51, and the anxious EIC reacts for Md Ali 52-95 and Nasir Jung 48-50, fearing lost trade.
→ The French strike first, and win.

Phase 1: the French kingmaker.
At Ambur in 1749 Anwaruddin 44-49 dies and Chanda Sahib 49-52 is made Nawab; by December 1750 Nasir Jung 48-50 is dead and Muzaffar Jung 50-51 is Nizam. Muzaffar Jung 50-51 is killed in February 1751 at Lakkireddipalli Pass, so Bussy installs Salabat Jung 51-62. The French gain a resident and an army at Hyderabad, paid for with the Northern Sarkars, 2,00,000 pounds and jagirs, and Dupleix 42-54 styles himself Nawab from the Krishna to Cape Comorin. His four steps are a model: a succession dispute, an army at the State's cost, territory as payment, a Resident.
→ But a model that works once can be matched by a rival.

Phase 2: Arcot, 1751.
Dupleix 42-54 fixes on Trichinopoly, where Md Ali 52-95 holds out, and leaves Arcot unguarded, so Clive 57-67 takes it from Madras with about 200 Europeans and 300 sepoys and holds it for 53 days. Paris, wanting to honour the 1748 treaty and keep America, refuses to help. By the Treaty of Pondicherry (1754) Dupleix 42-54 is recalled, Godeheu replaces him, the French keep Hyderabad influence and Md Ali 52-95 becomes Nawab of Carnatic; Chanda Sahib 49-52 is beheaded at Tanjore by Pratap Singh 39-63.
→ Now Europe's wars bring royal armies to India.

The 3rd war and Wandiwash.
The Seven Years' Global War (1756-63) brings royal armies for the first time: Count de Lally with Bussy for France, Eyre Coote with Clive 57-67 for Britain. Bussy leaves the Northern Sarkars to help Lally, so Clive 57-67 takes them in 1759, and Lally's rude conduct and unpaid soldiers weaken the French, who also face a superior British navy. Eyre Coote wins the decisive battle of Wandiwash on 22 January 1760 and Pondicherry falls in 1761.
→ The treaty table closes the book.

Paris, 1763.
France loses all gains since 1749, keeps five posts (Pondicherry, Mahe, Karaikal, Yanam, Chandernagore) and may not keep a strong army or fortify its bases; in 1769 the French EIC is abolished. Having countered the Portuguese by 1612 and the Dutch by the 1650s, the British EIC now has a monopoly over India's international trade. It won all three wars because France starved Dupleix 42-54, had weaker leadership and a weaker navy, and could not match a private joint-stock firm with deep capital.
→ But the real result is bigger than trade.

From Carnatic to Plassey.
The 3rd war brought large royal military forces to India, and that strength plus Clive 57-67's shrewd diplomacy made Plassey 1757 possible. In 1766 Hyderabad ceded the Northern Sarkars to the EIC for Rs 7 lakh a year; Hyderabad signed the first Subsidiary Alliance in 1798, Mysore in 1799, Travancore in 1805, and Carnatic was annexed in 1801. The French founded the model of empire building and the British implemented it.

10.spine: Abuse, then conquest, then plunder, then legalise: each step makes the last step's abuse legal. Farman rights are abused through Dastaks (abuse); Plassey wins Bengal by conspiracy (conquest); the Bengal treasury is looted (plunder); Buxar and the Treaty of Allahabad 1765 make the loot a legal right (legalise).
beats:
The Doctor's gift (1717).
The EIC is just a trader with a few Farmans: 1613 a factory at Surat, 1618 factories across the empire (Thomas Roe), 1691 duty-free trade in Bengal for Rs 3,000 a year. Then the EIC surgeon Dr William Hamilton cures Emperor Farrukhsiyar 13-19, and the reward is the 1717 Farman, the Magna Carta of the Company: duty-free trade, the Royal Mint, and rent of 38 villages around Calcutta.
→ But the Nawab of Bengal has to honour it.

The Nawab says yes, but.
MQK 17-27 allows duty-free trade but no Dastak misuse; refuses the Royal Mint (it hurts sovereignty and his commission); allows renting villages but not buying them.
→ So the EIC's officers look for other ways to profit.

The cheating begins.
Officers use the Dastak, a duty-free pass meant for EIC goods, to do private trade. By 1750 private trade is 1,00,000 pounds a year, about 50 times their salaries, and Bengal loses duty revenue. Interlopers break the Royal Charter; free merchants sell to the EIC in India; Dastak misuse breaks Indian law.
→ Bengal's rulers must decide how long to tolerate this.

A young Nawab says enough (1756-57).
Alivardi Khan 40-56 had tolerated the EIC (he was pragmatic, and Adyar 1746 had shown the strength of European infantry). His grandson Siraj 56-57, young and disliked at court, stops the Dastak misuse. The EIC shelters Krishna Ballabh and adds fortifications, so Siraj seizes Kasimbazar and then Calcutta, which he renames Alinagar. The Black Hole story is born (146 locked in and 123 dead in Holwell's account; modern estimate 30 to 40).
→ The EIC calls Robert Clive back.

Clive returns.
Clive 57-67 arrives from Madras with the Royal military, recaptures Calcutta, signs the Treaty of Alinagar (all EIC privileges restored), destroys Hugli and beats the French at Chandarnagar (the Seven Years' War is on).
→ Now he needs a way to beat Siraj without a real fight.

Plassey, 23 June 1757: the conspiracy.
Mir Jafar 57-60, Siraj's Bakshi (bag = war paymaster, binoculars = head of military intelligence), makes a deal with Clive. At Plassey the bulk of the army does not fight; Siraj flees and is beheaded on the orders of Miran, Mir Jafar's son. The EIC has conquest, not rule.
→ Now comes the reward.

The loot.
Plunder 1757-65: 2,75,000 pounds to the Royal military, 2,34,000 pounds plus a jagir of 35,000 a year to Clive 57-67, Rs 2.25 crore to the EIC, and 2.5 million pounds of political gifts. Gomastas run untaxed private trade; Bengal's treasury buys Indian and Chinese goods and sends gold to Britain: the Drain begins; a large army is built. When Mir Jafar 57-60 cannot pay more, Mir Qasim 60-63 replaces him.
→ But Mir Qasim does not want to stay a puppet.

The puppet rebels.
Mir Qasim 60-63 shifts his base to Bihar, punishes zamindars who underreported revenue, abolishes all internal duties. He is defeated in 1763, escapes to Awadh, and forms a league with Shuja 54-75 and Shah Alam II 60-06 (who is in Awadh because he left Delhi fearing Imad-ul-Mulk).
→ Three armies now face the EIC.

Buxar, 1764: the real battle.
Seven years after Plassey a closely fought battle is won by Hector Munroe (Clive 57-67 is in London). Shuja 54-75 had attacked the fort against Mir Qasim's advice. This is the EIC's first real military victory.
→ Now the EIC dictates terms: the Treaty of Allahabad.

Allahabad, 1765: Paper, Power, Pay.
Paper: the Emperor gets promises (Rs 26 lakh tribute, help to retake Delhi) that are never kept, plus Allahabad and Kora. Power: the EIC gets the Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa (Nizamat stays with the Nawab): the Dual Government, with Md Reza Khan. Pay: Awadh pays Rs 50 lakh, loses Benaras, and becomes the buffer (Ring Fence, mini Subsidiary Alliance). Indirect Rule, Ring Fence and the mini SA are Clive 57-67's toolkit.
→ Power without responsibility cannot last.

The bill comes due (1770-73).
The Great Bengal Famine 1770 kills about one-third of the population while neither the EIC nor the Nawab takes charge. Land revenue and law and order collapse and the EIC goes bankrupt (1772). The EIC takes over the Nizamat; W. Hastings 73-85 carries Direct Rule: the Company State stands.

11.spine: Money rules the chapter: high war expenditure produced the ban on conquest (1784), Wellesley 98-05 got round the ban with the Napoleon threat and the Subsidiary Alliance (control without annexation), and high war expenditure again got him recalled.
beats:
Three brothers, one mission.
Richard Wellesley 98-05 becomes Governor General of Bengal in 1798, an empire builder who knows expansion raises his profile with a nationalistic British public. His brothers join him: Arthur, a Royal Army officer commanding the 33rd Regiment of Foot (not an EIC officer), and Henry, who handles the administration and diplomacy of the EIC. In 1800 Richard founds Fort William College, Calcutta, to train British civil servants in Indian languages, laws and customs.
→ But Richard has a legal problem: conquest is banned.

The money rule.
GBF 1770 leads to the EIC's bankruptcy by 1772; the British State lends money but brings the EIC under supervision through the Regulating Act 1773, so it will not waste taxpayers' money on wars. Then the 1st Anglo-Maratha War (1775-82) and the 2nd Anglo-Mysore War (1780-84) mean high war expenditure, and Pitt's India Act 1784 bans conquest: the Governor General may fight only in defence, otherwise he needs the Court of Directors or the Board of Control.
→ So Richard needs a threat big enough to justify fighting.

Napoleon knocks at Egypt.
In 1798 Napoleon attacks Egypt to control the Middle East and hurt British trade, and he is in contact with Tipu 82-99 of Mysore. Wellesley 98-05 overhypes a Napoleon and Tipu 82-99 alliance. The threat was there but not real: Britain's navy was superior, and the British had already burnt French ships in the Mediterranean.
→ But the British State agrees anyway, and wants a cheaper path.

The middle path.
Protecting India from European rivals is the primary goal of British foreign policy, so the State does not take risks. Wellesley 98-05 offers the Subsidiary Alliance: political domination without the cost, administrative burden and symbolism of full annexation. The teacher's line: SA = control without annexation. The idea is older: Dupleix 42-54 at Hyderabad in 1751 and Clive 57-67 at Awadh in 1765 (a mini SA).
→ Now Wellesley 98-05 turns the idea into a policy, written down.

The model treaty.
Wellesley 98-05 formalises the relationship in a written treaty, takes over Foreign Policy and disbands the State's army, State by State. The EIC gets five things: a Resident, a military alliance, the State's army disbanded and replaced, an annual subsidy and Foreign Policy. The ruler gets two promises: protection, and non-interference in succession, Diwani and Nizamat (minus military). Taking Foreign Policy closes a loophole: the army was paid by the State's subsidy, so only war and peace in EIC hands gave the EIC the right to deploy it.
→ So why would any ruler sign?

Why rulers walked in.
Five arguments: protection against internal revolts, protection against external threats (Chauth raids, Mysore, Rohillas), a subsidy cheaper than annexation, royal dignity preserved, and help in succession disputes and against neighbours. The EIC made military help conditional on signing. The teacher tags the fifth argument FACTIONALISM.
→ But once signed, the chain starts to bite.

The vicious chain.
The State's army is disbanded and Mansabdars lose their military role; the EIC army grows free of cost; the subsidy is high and rising (Drain of Wealth); taxes rise and peasants revolt; the EIC charges maladministration though the ruler has no power; territory is taken in lieu of cash (half of Awadh 1801, Berar 1853); and no alliances against the EIC remain possible. The teacher compares it to Bali of Ramayana: a military power shift.
→ Let us see who signed, and why.

The signing spree, 1798-1805.
Hyderabad signs first in 1798, for protection against the Marathas and Mysore. Mysore signs in 1799 after Tipu 82-99 is killed at Seringapatam. Awadh in 1801: Sadat Ali Khan II had offered Rs 76 lakh in 1798 for John Shore 93-98 removing his nephew Wazir Ali (1797-98); he defaulted and Henry Wellesley imposed a full SA. The Gaikwad signs at Cambay in June 1802, the Peshwa Bajirao II 96-18 at Bassein in December 1802 after Yashwantrao Holkar defeats him, Scindia in 1803, the Jats, Rajputs and Bundelas in 1803-05, and Travancore in 1805 after a Nair mutiny.
→ But some land was not left to alliances at all.

Land taken outright.
Wellesley 98-05 also annexes directly: Mysore territory in 1799 (to the Madras Presidency), half of Awadh in 1801 (the Doab, Gorakhpur, Rohilkhand: revenue twice the Rs 76 lakh subsidy, later the Ceded Districts, NWP 1836), and the Carnatic in 1801 (maladministration on record, the Nawab's many loans as context). In the 2nd Anglo-Maratha War (1803-05) Bhonsle loses Orissa and Scindia loses Gujarat and everything north of the Yamuna, including Delhi.
→ But every war costs money.

The bill, and the recall.
Wars are expensive for both winner and loser. The board repeats: loan and Regulating Act 1773, but still wars; Pitt's India Act 1784, but still wars. Under Wellesley 98-05 the 4th Anglo-Mysore War 1799 and the 2nd Anglo-Maratha War 1803-05 again mean high war expenditure, and he is recalled to London. Travancore in 1805 is the last SA of his term.
→ The last two signatories come under his successor.

The last two of ten.
Under Francis Hastings 13-23, the Bhonsle of Nagpur signs in 1816 (Appa Sahib wins the Nagpur regency fight with EIC backing) and Holkar of Indore signs at Mandsaur in 1818 after defeat in the 3rd Anglo-Maratha War. The teacher's count: ten SAs in 20 years, eight under Wellesley 98-05 and two under Francis Hastings 13-23. Factionalism brought the Peshwa, Bhonsle and Gaikwad; war brought Scindia and Holkar.

12.spine: Mysore built a war machine and a trading State that frightened every neighbour, so the EIC kept building coalitions against it; across four wars Mysore went from winning to losing, and with its fall the Carnatic was annexed and Travancore was pulled into a Subsidiary Alliance, completing the south by 1809.
beats:
A State that frightened everyone.
Hyder Ali 61-82 and Tipu 82-99 followed Military Fiscalism: the goal was a stronger military and the tool was maximising revenue. France gave arms and support in exchange for trade concessions, and Tipu ran a State-owned trading company and put an embargo on pepper, cardamom and sandalwood. The teacher's four anxious neighbours were the Marathas, Hyderabad, Travancore and the Carnatic.
→ So in 1766 the EIC and its friends moved.

1766: the first alliance.
Hyder Ali 61-82 had a modern arsenal at Dindigul Fort (1755) and in 1766 annexed Malabar and Calicut. The same year, under the Treaty of Hyderabad, the EIC promised to help Hyderabad invade Mysore and received the Northern Sarkars (4 of 5 districts, Guntur kept) for Rs 7 lakh a year. The Marathas joined, giving the triple alliance of EIC, Hyderabad and Marathas.
→ But Hyder knew how to buy a coalition apart.

The bribe and the gates of Madras.
In 1767 Hyder paid the Marathas Rs 35 lakh to exit, and gave the Nizam Rs 20 lakh plus a promise of the Carnatic Nawabi for his son. Hyderabad made peace with the EIC in 1768. In 1769 Hyder reached the gates of Madras while the Bombay navy took coastal Mysore (Mangalore). The EIC signed the Treaty of Madras: territories returned and a defensive alliance. The teacher marks the 1st war as won by Mysore.
→ But a defensive alliance is only as good as who attacked whom.

A promise broken.
In 1771 the Marathas attacked Mysore and the EIC refused its 1769 duty, so the alliance was a paper one. France then joined the American War (1778) and in 1779 the EIC seized the French port of Mahe, under Mysore's protection and Hyder's arms route.
→ Hyder struck back in 1780.

Pollilur and the Confederacy.
Hyder invaded the Carnatic and took Arcot. At Pollilur (September 1780) his iron-cased rockets annihilated Colonel Baillie's infantry, one of the worst defeats ever suffered by a European army in India. Nana Fadnis, the first Indian statesman to grasp the EIC's empire ambitions, built the Triple Confederacy of Marathas, Mysore and Hyderabad (1780-82); Hyderabad joined over Guntur and the unpaid 7 lakh.
→ Warren Hastings answered with diplomacy.

Hastings splits the coalition.
Warren Hastings 73-85 returned Guntur to Hyderabad and signed the Treaty of Salbai (May 1782) with the Marathas, ending the 1st Anglo-Maratha War. Mysore was left isolated. Hyder died of cancer in December 1782 and Tipu 82-99 continued, until the Treaty of Mangalore (1784): a stalemate, territories returned.
→ Tipu kept growing, and the EIC found a pretext.

The Travancore trigger, 1790-92.
Tipu 82-99 attacked Travancore, a formal EIC ally (1789), and Cornwallis 86-93 used it to declare war. The EIC formed a Triple Alliance with the Marathas and Hyderabad in 1790, and Mysore faced a three-front campaign. By the Treaty of Seringapatam (1792) Tipu lost half his Kingdom (Malabar, Dindigul, Baramahal), paid 3 crore and gave two sons as hostages. The teacher: notice the encirclement by the EIC.
→ Seven years later came the last war.

Napoleon and the fall, 1799.
Tipu 82-99's talks with Napoleon gave Wellesley 98-05 his pretext in London. Hyderabad had to fight because of its SA of 1798, the Peshwa sent no army on Nana Fadnis's advice, and Arthur Wellesley, with his Royal regiment, was among the key commanders at the siege. Tipu died defending Seringapatam. Kanara and Coimbatore went to the EIC and Hyderabad, and the Wodeyars returned under an SA with five-year-old Krishnaraja III.
→ So why did Mysore lose?

Four reasons and one answer.
Mysore had no stable alliance (its external ally was weak and its Indian neighbours were rivals), a French naval gap (France was busy in 1776-83 and 1792-1804 and its navy could not match Britain's), Military Fiscalism over-extension (the war fine drained the treasury: the teacher's BUT), and a Seringapatam that three coalition armies could surround. Cornwallis 86-93 and Wellesley 98-05 judged it too strong for Indirect Rule: it fought well but largely alone. The teacher's Mains skeleton generalises this to why Indian States lost: factionalism, war defeats and fear of neighbours, internal revolts.
→ After the fall came the clean-up.

Clean-up in the south.
Dhondia Wagh, a former prisoner of Tipu 82-99, raised a mounted force from soldiers disbanded under the SA, raided the Mysore-Maratha borderlands (1799-1800) as 'King of Two Worlds', and was killed in 1800 by Colonel Arthur Wellesley. In 1801 Wellesley 98-05 annexed the Carnatic, whose Nawabs had borrowed from private EIC officials against their Jagirs (the Carnatic Debts), citing financial maladministration and secret contact with Tipu. It became direct EIC territory, not an SA State.
→ One southern State was still outside: Travancore.

Travancore pays for help.
Marthanda Varma 29-58 had built the State and beaten the Dutch at Colachel (1741), and Rama Varma 58-98 kept the EIC alliance as a hedge against Mysore, which triggered Tipu's 1789 attack. Travancore signed a Treaty of Perpetual Friendship in 1795, took a British Resident in 1800, and in 1805 signed a proper SA with Wellesley 98-05, extracted in exchange for crushing a revolt by its own Nair troops over unpaid salary.
→ The price proved unbearable.

Kundara, 1809.
Velu Thampi Dalawa, Prime Minister 1802-09, led an armed revolt against heavy subsidy demands and constant interference, and in January 1809 issued the Kundara Proclamation calling all Travancoreans to rise. It was crushed within months and he died that year. With the Cochin SA of 1809, the EIC was paramount from the Krishna to Kanyakumari, setting up the 2nd and 3rd Anglo-Maratha Wars.

13.spine: A divided Maratha house kept inviting the EIC in (Surat 1775, Bassein 1802), the Subsidiary Alliance then took away the Peshwa's own army, and the EIC's Paramountcy turned the loophole of 1816 into the war that ended the Peshwaship in 1818.
beats:
The whole story on one board.
The teacher puts the three wars on one line. The 1st war (1775-82): reason factionalism, it began at Surat 1775, the EIC 'won' and it ended at Salbai 1782 with a military alliance. The 2nd (1803-05): reason factionalism, it began with Bassein 1802, an SA signed for the Svarajya, and the Marathas lost. The 3rd (1817-19): reason a breach of the SA by the EIC, and the Marathas lost, with the Swarajya annexed.
→ So why did the EIC care so much about the Deccan?

Why the Deccan mattered.
The Deccan and the Konkan coast were commercially critical to the EIC: a large coastline, a major cotton trade from Gujarat to China, and Maratha control over parts of the Malabar coast. The Maratha Confederacy and Mysore were the last major powers able to check the EIC. Three Anglo-Maratha Wars and four Anglo-Mysore Wars decided the outcome.
→ The first of the three wars began inside the Maratha house itself.

A claimant and a treaty at Surat.
In 1773 Raghunath Rao 73-74 became Peshwa after the murder of his nephew Narayan Rao 72-73. In 1774, in the Baarbhai Conspiracy, Nana Fadnis and eleven other ministers removed him. He went to the EIC's Governor of Bombay, William Hornby, and in 1775 signed the Treaty of Surat: EIC help in return for Salsette, Bassein and some revenue from Bharuch and Surat.
→ But Calcutta did not like the bill.

Warren Hastings cancels, then Purandhar collapses.
Warren Hastings 73-85, the Governor General in Calcutta, overturned Surat to avoid expensive war expenditure and negotiated the Treaty of Purandhar (1776) with Nana Fadnis. Madhav Rao II 74-95 was recognised, Raghunath Rao 73-74 pensioned, Salsette and Bharuch went to the EIC, and no French presence was allowed. But Bombay kept sheltering Raghunath, Nana Fadnis offered the French a port, and the war resumed.
→ Now the Marathas gave the EIC a bloody nose.

Wadgaon and the peace of Salbai.
At Wadgaon (1779), near Pune, Nana Fadnis, Mahadji Scindhia and Tukoji Rao Holkar defeated the EIC and Raghunath Rao 73-74. The war then stalled, with both sides in difficulty, the Marathas also being tied to the 2nd Anglo-Mysore War (1780-84). In 1782 Mahadji Scindhia signed the Treaty of Salbai at Gwalior: a military alliance against Hyder Ali 61-82's retention of territories, Salsette and Bharuch to the EIC, no French, territory returned, Madhav Rao II 74-95 recognised and Raghunath pensioned.
→ Peace came, but the glue holding the Marathas together began to dissolve.

Twenty-one years of decline.
Between Salbai (1782) and Bassein (1802) the Marathas declined. Mahadji Scindhia died in 1794, Madhav Rao II 74-95 committed suicide in 1795, Bajirao II 96-18 became Peshwa in 1796, and Nana Fadnis, the one man who held the Confederacy together for two decades, died in 1800. Wellesley 98-05, the empire-builder, was waiting for exactly this opportunity.
→ Then a Holkar execution lit the fuse.

Bassein: the Peshwa signs an SA.
In 1801 Vithoji Rao Holkar was captured and executed on the orders of Bajirao II 96-18. To avenge his stepbrother, Yashwantrao Holkar defeated the Peshwa and Daulat Rao Scindhia in October 1802. Bajirao fled and signed the Treaty of Bassein (December 1802), an SA in which the army of the Svarajya was to be disbanded once the EIC restored its puppet Peshwa. The Gaikwad had already signed the Treaty of Cambay in June 1802.
→ Ironically, the SA united the old rivals.

Assaye and a lost war.
Scindhia, Holkar and Bhonsle united against the EIC. Arthur Wellesley fought them at Assaye (1803), which he called the toughest fight of his career, harder than anything against Napoleon. The Marathas lost: the Peshwa was a puppet; Scindhia lost all north of the Yamuna (Delhi, Agra) and all of Gujarat and signed an SA, with a British Resident in Delhi putting Shah Alam II 60-06 effectively under EIC indirect control; Bhonsle lost Orissa and signed only a mini alliance. Wellesley 98-05 was recalled for the war's cost, and Cornwallis 86-93 arrived in July 1805 and died in October.
→ After Wellesley the EIC pulled back, and trouble gathered at its edges.

Pindaris, Paramountcy and a loophole.
After Wellesley 98-05 the EIC followed non-intervention, giving Bhonsle and Holkar time to rebuild. Pindaris, disbanded soldiers of Scindhia and Holkar, raided the Northern Sarkars and Madras. Francis Hastings 13-23 crushed them and launched the Policy of Paramountcy (1813-58): the EIC was to be supreme and could even annex. Residents treated Bajirao II 96-18 as a puppet. In Nagpur Appa Sahib signed an SA in 1816 but, using the loophole that retainers were allowed, secretly recruited Arab and Rohilla mercenaries and had Parsoji murdered.
→ The loophole turned into a battlefield.

The third war: Sitabuldi, Mahidpur, Koregaon.
In late 1817 Bajirao II 96-18, Appa Sahib and Yashwantrao Holkar rose together. Appa Sahib, as Senapati, used his Arab mercenaries at Sitabuldi (November 1817) but was defeated. Holkar fell at Mahidpur (December 1817). At Koregaon (1 January 1818) a small EIC force of Mahar soldiers held off a much larger Peshwa army. The EIC used its largest force ever, about 1.2 lakh, and Bajirao surrendered in June 1818.
→ Now came the settlement.

The settlement of 1818.
The Peshwaship was abolished and Bajirao II 96-18 pensioned to Bithur near Kanpur, where his adopted son Nana Sahib would later lead the Kanpur revolt of 1857. Svarajya was annexed into the Bombay Presidency. Appa Sahib was deposed, and Bhonsle lost huge territory. Holkar signed an SA at Mandsaur (1818). Satara and Kolhapur were spared as the Chhatrapati's symbolic line; Satara was annexed in 1848 under Dalhousie 48-56's Doctrine of Lapse.
→ Why did such a great power fall, and where did the EIC look next?

Why they lost, and the next wars.
The Marathas lost for four reasons: factionalism, no unified command (Scindhia, Holkar, Bhonsle, Gaikwad), the EIC's finances, and its naval and logistics advantage. The EIC's army, with a vested interest in big threats, then overhyped border dangers: Nepal 1814-16 (Sugauli, a protectorate), Burma 1824-26 (Yandabo), Coorg 1834, Afghanistan 1838-42 (20,000 dead), Sindh 1843 (Napier's Peccavi), the Sikh wars and Burma II 1852-53.

14.spine: Paramountcy made British interests supreme, so Dalhousie 48-56 used Lapse, war and unpaid subsidy to take the Company State to 63% of the land; the same annexations, from Jhansi to Awadh, cost it the legitimacy that 1857 then tested.
beats:
A trading company that wanted to be left alone.
In 1600 the EIC was a trading company, here for business and not for ruling. Its army was small (the Child's War 1686-90 showed it), so it stayed out of Indian politics, but not absolutely: when an opportunity came, as after Buxar 1764, it interfered, took a benefit and went back. After 1757 its power kept rising, and so did its interference.
→ So by 1813 interference became a declared policy.

Paramountcy: British interests first.
Francis Hastings 13-23 began the Policy of Paramountcy in 1813: among all States in India the Company State is supreme, British interests come first, and the EIC will annex if it must. Every State was locked in a sealed bubble with the EIC as gatekeeper. Paramountcy was the Subsidiary Alliance minus the rights of the Indian State.
→ Into this policy walks Dalhousie 48-56.

Three roads to expansion.
Dalhousie 48-56 used Paramountcy in three ways: the Doctrine of Lapse, wars (Punjab 1849, Pegu 1852-53) and annexation in lieu of subsidy (Berar 1853). By 1856 the Company State held 63% of India and 78% of its people, and no more mainland was annexed after him. The teacher's logic: a succession dispute means instability, which hurts British business, and British interests are paramount.
→ The first road was a rule about heirs.

The Doctrine of Lapse.
The Court of Directors formulated it in 1847; Dalhousie 48-56 implemented it. If a ruler died without a biological heir his rights lapsed, overriding adoption under Hindu law. Seven States fell in seven years: Satara 1848, Sambalpur and Jaitpur 1849, Baghat 1850, Udaipur 1852 (in Chhattisgarh), Jhansi and Nagpur 1854. The Inam Commission of 1852 applied the same logic to land, seizing about 20,000 estates in the Bombay Presidency, and the pension of Bajirao II 96-18 was refused to Nana Sahib.
→ The second road was unpaid subsidy.

Berar and Awadh: subsidy turns into land.
Hyderabad signed the first Subsidiary Alliance in 1798; by 1853 it could not pay, so Dalhousie 48-56 annexed Berar. Awadh followed the same chain: Clive 57-67's treaty of 1765, Shore's swap of Wazir Ali 97-98 for Sadat Ali Khan II in 1798 for Rs 76 lakh, half of Awadh taken in 1801 under Wellesley 98-05, and in 1856 the rest, on maladministration. Wajid Ali Shah had heirs, so this was not Lapse.
→ The third road was war, and its first target was the Sikh State.

The Sikh State: from buffer to target.
Under Ranjit Singh 01-39 the Sikh State was the ideal stable, strong, friendly buffer. After 1839 four factions tore it apart: the royal family, the Sindhanwaliyas, the Dogra Rajputs and the Khalsa Army. The Treaty of Lahore (9 March 1846) cut the army, took the Jalandhar Doab, and sold Kashmir to Gulab Singh for 75 lakh Nanakshahee rupees against a 1.5 crore indemnity, formalised by the Treaty of Amritsar (16 March 1846).
→ But a Resident and a reduced army were not the end.

Punjab annexed, the Koh-i-Noor taken.
In 1848 the Sikh Governors Mulraj (Multan) and Chattar Singh (Haripur) revolted, the opportunity the empire-builder Dalhousie 48-56 needed. Punjab was annexed in 1849 from Duleep Singh 43-49, a child of 5 at accession; the Koh-i-Noor went to the British Crown and a Board of Administration (the Lawrence Brothers and Charles Mansel) ruled. The frontier now touched the Afghan foothills.
→ War also reached the eastern shore.

Pegu and the sea ring.
The 2nd Anglo-Burmese War 1852-53 annexed Pegu; with Arakan and Tenasserim (1824-26) the Bay of Bengal became a British lake. The Bay's coast fell clockwise from Bengal 1757 to Pegu 1853, and the Arabian Sea anticlockwise from Bombay 1668 to Sindh 1843 (not Dalhousie 48-56's, but Ellenborough 42-44's). Beyond India came Kalat 1854, Jacobabad 1876, Persia 1856-57, 1907 and 1909.
→ But Dalhousie 48-56 did not only annex.

The moderniser.
A follower of Utilitarianism, Dalhousie 48-56 built the skeleton of modern India: railways from 1853 (Bombay-Thane first), the telegraph (about 4,000 miles), the Post Office Act 1854 with a half-anna rate, a civilian PWD and the restored GT Road, and Wood's Despatch 1854. The motives: troops, cheaper administration, raw materials and markets. The three universities came in 1857 under Canning 56-62.
→ Yet each annexation was adding to a hidden bill.

The five policies and the hidden bill.
The arc ran from Relative Isolation through PoIR and PoRF, the Subsidiary Alliance 1798 and Paramountcy 1813 to Subordinate Union 1858; each step built on the last, which is why 1857 came when it did. Dalhousie 48-56 consolidated the Company State but destroyed its legitimacy: Rani Lakshmibai (Lapse 1854), Nana Sahib (pension 1851), Bahadur Shah Zafar 37-57, the Awadh court, disbanded Sikh soldiers, talukdars and inam-holders were all aggrieved.
→ And then the Crown had to clean up.

1858: the reversal.
Dalhousie 48-56 handed over to Canning 56-62 in 1856, who inherited the revolt. The Government of India Act 1858 abolished the Company State, and Queen Victoria's Proclamation of 1858 ended the Doctrine of Lapse and pledged respect for the treaties and rights of Indian rulers. Paramountcy gave way to Subordinate Union, Indian Kings became Indian Princes, and there were no further annexations.
