15.spine: The British told themselves that ruling India was moral (the White Man's Burden), and each ideology under that roof rose or fell with the EIC's confidence: Orientalism while it was unsure, Authoritarianism under Cornwallis 86-93, the three reform ideologies after 1813, and Racism once 1857 had shocked them.
beats:
A nation sure of itself.
Britain had reasons for pride: the first modern democracy, the Industrial Revolution (c. 1750-1850), victory in the Seven Years' Global War (1756-63), Napoleon beaten (Leipzig 1813, Waterloo 1815) and the rise of capitalism and science. Within 150 years it could convince itself it was destined to lead, and that it owed the world its civilisation. This is the White Man's Burden.
→ So what should the British do in India?

Scared, so Orientalist.
Before 1813 the EIC was not militarily confident, and one badly handled insult could trigger mass resistance. Scholars like William Jones found Sanskrit older and more sophisticated than Greek and Latin. So Orientalism said: rule India the India way, with Hindu law, Islamic law, Indian languages and an Indian syllabus. Warren Hastings 73-85 was its champion.
→ Institutions followed the idea.

Four Orientalist institutions.
The Calcutta Madrasa came in 1781 (Warren Hastings 73-85), the Asiatic Society of Bengal in 1784 (Sir William Jones), the Sanskrit College at Banaras in 1791 (Jonathan Duncan) and Fort William College in 1800 (Wellesley 98-05) to train British civilians. The Aryan Invasion Theory and kinship through language added a rhetoric of love: we are cousins who have come home.
→ But Orientalism had critics from the start.

My way or highway.
The critics said the study of India showed a glorious past and a degenerate present, so restoring the past was pointless. Cornwallis 86-93 ruled India the English way: all-British senior posts, rule of law with the Collector no longer also Judge (Charter Act 1793), the Permanent Settlement 1793 and an Aloof Elite. He had lost America and did not want settlers putting down roots.
→ Between the two, a hybrid appeared.

Indian coat, British hand.
Thomas Munro, Governor of Madras 1820-27, governed through Indian forms but kept all power with the EIC: Orientalist in form, Authoritarian in substance. His Ryotwari Settlement copied the ancient State-peasant model but all collection was by EIC officials. Elphinstone, Malcolm and Metcalfe followed him.
→ Then, by 1813, the EIC stopped being cautious.

1813: confidence, then three ideas.
Indian powers had been beaten except Holkar, Bhonsle and the Sikh State, the army was huge, Napoleon was beaten and the Industrial Revolution was in full swing, with a market for British goods to win. Liberalism (Macaulay: Law Commission 1834, Minute on Education 1835, Brown Sahibs), Utilitarianism (Bentham and James Mill: good laws, a strong State, the schoolmaster) and Evangelicalism (Charles Grant, Charter Act 1813, Lex Loci Act 1850) filled the space.
→ Bentinck 28-35's years were the high-water mark.

The Liberal window, 1828-35.
From Bentinck 28-35 through the Charter Act 1833 to Macaulay's Minute 1835, Liberal confidence peaked: the Sati Abolition Act 1829, Thuggee suppression under Captain Sleeman (three tools: informants, approvers, swift commissions; over 3,000 Thugs convicted 1831-41), English replacing Persian in higher instruction, and Cornwallis 86-93's Code revised into uniform criminal procedure.
→ Then 1857 broke the story.

The shock of 1857.
The Revolt shook the British psychologically and broke the paternalistic narrative. Six fronts shifted: reform retreated, race was read by physical features, the Aryan theory was twisted, Dogs and Indians not allowed, Authoritarianism rose and social reforms slowed after Queen Victoria's Proclamation of 1858. Lytton 76-80 (Vernacular Press Act and Arms Act 1878) and Curzon 99-05 (Partition of Bengal 1905) were its architects.
→ The same hard mood showed on the frontiers.

The Forward Policy and the Great Game.
Fearing Tsarist Russia, the British pushed the frontier into Afghanistan: Auckland 36-42's 1st Anglo-Afghan War 1839-42, Ellenborough 42-44's punitive return to Kabul, Lytton 76-80's 2nd war 1878-80 and the Treaty of Gandamak 1879, then Ripon 80-84's reversal. The defensive twin was the Ring Fence, and the Persian flank ended with the Anglo-Russian Convention of 1907.
→ And the land-grab ended in Burma.

Upper Burma and Imperial Preference.
Dufferin 84-88 annexed Upper Burma in January 1886, the last major extension, deposing King Thibaw. Trade was also bent to the empire: Imperial Preference, formalised at Ottawa in 1932, let British goods enter Indian ports at lower tariffs than German, Japanese or American goods.
→ But the empire's own claims came back to haunt it.

The ideas come home.
The White Man's Burden produced its opposite: the American Revolution, the French Revolution 1789, the European revolutions of 1830 and 1848 and the Irish struggle. Later shocks added deindustrialisation and the Drain Theory, the Russian Revolution 1917, Wilson's self-determination and anti-racism. They travelled through people: Gandhi from South Africa (1893-1915) and Nehru from Cambridge.

16.spine: Every system answers five questions (landowner, assessment, settlement, collection, tenants' rights), and every British answer left the ryot worse off than the Mughal patta: auction, then a fixed-forever Zamindar, then an over-assessed ryot, then an unsurveyed Mahal, with cash revenue pushing him to cash crops and famine. Each failure forced the next experiment.
beats:
The Mughal patta.
The Khudkasht (cultivator) holds customary occupancy rights and pays by a patta, a written record of what he owes, plus abwabs to his Primary Zamindar. The chain runs Khudkasht, Primary Zamindar, Intermediary Zamindar, then the Jagirdar or State, with Amils and Amalguzars checking. The Zamindar is a commission collector (Vatan right, 10%) and not the owner: only the King is legal owner. When the State needs money in a hurry it auctions the collection (Ijaradari).
→ But in 1765 the EIC takes over the collecting.

Diwani, but the old chain (1765-70).
The Treaty of Allahabad gives the EIC the Diwani of Bengal, Orissa and Bihar. It keeps the Mughal collection (Orientalism) under Deputy Subadar Muhammad Reza Khan as Diwan. But the patta is ignored and rents run far beyond the record, then back-to-back droughts strike: the Great Bengal Famine of 1770 kills 50 lakh to 1 crore, the demand is doubled and brutality is used. Reza Khan is jailed without trial 1772-74 as scapegoat.
→ By 1772 the EIC is in trouble itself.

Bankrupt (1772).
Since 1757 the EIC bought Indian goods with India's own land revenue, so the famine hit its income directly. Nabobs' corruption, the famine and the army and Dual System expenses bring it to the verge of bankruptcy. Parliament lends 1.4 million pounds at 4% on condition of parliamentary oversight, which leads to the Regulating Act 1773.
→ Meanwhile Warren Hastings 73-85 tries to squeeze more.

The auction year (1772).
Warren Hastings 73-85, an Orientalist, revives Ijaradari as the Farming System: each district's collection is auctioned to the Revenue Farmer, who works under a European District Collector. The farmers squeeze the ryots to recover their bids, the demand is so high that peasants pay nothing, and revenue does not improve.
→ Now the EIC wants certainty and a loyal landlord class.

Cornwallis 86-93, the Believer (1793).
Cornwallis 86-93 comes from a landlord family and believes in English landlordism ('my way or highway'). His Permanent Settlement Act 1793 covers Bengal, Orissa, Bihar, North Madras and Benaras. Four pillars: the Zamindar becomes legal owner; settlement is with him; LR is fixed at 10/11 of the 1789-90 revenue forever (Rs 66 becomes Rs 60); and the Sunset Clause auctions his land if he misses the evening deadline.
→ But the results diverge from the intentions.

What the Permanent Settlement did.
Frequent auctions at first (Jotedars and the Zamindar's family buy), later loyal Zamindars (largely on the British side in 1857) and certain revenue. But Zamindars do not invest, become absentee, and the ryot is a tenant at will with the patta ignored. Wellesley 98-05 gives back seizure, imprisonment and rent rises (Regulation VII of 1799), and the Cornwallis 86-93 Code clogs the courts.
→ Ryots revolt and the British have to act.

Patching the ryot's rights (1859 and 1885).
The Rent Act 1859 gives occupancy rights after 12 years on the same plot, revives the patta and bans imprisonment, but Zamindars evict at year 11 and keep lathiyals; the Indigo Revolt 1859-63 and the Pabna Agrarian Leagues 1873 follow. After Ripon 80-84's Rent Commission of 1880, the Bengal Tenancy Act 1885 under Dufferin 84-88 counts 12 years across plots in a village and is implemented sincerely.
→ Meanwhile, in the south, Munro rejects the Bengal model.

Munro's Ryotwari (1792-1820).
Cornwallis 86-93 and Wellesley 98-05 tried to create big Zamindars in Madras through the Poligars; it failed. Thomas Munro convinced the Court of Directors in 1801: Read had begun in Baramahal in 1792, Munro applied it 1801-07, and as Governor of Madras 1820-27 re-established it. His reasons: Scottish yeoman ideology, no big Zamindars, stressed finances, eliminating Poligars, political stability. The ryot owns, is settled with directly, after a field survey (SCAM-B).
→ But the survey is the hard part.

Over-assessment and the Deccan riots.
Phase 1 took 33% to 50% of gross produce and ignored costs: ruin, abandoned land, moneylender debt. Phase 2 used net produce (Ricardian Economic Rent): Pringle 1830 reached 55%, the Wingate Settlement 1835 fixed it for 30 years; in Madras the Torture Commission 1855 led to a 50% cap. Mirasidars wore three hats, Patils were demoted, and when the cotton boom of the US Civil War years (1861-65) collapsed, debts to Marwari and Gujarati moneylenders plus crop failures led to the Bombay Deccan Peasant Riots of 1875.
→ In the north, a third answer is built for Awadh.

Mahalwari (1822-1856).
In Awadh half came under British rule in 1801 and the Taluqdars were crushed 1801-22. Holt Mackenzie's recommendations became Regulation VII of 1822: settlement with the Mahal through its Lambardar, a hybrid where the Taluqdar owns in some areas. R.M. Bird's Revised Mahalwari of 1833 assesses at Mahal level, 66% of rental value for 30 years; Dalhousie 48-56 carries it to Punjab and Central India (CUP). Improper surveys and the summary settlement of Awadh in 1856 feed the 1857 revolt.
→ One more pressure squeezed all three systems: cash.

Cash instead of grain.
The Mughals took much in kind; the British demanded cash. Ryots, compelled or induced by moneylenders and traders, shifted from food crops to indigo, cotton, opium, jute and sugarcane. Land that grew rice, wheat and millets served British factories (after the Industrial Revolution India became an export market and a source of raw materials). Less grain in reserve fed the famines of the late 19th century.
→ So whichever system, the ryot lost.

Why three systems, and why the ryot lost.
Cornwallis 86-93 the landlordist made PS, Munro the yeoman man made Ryotwari, and Mahalwari was a practical compromise: ideology, geography and fiscal pressure. In all three, high demand, faulty surveys, legal vulnerability and predatory moneylending left the cultivating class worse off than under the Mughal patta.

17.spine: London first let the Company rule, then took its powers one by one: it regulated the political (CMR) side in 1773, controlled it in 1784, took the head in 1793, the trade in 1813 and 1833, the jobs and the Budget in 1853, and the body in 1858. Each Act moved power from the EIC to the Br State, so 1857 was the final nail, not the first wound.
beats:
A trader turned ruler (1765).
The EIC has done business since 31 December 1600; since the Treaty of Allahabad in 1765 it also runs Civil, Military and Revenue (CMR) affairs, a Company State. The Br State has no problem with a trader but 'problem and anxiety' with a Company State, since only a State holds power over territory. Yet it does not end it: the EIC brings two incomes (trade and land revenue), bears the burden of ruling far-away India, and raises Britain's empire and geopolitical power indirectly. So from 1773 the State regulates the EIC's political matters.
→ But why was London so nervous?

Five worries.
Money: in 1767 the State demanded 400,000 pounds a year. America: the revolution of 1765-83 ended with the USA in 1783, so what if EIC men did the same? The taxpayer: the EIC went bankrupt in 1772 and was lent 1.4 million pounds. Conscience: the Great Bengal Famine of 1770 and the Nabobs. Careers: Clive 57-67 and Hastings 73-85 wanted a Crown link. The Select Committee of 1772 kept the EIC's trade monopoly but made the Court of Directors accountable for its political functions.
→ So Parliament passes the Regulating Act of 1773.

The Regulating Act 1773 in India.
The Governor of Bengal becomes GG(Bengal) and is made senior to Bombay and Madras in war and peace, except in emergency; commerce is untouched. A Supreme Council of GG + 4 decides by majority and the GG has only a casting vote, so he needs at least two councillors: a check on an empire-builder. Law-making for Bengal and on war and peace goes to the council.
→ And in London the State gets its own hooks.

The Regulating Act 1773 in London.
For the first time Parliament's right to regulate the EIC's political affairs is recognised. The GG sends information to the Court of Directors and the Directors send political matters to the State. A Supreme Court at Calcutta (a Chief Justice and three puisne judges, all chosen by the Crown, Elijah Impey first in 1774) is created, officials may not take gifts, and the tenures are 4, 5 and 4 years.
→ But the Act leaks.

The leaks of 1773.
The Supreme Court clashes with the GG's council over officials' official acts; distance blunts supervision; Bombay signs the Treaty of Surat in 1775 without the GG, starting the 1st Anglo-Maratha War (1775-82). With no veto, the GG is blocked by factions: Philip Francis opposes Hastings 73-85 and Edmund Burke leads an impeachment, which ends in acquittal. The Amending Act of 1781 fixes the Supreme Court's jurisdiction.
→ Having lost America, London moves from supervision to control.

Pitt's India Act 1784.
Britain lost 13 colonies in 1783, so the State fears an Indian declaration of independence. A Board of Control (six members, a ministry for Indian affairs) takes political affairs while the Court of Directors keeps commerce: Double Government 1784-1833. The BoC can also order the GG directly: Dual Control 1784-1858. The council shrinks to GG + 2 + CIC and the GG gets a regular and a casting vote. Conquest is declared 'repugnant'. The Amending Act of 1786 gives a veto and lets Cornwallis 86-93 hold both GG and C-in-C.
→ Still, the Company appoints its own top men.

1793: the Crown takes the head.
Subjects of the Crown cannot acquire sovereign power except on behalf of the Crown, so the EIC is an agent. Principal Servants (GG, Governors, C-in-C, Councillors) are appointed by the EIC but only after Crown approval, and Parliament renews the Charter for the first time. The head of the Company State belongs to the State while the body stays with the EIC. In India the GG can supersede Governors, the CIC becomes an extra-ordinary member, and Cornwallis 86-93's Code makes law written.
→ Next, free-trade ideas knock on the door.

1813: the monopoly breaks.
Adam Smith (1776), Liberals, Utilitarians and Evangelists, and lobbying manufacturers attack the monopoly; the Industrial Revolution makes Britain want India's raw material and an export market. The India trade monopoly ends (Tea, Opium and China stay), Crown sovereignty is stated as undoubted, missionaries enter with a licence and Rs 1 lakh a year goes to education. The Act contributes to 1857.
→ The rest of the trade follows in 1833.

1833: one India, one law.
The St Helena Act ends the EIC's commercial function: no more business, only a political agent. The BoC supervises all administration and its President is renamed Minister for Indian Affairs. The GG(Bengal)-in-Council becomes GG(India)-in-Council (Bentinck 28-35 first), the Governors of Bombay and Madras lose law-making, Macaulay joins as Law Member, the Law Commission of 1834 begins codification and the UCS opens to Indians. Centralisation peaks.
→ 1853 takes the jobs and the purse.

1853: no term, no jobs, no Budget.
The Charter lasts only 'till Parliament specifies otherwise'; a Civil Services exam (first held in London in 1855) ends the EIC's patronage and opens the CCS to Indians; the Budget goes to Parliament. Six Legal Members (four provincial, a Chief Justice and a judge) make a legislative council of twelve, and in 1854 Dalhousie 48-56 appoints Halliday as first LG of Bengal.
→ Then 1857 arrives.

1858: the Crown takes the body.
The EIC is blamed for 1857; the public, free traders and the western-educated middle class want direct rule. The GOI Act 1858 ends Company rule: a Secretary of State with a 15-member India Council replaces the BoC, Dual Control ends, and Canning 56-62 is first Viceroy. Mughal sovereignty is ended (Zafar 37-57 goes to Rangoon) and the princes of the 565 PS live under Paramountcy. The Proclamation promises no annexation, Crown administration, religious non-interference and amnesty; the Royal Titles Act 1876 makes Victoria Kaesar-i-Hind.
→ But who was responsible for the conquest itself?

Whose conquest?
Britain claimed no official policy of conquest; Sub-Imperialism by EIC officials drove it, and Pitt's India Act 1784 banned it. Yet the State gave the Charter (the tools), sent the Royal Military at Plassey and in October 1857, financed the EIC, followed the money, controlled the empire-builders and used the EIC as a foreign-policy tool (the 1st Afghan War, the Great Game).

18.spine: The EIC kept the Mughal frame for courts, services and police until a crisis (the 1770 famine) forced it to take control; Cornwallis 86-93 then built the structure, and Indians were let in only as far as cost or pressure from the Indian movement forced, leaving independent India with codified law, an organised civil service and a hierarchical police.
beats:
A trading company must run a state.
Administration is the machinery by which a State carries out its policies, laws and schemes on the ground. When the EIC turned from a trading company into a Company State (1765-1858; the Charter Act 1833 ended its commercial function) it had to decide how much Indian machinery to keep and how much to replace. Three pillars carry the story: judiciary, civil services and police. The teacher calls the whole chapter the history of Public Administration in British India.
→ First, what court system did the EIC inherit?

The Mughal ladders of Bengal.
Before 1772 Bengal had two separate hierarchies. In civil matters (Diwani) courts ran up to the Sadar Diwani Adalat, with Pandits and Maulvis judging personal law and the Zamindar's Kachari handling land revenue disputes. In criminal matters (Nizamat) Islamic law applied to everyone: the Kazi judged, the Mufti interpreted and the Faujdar, like today's SP, caught the accused and carried out the sentence.
→ Then the EIC took over the revenue, but not the rest.

One man, two hats.
After the Treaty of Allahabad 1765 the EIC held the Diwani and the Nawab kept the Nizamat: a Dual Government. Guided by Orientalism, the EIC let Muhammad Reza Khan head both and cared mainly about revenue. Revenue fell, law and order broke down, and the Great Bengal Famine of 1770 killed about one-third of Bengal.
→ So the EIC decided to rule directly.

Hastings 73-85 steps in.
In 1772 Hastings 73-85 ended the Dual Government. The British DC sat as judge in the civil courts, while in criminal courts the Kazi and Mufti stayed as judges under the DC's watch, because law and order was too sensitive to replace. The Regulating Act 1773 led to the Supreme Court at Calcutta in 1774 for British subjects under British law, with Madras (1800) and Bombay (1823) to follow. Laws were written down too: the Gentoo Code (1776), the Hedaya (1791) and the Code of 1781.
→ But the DC was still both collector and judge.

Cornwallis 86-93's Code of 1793.
With the Permanent Settlement of 1793, zamindars became property owners and needed courts they could trust: if the DC auctioned an estate and then judged the owner's appeal, there was a conflict of interest. Cornwallis 86-93 stripped the DC of all judicial power (the Prelims 2010 answer), divided Bengal into four divisions with Provincial Courts of Appeal and Courts of Circuit, created Anglo-Muhammadan law, removed Indians from all senior posts and permitted lawyers.
→ Yet the new system clogged, and the model did not fit everywhere.

Ryotwari, Bentinck 28-35 and the codes.
Courts clogged after 1793: the DC could no longer settle disputes on the spot, court fees were abolished (back in 1795), and lawyers prolonged cases. In Ryotwari areas, with many small landowners, Madras (1814, on Munro's advice) and Bombay (1819, Elphinstone) merged the DC's roles again. Bentinck 28-35 abolished the divisional courts, replaced Persian in 1835, and the Charter Act 1833's Law Commission under Macaulay led to the CPC 1859, IPC 1860 and CrPC 1861. High Courts came in 1862 and the Federal Court in 1937.
→ Now the people who staffed the courts.

From patronage to a service.
A service means a career ladder with rules, not total discretion. Early EIC officials came by nomination and patronage, and Directors lobbied Parliamentarians with jobs for their sons. Cornwallis 86-93 organised them into the Covenanted Civil Service (senior, signed a covenant in London, Europeans only, like Group A) and the Uncovenanted (junior, hired locally, where Indians served, like Group B), with higher pay, curbed private trade and strict seniority; but entry stayed by nomination until the Charter Act 1853.
→ Then came the exam, with three locks on the door.

The exam and its three locks.
The Charter Act 1853 mandated an exam for the CCS and the first exam was held in London in 1855. Indians were eligible on paper, but the age limit was kept low, the syllabus was dominated by English Literature (to produce Macaulay's Brown Sahibs) and the venue was London. Satyendranath Tagore became the first Indian to clear it in 1864 and four more followed in 1867.
→ The western-educated Indians began to push back.

The long fight for Indianisation.
From 1860 the WEMC demanded a simultaneous exam in India and a higher age limit. The British answered with Lytton 76-80's lateral entry for loyal elite Indians (a Statutory Civil Services Act the teacher calls unimportant). Aitchison 1887 led to the three tiers ICS, PCS and Subordinate in 1892 by executive order under Lansdowne 88-94; Islington (1912, report 1917) offered 25% yet refused a simultaneous exam, which the teacher marks as a CONTRADICTION; the GOI Act 1919 brought the exam to India in 1922, the PSC in 1926 and a 33% target; Lee (1923-24) set 20-40-40 and the PSC came in October 1926 with Ross Barker as first Chairman; the GOI Act 1935 gave the Federal PSC (1937), over 50% were Indianised by 1947, and Article 378 made it the UPSC in 1950.
→ The third pillar, the police, followed its own path.

From Faujdar to Daroga.
Under the Mughals the chain ran Naib Nazim, Faujdar, Kotwal, Zamindar. After the 1770 famine raised crime, Hastings 73-85 put English Magistrates in place of the Faujdars in 1781. Cornwallis 86-93 ended the zamindars' police powers in 1793: thanas of 30 square miles under an Indian Daroga, the DM supreme in his district. But a Daroga-Zamindar nexus of bribes and lathiyals oppressed the rural poor; Wellesley 98-05 restored the zamindars' powers in 1799, and the Madras trial of 1802 ended in the Torture Commission report of 1855.
→ The British then went looking for a proven model.

The Police Act 1861.
The British turned to the Irish Constabulary model, a centralised, quasi-military force built as much for political control as for crime. It was road-tested in Sindh (1843, Charles Napier), Punjab (1849), Bombay (1853) and Madras (1859); M.H. Court's 1st Police Commission (1860), set up by Canning 56-62, borrowed from Sindh, and Napier did not head it. The Police Act (March 1861), passed by the GG's Council, set up the IG, SP and SI hierarchy (the SI reports to the SP, not the DC) but only posts, not a service. Fraser's commission (1902-03) created the Imperial Police cadre, closed to Indians; direct entry opened to Indians in 1920, yet only 20% of SPs were Indians by 1931; the IPS came in 1948 and the AIS Act in 1951.
→ What did all three pillars leave behind?

Crisis or pressure.
Each major reform followed a crisis (the 1770 famine, the 1857 revolt) or a concession won by the Indian National Movement. The British Indianised only as far as cost or politics demanded. What they left behind, however inadvertently, was codified law, an organised civil service and a hierarchical police, which independent India inherited and adapted.

19.spine: Reason met a religious society: reformers who joined reason to scripture (Roy, Vidyasagar) won laws but not the masses, because reform was elite, top-down and gradual. The colonial school and press that carried the Doctrine of Reason made the educated 8% who finally turned it on British rule itself.
beats:
Europe's rebirth, Bengal's mirror.
The Renaissance was Western Europe's 14th-century rebirth, driven by reason and aimed at human welfare, and it set off the Reformation, the end of feudalism, capitalism, the Enlightenment and the Industrial Revolution. 19th-century Bengal looked similar: an oppressive priestly establishment, no modern education, birth-based privilege and poverty. The response was the same too: reach back to the scriptures for what was great and use reason to remove what was not.
→ But why did reform begin in the 19th century, and in Bengal?

The Raj opens the door.
After 1813 the British moved from Orientalism to Liberals, Utilitarians and Evangelists, who backed Western education and reform, while Evangelist conversion frightened Indians into reforming from within. The British called ancient India a myth, and cultural nationalism was the reply. Western education (1835) gave the Doctrine of Reason, and Bengal led because the Governor General sat there.
→ Now, who would use that reason, and how?

Logic alone, or logic plus scripture?
In India religion determined social practice, and the masses were deeply religious, so a reformer had to reform or reinterpret religion. Derozio's Young Bengal used only logic, ate beef and drank wine, and won a great controversy but poor mass politics. The socio-religious reformers used the Ctrl+F method: find the logic in the scripture and show it to the people.
→ One man did this best: Roy.

Roy, the bridge.
Roy, the Father of Modern India, held universalism and found monotheism in the Upanishads; he used the Doctrine of Reason against other-worldliness, Karma and Incarnation. He opposed the Sanskrit College of 1824, wanted Western sciences, and worked with Bentinck 28-35, Macaulay and David Hare. His political demands, shared with Young Bengal, were Separation of Powers, a free Press, Indianisation and Trial by jury.
→ His first great test was Sati.

Sati: the first law.
By the 19th century Sati was driven by property, burden, honour and glory, and lower castes in Bengal had begun to copy it through Sanskritisation. Bentinck 28-35 demanded scriptural proof, so in 1828 the Brahmo Samaj beat Radhakanta Deb in debate, and in 1829 Regulation XVII made Sati culpable homicide. Radhakanta Deb's Dharma Sabha appealed to the Privy Council in 1830 and lost.
→ Roy now had a law, and needed a body to carry the work on.

The Brahmo Samaj splits.
The Brahmo Samaj (1828) took the low-hanging fruits first and stayed an upper-caste, urban body; after Roy's death in 1833 Debendranath Tagore, the organisation man, held it together. Keshab Chandra Sen wanted a mass, all-India movement and a new religion, so 1866 gave the Brahmo Samaj of India and the Adi Brahmo Samaj; he also drove the Brahmo Marriages Act 1872. In 1878 he married off his minor daughter and the Sadharan Brahmo Samaj split away.
→ Meanwhile Maharashtra took up the work, from the elite and from below.

Maharashtra and the voice from below.
The Paramhansa Mandali (1849) copied Young Bengal and failed the same way; the Prarthana Samaj (1867) of Atmaram Pandurang, Ranade, Bhandarkar and Telang was Brahmoism for Maharashtra, with Keshab's help. Ranade also built the Poona Sarvajanik Sabha and the National Social Conference (1887). Phule opened a girls' school in Pune (1848), wrote Gulamgiri and founded the Satyashodhak Samaj (1873): he spoke for the oppressed and organised them.
→ But the hardest customs lay inside the home.

The home front: marriage, age, infants.
Child marriage had religious sanction in the Garbhadhan ceremony, so the IPC 1860 set only age 10 and the Rakhmabai case (1884) split opinion. After the death of 11-year-old Phulmoni, Lansdowne 88-94 raised the age to 12 in 1891; Tilak said reform must come from society, Bhandarkar showed the Dharmashastras allow marriage after puberty, and census data showed the practice went on. The Female Infanticide Act 1870 could not reach dowry and hypergamy, nor the nutritional neglect of girls.
→ Vidyasagar took on the widow.

Vidyasagar's war on widowhood.
Vidyasagar changed Sanskrit College from within, opened 25 girls' schools in 1857-58, and sent a petition with 1,000 signatures; the Hindu Widow Remarriage Act came on 26 July 1856 and he married his own son to a widow. But a widow lost her husband's property on remarriage, orthodox Hindus won the scripture debate after 1857, and Maharashtra saw only 38 widow remarriages by 1900. Early reform failed because it was elite, top-down, gradual and silent on caste.
→ So a second wave tried the masses, and the faiths answered each in their own way.

Pride, revival and other answers.
Dayanand's Arya Samaj (1875) said the Vedas were infallible, rejected idols and rose in Punjab, while Ramakrishna and Vivekananda offered spiritual pride and Vivekananda accepted idols and won the masses. Revivalism had a positive face and a negative one (aggressive Shuddhi, cow protection and communal tension). Sir Syed built Aligarh (1875) on modernisation without surrender of faith, and Narayana Guru consecrated an Ezhava's Shiva at Aruvippuram in 1888.
→ All of this stood on a schoolroom built by British policy.

Schools: from Orientalism to Sargent.
Orientalists (Warren Hastings 73-85, Jones, Wellesley 98-05) governed the Indian way until Macaulay's Minute settled the debate in 1835 for a Western syllabus in English, making Brown Sahibs and a downward filtration that never reached the masses. Wood's Despatch 1854 gave the vernacular-to-English ladder, grants-in-aid and three universities (1857), then came Hunter 1882, Curzon's Act 1904, Sadler, Hartog, Wardha 1937 and the unfunded Sargent Plan 1944. By 1921 only about 8% were Western educated and 92% were illiterate.
→ Those few read, and wrote, in the press.

The press and the educated eight per cent.
The press began in 1780 with Hicky's Bengal Gazette, shut down in 1782 by Warren Hastings 73-85, and then ran a cycle of repression (1799, 1823, 1878, 1908-10) and concession (Metcalfe 1835, Ripon 80-84's repeal in 1882). Indian-run papers carried reform and then nationalism, and the WEMC's method from 1857 to 1905 was pen and press. The Doctrine of Reason that was meant to make Brown Sahibs ended by making the leaders of the Indian National Movement.

20.spine: Peasants and tribals lose their security (land revenue, forests, religion), so they rise first, led by elites, peasants, sects or chiefs. The revolts are local, uncoordinated and not democratic, yet political and public, so they are the pre-history of modern nationalism and the culmination of a hundred years before 1857.
beats:
The bottom of the order moves first.
The Western Educated Middle Class believes in the benevolence of British rule and answers it with socio-religious reform. Peasants and tribals, at the very bottom of the new colonial order, answer with defiance and often violence. The teacher's one-line logic: the common man wants security, economic, physical and socio-cultural.
→ But what exactly did the peasant lose?

The peasant's squeeze.
The Farming System of 1772 auctions land revenue to a revenue farmer (ijaradar). PS1793 makes the zamindar owner, with high rents, illegal abwabs and no occupancy right. The Rent Act 1859 promises occupancy after over twelve years but is ineffective in Bengal. In Ryotwari and Mahalwari areas the road is auction, moneylender, then landlessness.
→ And in Bengal and Bihar a planter adds a second trap.

The indigo trap.
The European planter gives a loan at the start, sells inputs to the ryot and buys the indigo back at a price below market. The ryot cannot pay rent and loan, the soil is exhausted, and he must borrow and grow indigo again, or face eviction. The teacher's two systems: Bengal Ryoti (a quadrant of the plot, Indigo Revolt 1859) and Bihar Tinkathia (3/20th, Champaran Satyagraha 1917).
→ Then fear for faith adds fuel.

Religion adds fuel.
As a grievance: temple and mosque lands are taxed, revenue-free tenures end, missionaries may enter after 1813, and Sati 1829, Lex Loci 1850 and Widow Remarriage 1856 are seen as interference. As an organiser: with no parties or newspapers, a sect already has a leader, a philosophy and unity.
→ Meanwhile the tribals, in their forests, lose even more.

The tribal's world turned upside down.
Tribals lived by cultivation, hunting and gathering, under their own tribal law and chief. The British pushed land revenue in through four routes (zamindars as owners, revenue farmers, the chief made a zamindar, ryots made individual owners), demanded cash, and banned Jhum and hunting because they wanted settled peasants paying LR regularly.
→ Then the law takes the forest itself.

The forest is fenced (1878).
Under Lytton 76-80 the Indian Forests Act 1878 splits forests into Reserved, Protected and Village, driven by the railway need for timber (about 2,000 sleepers a mile). Customary rights become privileges, and millions become trespassers on ancestral land. The Abkari system adds an auctioned liquor monopoly, second only to land revenue.
→ Now the elites, too, have lost something.

The elites rise: civil uprisings.
Raja Chait Singh of Benaras (1778-81) loses his estates for unpaid LR. Wazir Ali 97-98, the Poligars, the Bundelas and Veluthampi (1809) each lose status, land or autonomy to British rule or its Resident. The Paikas of Odisha (1817) draw multi-class support and are debated as a candidate for the true First War of Independence.
→ Peasants, meanwhile, begin to lead themselves.

Peasants lead: Rangpur and Mysore.
In 1783 the Rangpur peasants, hurt by the Farming System and the 1770 famine, loot the grain stores of Debi Singh and Gobinda Singh, free prisoners, attack courts and run their own government. In Mysore (1830-31) peasants rise against the Wodeyars and British agents because the SA 1799 subsidy forced high LR.
→ Elsewhere the leader comes from religion.

Religion leads.
Dasnami Sanyasis and Madari Fakirs (1760-1850s, peak about 1800 with 50,000) inspire Anandamath. Karim and Tipu Shah lead the Pagal Panthis. Titu Mir builds a bamboo fort, the Faraizi (Dudu Mian) say land belongs to God, and the Moplahs lose rights because the British recognise only the Janmies.
→ In the hills and forests, the tribals rise in a chain.

The tribals rise, ending in the Hool.
Pahariya 1778, Bhil 1818-31, Ramosi 1822, Khasi 1829-33, Kol 1831-32 and Kandh 1837-56 each rise against loss of land, forest rights or religion. The Santhals (1855-56) give a public prior warning, rise with bows and arrows against the unholy trinity of British, zamindars and moneylenders, and about 50,000 are killed. The Santhal Parganas follow, with a bar on land transfer to non-Santhals.
→ Two more risings come after 1857.

After 1857: Birsa and Rampa.
Birsa Munda's Ulugulan (1899-1900) begins on Christmas 1899, with a belief that British bullets turn to water. The Rampa revolt, led first by Muttadars and crushed by 1880, merges into the NCM in 1920. After 1922 Alluri Sitarama Raju restarts the Fituri and is executed in 1924.
→ So what do all these revolts add up to?

The verdict.
They were not all-India, not coordinated, with local leaders, no plan and no democratic goal, so not modern nationalism. But they had ideology, organisation, programme, awareness and symbolism, and crimes hide while politics shows. Hence the pre-history of modern nationalism, and the culmination of a hundred years before 1857.

21.spine: Pressed on every side (pay, caste, Awadh, land, religion), the Bengal Army and the dispossessed villages rose together; they lost for lack of money, command and unity; and the Crown that replaced the Company rebuilt the army, police and services to prevent a repeat, shutting the very door that created modern nationalism.
beats:
A village in uniform.
The Bengal Army is the largest of the three armies, filled with upper-caste sepoys from Awadh and some from Bihar, and Indians far outnumber the British in it. The sepoy is a peasant in uniform: he is paid less than a European, is called Suar, and cannot rise beyond Subedar at 60 to 70 rupees a month.
→ But the British were about to press on every sore at once.

1856: four blows.
To offset war costs the British cut sepoy pay and abolish the allowance for serving outside the home region, a loss of money and of caste. Awadh, the biggest recruiting ground, is annexed on grounds of maladministration and feels like personal betrayal. The Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act is passed, and Canning 56-62 announces that the Mughals will be only 'Princes'.
→ All that was missing was a spark.

The fat on the cartridge.
The new Enfield rifle replaces the Brown Bess, and its cartridge, greased with cow and pig fat, must be bitten before loading. With rumours of cow and pig bone dust in flour, and missionaries in cantonments since the Charter Act 1813, sepoys fear a plot against Hindu and Muslim identity. The teacher is clear: the cartridge was only the trigger.
→ And the first sepoy fired.

Barrackpur to Delhi.
On 29 March 1857 Mangal Pandey of the 34th BNI fires at European officers; he is hanged on 8 April and Jemadar Ishwari Prasad on 22 April, and the 34th BNI is disbanded. On 10 May Meerut mutinies and on 11 May the sepoys reach Delhi and proclaim Bahadur Shah Zafar 37-57 Emperor of Hindustan. Delhi is held until 20 September, and for the first time in a century the British monopoly of organised violence is broken.
→ Now the villages were waiting.

The village joins.
Annexation and the Doctrine of Lapse have stripped rulers and their courts; Mahalwari, disbanded forts and equality before law have stripped the taluqdars of estates, arms and status; high land revenue, moneylenders and courts that side with lenders have ruined the peasants. Cheaper British goods ruin the artisans. Above all, the whole countryside fears for its religion: missionaries 1813, Sati 1829, Lex Loci 1850, Widows 1856.
→ Each region found its leader in the dispossessed.

Lamps in eight hands.
Nana Sahib rises at Kanpur, Hazrat Mahal at Lucknow, Khan Bahadur Khan at Bareilly, Lakshmi Bai at Jhansi, Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah at Faizabad, Kunwar Singh at Jagdishpur in Bihar and Zafar at Delhi, with Tantia Tope as the great guerrilla. Lakshmi Bai dies at Gwalior in June 1858; Tantia Tope is betrayed by Man Singh and hanged in April 1859; Zafar is exiled to Rangoon and dies in 1862.
→ Yet eight lamps are not one flame.

Why the flame went out.
The rebels have no money, weapons or training, and no central command. The teacher's board shows the mistake: all the sepoys go to Delhi, so the fall of Delhi is the fall of the sepoy mutiny and of the revolt. The revolts are local, with no control of the telegraph; Bombay and Madras stay quiet and Punjabis and Gurkhas help the British.
→ Whatever it was, what do we call it?

Mutiny, war or more?
The colonial view says sepoy mutiny; Savarkar (1909) and Marx say war of independence; mainstream historians say far more than a mutiny but without modern nationalism. Against the war: Scam B areas, Punjab, Bengal, the WEMC, loyal princes (Kota the exception), no manifesto, an old-order goal. For more than a mutiny: a common enemy, Hindu-Muslim unity (Aitchison), a federal vision, a mass movement.
→ Whatever the name, Britain could not go back to the Company.

The Crown takes over.
The GOI Act 1858 ends the EIC: Queen Victoria is sovereign and a Cabinet-rank Secretary of State replaces the President of the Board of Control. The Proclamation of 1 November 1858 promises tolerance and shelves social reform; the teacher adds no more annexations, with British India holding 63% of the territory. Britain now sees Indians as racially inferior and more authoritarian rule follows.
→ And the state itself was rebuilt: police, services, army.

A Police Raj and a shut door.
Canning 56-62's 1st Police Commission of 1860 leads to the Police Act of March 1861: Inspector General, Superintendent of Police, Sub-Inspector, with Indians excluded from important posts. The civil services exam is no longer held simultaneously in India, the age cap is 19 to 23, and the Statutory Civil Service of Lytton 76-80 admits only hand-picked elites: co-option, not inclusion.
→ But the deepest reform was the army.

The coup-proof army.
The Peel Commission (appointed July 1858, report March 1859) leads to the European Forces (India) Act 1860, ratios of 1:2 in Bengal and 1:3 in Madras and Bombay, and an Indian ban on artillery. Regiments mix castes and religions, recruitment favours martial races, loyalty to the salt is taught, and the army is kept in barracks and used against peasant revolts and the INM.
→ Yet the shut door had made a new class.

The door that made its own key.
The WEMC, schooled in British liberalism, had wanted a share in governance and was locked out. That frustration became the seed of the modern nationalism-based INM, and by 1929 its demands would escalate into Purna Swaraj. 1857 was the hinge: more efficient and more repressive reforms that planted what would later demand independence.

22.spine: The peasant now used the master's law and the educated gave him a voice, so each revolt (Indigo, Pabna, Deccan, Punjab) ended in a legal relief and left behind organisation and voice: the rehearsal, and the soil, for the national movement.
beats:
1857 changes the way of resisting.
After 1857 the peasants did not just pick up weapons: they filed court cases and organised themselves, using the colonial legal system against colonial rule. The Western Educated Middle Class (WEMC) began to speak for the ryot in newspapers, courts and associations. The teacher's ladder says modern politics tries non-violent methods first: courts, press, peaceful protest.
→ So the first great test came in Bengal, over a blue dye.

1788: a trap that looked like a contract.
The EIC began promoting indigo in Bengal in 1788 with loans to ten European planters, preferring them to zamindars. Nij farming (the planter buys land) was costly, so planters moved to the Ryoti system: lease land from zamindars, then contract with ryots to grow indigo on at least 25% of their land, with low-interest loans, seeds and seed drills, and the planter buying the crop.
→ But the contract turned into a noose.

The squeeze.
Indigo ruined the soil, the price was not remunerative, and the ryot borrowed one loan to repay another, tied by force of finance. A Stock Exchange crisis then cut global indigo prices, and a sympathetic Lieutenant Governor of Bengal told Collectors to side with ryots against forced cultivation.
→ So the ryots finally had room to act.

The ryots go to court.
They refused new loans and indigo, boycotted the planters' Indian agents, and began a no-rent campaign when planters sued (the teacher: the contract was legal). When planters tried eviction, the ryots organised and went to court under the Rent Act of 1859. This was Non-Cooperation decades before Gandhi.
→ Then the educated took up their pens.

The educated join.
DeenBandhu Mitra's play Neel Darpan (1860) shocked the public; Michael Madhusudhan Datta translated it and James Long published it, and for that Long was convicted of libel, fined Rs 1,000 (paid by Kaliprasanna Sinha) and jailed a month. Hindu Patriot and Somprakash ran editorials, and the British Indian Association (1851) of educated zamindars backed the ryots, partly from self-interest.
→ Now the system had to give way, but not all at once.

Indigo ends slowly.
The Indigo Commission (1860) said honour old contracts, refuse new ones. By 1863 indigo moved to Bihar as Tinkathia (3/20th of land). The long-term death blow was BASF's synthetic indigo in 1897 (Prelims 2020), with a short WWI revival, and Champaran (1917) and the Act of 1918 ended Tinkathia.
→ Meanwhile in Bengal another villain appeared: not a European, but an Indian zamindar.

Pabna, 1873: a league and a split.
Zamindars violated the occupancy rights of the Rent Act 1859, raised rents illegally and collected Abwabs. The ryots formed Agrarian Leagues, pooled money for court, and Ishan Chandra Roy spread them. The WEMC split: Hindu Patriot and Amrita Bazar Patrika for the zamindars, Bengalee (SNB) and the Anglo-Indian press for the ryots. Ripon 80-84's Rent Commission (1880) led to the Bengal Tenancy Act 1885: occupancy rights after more than twelve years.
→ Now across to the Deccan, where the villain was the moneylender.

The Deccan's bond trap.
No-tax came in 1873-74 against a Land Revenue hike. The Limitation Law 1859 allowed interest for three years only, so moneylenders made a fresh bond with the interest added to the principal. The Poona Sarvajanik Sabha (1870) gathered 17,000 signatures; moneylenders refused loans; in 1875 the ryots burned debt bonds, not lives. The Relief Act came in 1879, and a second no-tax campaign in 1896-97 over refused remission.
→ Then to Punjab, where religion and canals shaped the revolt.

Punjab: a sect and a canal bill.
The Namdhari (Kuka) sect under Baba Ram Singh turned from violence against cow slaughterers and priests to violence against the British, and he was exiled to Burma in 1872 (the teacher: not imp). In 1907 a bill to control inheritance and raise water rates in the canal colonies brought the Lahore Indian Association, the Arya Samaj and the Singh Sabha into a no-tax campaign. The British repressed, then quietly withdrew it, fearing the Army, recruited heavily from Punjab, might follow.
→ Put the pieces together and a pattern shows.

The rehearsal.
Across Bengal, Maharashtra and Punjab, peasants organised, used the colonial legal system and found the WEMC lending its voice. It was not yet the national movement but the soil in which it would grow: non-cooperation, no-tax, boycott and legal challenge were all rehearsed here before Champaran (1917) and Non-Cooperation (1920).

23.spine: Petition, then provoke, then organise, then converge: the landed class petitioned for itself and got nothing; the Raj's own tools (education, press, rails) built the WEMC and its racism provoked it; the WEMC organised for everyone from 1870; and five roots converged in the INC of 1885.
beats:
The landlords petition (1851-52).
The first organised political voice is not the middle class but the educated landed class. The British Indian Association (BrIA 1851) is set up in Calcutta with Radhakanta Deb as first president; the Bombay Association and the Madras Native Association follow in 1852. All three petition because Parliament is discussing the Charter Act of 1853, and they send three separate petitions, not one. They never oppose British rule: they call exploitation 'un-British'.
→ But nothing is granted.

Nothing is granted.
These conservatives have too much to lose: land revenue systems like the Permanent Settlement of 1793 created the landed class, the police protect them, and their status and security depend on the British. The teacher's board puts it as Of, By, For: their bodies were of, by and for the landed class, not for the people.
→ So a different class will have to carry the movement.

The Raj builds a class (after 1857).
Higher Western education after 1857 creates a politically conscious Western Educated Middle Class (WEMC), meant to be loyal Brown Sahibs. When it sees no real intent to share power, admiration turns into criticism and then a demand for Indian rights. But education is uneven (the Downward Filtration Theory of 1835 favoured Presidency Town elites; 1921 literacy is only 8%, female 2%), so the movement starts in Calcutta, Bombay and Madras.
→ Now this class needs tools.

The tools: press, rails, wires.
By 1875 India has over 400 newspapers and more than 1.5 lakh readers; the press turns regional leaders into national ones. From the 1850s railways and the telegraph let leaders from Bombay, Bengal, Madras and Punjab meet and coordinate. The infrastructure of empire becomes the infrastructure of anti-colonial politics.
→ But the Raj keeps handing out reasons for anger.

The villain does its work.
The 1850 Black Acts try to put Europeans in the mofussil under Indian judges and are suspended after a 'white rebellion'. The Lex Loci Act 1850 protects converts' inheritance over Indian opposition. Income Tax (1860, withdrawn, 1868) arrives during famines and draws 'No Taxation Without Representation'. In 1870 Bengal's higher-education budget is cut while military spending continues.
→ And then Lytton arrives.

Lytton antagonises everyone (76-80).
Lytton 76-80 cuts the ICS age from 21 to 19 (1876, exam only in London), holds the Delhi Durbar (1877) during the Great Madras Famine, passes the Vernacular Press Act and the Arms Act (1878), creates the nomination-based Statutory Civil Service, and fights the Second Afghan War (1878-80). The Amrita Bazar Patrika turns English overnight to escape the press law.
→ Then a liberal Viceroy is sent.

Ripon, the liberal contrast (80-84).
Gladstone's Liberals win in 1880 and send Ripon 80-84. The Rent Commission (1880) leads to the Bengal Tenancy Act 1885; the Factories Act 1881 bans labour under 7; the Vernacular Press Act is repealed and the Arms Act amended (1882); the ICS age goes back to 21. His key reform is Local Self-Government 1882: elected District Boards and municipalities with two-thirds elected. But Europeans in India oppose the simultaneous exam and it fails.
→ How far will Europeans let reform go?

The Ilbert Bill (1883-84).
Law Member C.P. Ilbert proposes that Indian district judges may try Britons in the mofussil. Europeans organise, lobby and protest, and the bill is withdrawn and amended to need a mixed jury. For the WEMC the last doubt is gone: the British will not treat Indians as equals. Its press campaigns are the biggest use of the press before 1885.
→ The WEMC decides to organise on its own.

The WEMC organises (1870 onwards).
The Poona Sarvajanik Sabha (1870, Ranade) petitions the House of Commons in 1875 for direct Indian representation. Surendranath Banerjee, who lost his ICS career over an age dispute, founds the Indian Association (1876); the Lahore Indian Association follows in 1877 and the Madras Mahajan Sabha in 1884. These bodies are of and by the WEMC but for all the people.
→ And they do real work.

More than talking shops.
The new associations lead peasants (Indigo Revolt 1859-63, Bombay Deccan Riots 1875, Punjab Canal Colony 1907), run famine relief and arbitration courts, protest the Plantation Labour Act of 1859 (serfdom), and demand Council seats, separation of powers, lower Home Charges and an extended Permanent Settlement. After the Indian Councils Act of 1892 they use the Councils themselves.
→ Now the roots meet.

Five roots, one Congress (1885).
Western education, a free press, racial provocation, organised WEMC associations, and railways and telegraphs all converge on the Indian National Congress at Bombay in 1885: the first all-India political party and the all-India culmination of the regional bodies.

24.spine: Decades of regional campaigns and attempts at all-India bodies prepared the ground; Hume, a Liberal retired civil servant, bridged Bombay, Calcutta and Madras and gave the INC protective cover, so the British 'Safety Valve' story is a friend's legend while the 'Lightning Conductor' reading is the sound one.
beats:
Small bodies, big complaints.
Long before 1885 regional associations protested the Lex Loci Act 1850 and the Income Tax of 1868, campaigned for Indianisation of the Civil Services (1877), against the Afghan War and the Vernacular Press Act (1878), for the Ilbert Bill (1883-84), and demanded the right to join the Volunteer Corps. None of their demands was met.
→ So the next logical step was a body that spoke for all of India.

The first attempts.
The British India Association (1851) tried branches in Bombay and Madras for a joint petition on the Charter renewal of 1853; journalists at the Imperial Darbar formed the Native Press Association (1877) with Banerjea as President; the Indian Association (1876) launched the Indian National Conference (1883); Madras hosted the Theosophical Society convention (1884); a National Fund followed in 1885.
→ But the regional bodies competed for leadership, and someone had to bring them to one table.

The retired civil servant.
A.O. Hume, a Liberal retired British civil servant, had worked under Mayo 69-72 (1871), was dismissed for opposing Lytton 76-80's Afghan War spending, and backed Ripon 80-84's reforms. He wanted the INC to be 'His Majesty's Opposition': a strong opposition party so that the government is accountable, with good governance and a responsive government.
→ And so in December 1885 the delegates met.

Bombay, December 1885.
The INC was founded in Bombay in December 1885 with W.C. Bonnerjee as 1st President. The teacher calls it the 1st all India ORG but not an all Indian one, since its founder was a Briton; and the President is not from the region of the session. Hume served as General Secretary, never as President.
→ The sessions then moved city to city, and the Presidents became the exam's favourite list.

Presidents and Firsts.
Naoroji 1886 (Calcutta), Tyabji 1887 (1st Muslim, Madras), Yule 1888 (1st non-Indian, Allahabad), Wedderburn 1889 and 1910, Webb 1894, Besant 1917 (1st woman), Das 1922 (from prison, Gaya), Naidu 1925 (2nd woman). Calcutta hosted the 2nd session, not the 1st; Tyabji died in August 1906, before the League of December 1906.
→ But why did this British friend help at all? One story says the British planned it.

The Safety Valve story.
Wedderburn's 1913 biography says Hume received seven volumes of secret reports in 1878 describing a conspiracy of the masses, met Dufferin 84-88, and together they founded the INC as a safety valve; R.P. Dutt agreed. The teacher draws a pressure cooker: Indians as steam, oppression as flame, the INC as the whistle.
→ But the story does not survive a check.

Why the story fails.
The seven volumes were never found in any archive; the only source is a friend's book written nearly four decades later. Dufferin 84-88 called the Moderates a 'microscopic minority of Babus working for self-interest', and quietly told the Governor of Bombay to be alert, fearing an Irish Home Rule League. The teacher: never in exam, always on YouTube.
→ So what was Hume really good for?

The bridge and the umbrella.
Wedderburn wrote to make his friend Hume a patriot. Hume's real usefulness was practical: a mediator who got Bombay, Calcutta and Madras to sit together, and, as Gokhale put it in 1913, a British founder gave protective cover because the British would never allow an all-India body under an Indian leader. If the British used the INC as a safety valve, Indians used Hume as a lightning conductor.
→ Hume had friends, and the handout names them.

The English friends.
Wedderburn (co-founder, 2nd non-Indian President 1889 and 1910, MP, with W.S. Caine set up the Indian Parliamentary Committee in 1893 for reforms in the Commons); Jardine (Judge, MP 1906-1918); Yule (1st non-Indian President, Andrew Yule and Company, an Agency House, 400 tigers); Webb (Irish MP, Madras 1894, invited by Naoroji, against racism and the opium trade).
→ One last check of how the exam turned the pieces into questions.

What UPSC asked.
Curzon 99-05 made the 'peaceful demise' remark (1998); the 1998 pairs trap is Tyabji and the Muslim League; 2000 asked Naidu, Das, Hume, Webb; 2004 and 2008 asked the first session (Bombay); 2011 the Wedderburn and Caine committee; 2015 the first woman and first Muslim Presidents. The teacher writes Mains - No Q, PRELIMS ticked.

25.spine: The British restructured the State in 1861 to look consultative while staying a despotism controlled from home: one council wore two hats, a nominated and rigged legislative ring was added, some provincial law-making was handed back, and the Viceroy kept every real power.
beats:
The despot at home.
After 1857 and the Crown takeover of 1858, the Secretary of State for India sits at the top of the chain in London. Charles Wood calls the Government of India a 'despotism controlled from home', and this stays the operating principle until 1947. The teacher: the Constitution of British India runs from the Regulating Act 1773 to the GOI Act 1935, and it is not a democracy.
→ So how was the machinery rebuilt in 1861?

Two laws, one year.
In 1861 the State is overhauled: the ICA 1861 restructures the Legislature and the Executive (L and E), and the Indian High Courts Act 1861 reorganises the Judiciary (J). Out of the Governor-General's Council come the VEC for executive work and the ILC for law-making.
→ But these are not really two bodies.

One room, two hats.
The VEC expands by adding 6 to 12 additional members for law-making: the VEC opens the doors of its room and the additional members join, and the room becomes the ILC. Every VEC member sits in the ILC, so the executive keeps an official majority. The same pattern appears in the provinces as PLCs and GECs.
→ Who sat in the executive room?

The cabinet takes shape.
Canning56-62 starts the Portfolio System in 1859 (departments allotted to individual members, decisions final subject to the Viceroy's veto) and the ICA 1861 makes it law. The 1857 debt brings a 5th ordinary member for Finance (James Wilson, income tax 1860, he dies 1860; the tax returns in 1868), so the VEC is GG + 5 + C-I-C. The C-I-C stays extraordinary so that one man does not hold both the office and the battlefield; a 6th member for Public Works comes in 1874.
→ Now, the legislative ring.

A grain of representation.
Of the 6 to 12 additional members the Viceroy nominates, half must be non-officials: for the first time non-officers can be lawmakers, and in 1862 three Indians join (the Raja of Banaras, the Maharaja of Patiala and Dinkar Rao of Gwalior). The goal is to reward those loyal in 1857 and co-opt the elites. Only 45 Indians are nominated until 1892.
→ But the arithmetic is rigged.

Seven beats six.
The VEC alone (GG + 5 + C-I-C = 7) matches or outnumbers the most non-officials possible (6). In the teacher's case of 6 additional members, officials are 10 (7 + 3) against 3 non-officials. The majority of officers is guaranteed, and 'official' means bureaucrat, PRO-British.
→ So what could the ILC actually do?

A legislature at the bottom of the ladder.
Of the ladder of legislative powers (discussion, questions, resolutions, bills, budget, create the Executive, dismiss it, amend the Constitution) the ILC has almost none: discussion and introducing bills only with the Viceroy's prior approval, no questions, no resolutions, no budget vote. The Viceroy holds an absolute veto and a 6-month ordinance. It is 'not a modern Parliament', all nominated, no elections.
→ And the provinces?

The first small step back.
The Charter Act 1833 had taken the law-making of Bombay and Madras to the Centre. The ICA 1861 restores it and proposes PLCs for Bengal, Punjab and the NWP (Bengal 1862, NWP 1886, Punjab 1897, the delays due to raw 1857 memories and a frontier province). On the teacher's board the Centre's share falls only from 100% (1833) to 90% (1861).
→ Yet the Viceroy keeps the keys.

BRASS: the Viceroy keeps the keys.
The Viceroy needs to sanction the Governor's nominations (ended by ICA 1892), frames the rules for all councils (ended only by GOI 1935), must approve certain bills before introduction (relaxed 1919 and 1935), keeps a single budget for all of British India (ended by GOI 1919) and can create provinces and appoint Lt Governors (to the Crown under GOI 1935). Giving with one hand and taking with the other.
→ So where does the story go next?

The long road to democracy.
The arc runs: centralisation began 1773, peaked 1833, decentralisation began 1861, Provincial Autonomy in 1935. The ladder of elections runs 1861 non-officers, 1909 first proper indirect election, 1919 first direct elections and elected majority. The expanded-council model lasts until GOI 1919 (CoS and CLA). The teacher's test of responsible government is that every minister is an MP or MLA first; the ICA 1861 fails it, and the Moderates ask for an ideal Constitution.

26.spine: The Moderates, shaped by Utilitarian and Liberal faith in laws and constitutions, asked the British for Limited Self-Government by petition and prayer. Because they were a narrow, elite, part-time body that distrusted the masses, their demands carried no pressure and none was met; yet they were building the culture of politics.
beats:
Limit the State, by law.
In the West the monarchy was limited step by step (Britain without a written Constitution, France with one). In India the opponent was a foreign power, so Step 1 for the Moderates was to limit the colonial State, with a good Constitution as the instrument. They drew on Utilitarianism (the greatest good of the greatest number, through laws) and Liberalism (rights, rule of law, a constitution).
→ So they chose methods that stay inside the State's own rules.

Only the State's own doors.
Constitutionalism meant Responsible Government, protected rights and Rule of Law. Constitutional methods meant using only the channels the State provides: elections, the Legislature, the Judiciary, RTI, CPGRAMS, Citizen Charters and petitions (the teacher adds FIR, Court case and NOTA). Gandhi's Non-Cooperation and Civil Disobedience sit outside, as extra-constitutional mass struggle.
→ But did they want the British gone?

Critics, not rebels.
The Moderates knew British rule was exploitative, yet they believed in its Providence: if pressurised, the British could modernise India. Their goal was Limited Self-Government within British rule, because the masses were not yet ready; the long vision was Canada or Australia with British citizenship. Banerjea wanted an end to Un-British Rule, and Bonnerjee called the INC loyal to the British and their well-wishers.
→ What, then, did they actually ask for?

Eleven asks, no answers.
Four were political: abolish the 15-member India Council, expand the ILC and PLCs with at least 50% indirectly elected members, give genuine powers, and Indianise the services (exam in India and Britain, age 23). Seven were economic: cut military spending (the Boxer Rebellion 1899-1901), a volunteer army, trial by jury, repeal of the Arms Act 1878, lower land revenue and no Salt Tax, PS 1793 extended, and an end to Assam tea indenture. None was met.
→ Who was asking, and for whom?

Who was in the room.
At the first session in 1885, 72 delegates came: Bombay 38, Madras 21, Punjab and NWP and Oudh 10, and only 3 from Bengal-Bihar-Orissa-Assam (the handout says Bengal about 5). They were upper-caste Western-educated professionals; Hindus were 90% and Muslims about 6.5% of the INC against 20% in the census. Tyabji, the first Muslim President (Madras 1887), was the exception.
→ Even that thin unity was guarded by a rule.

The 1886 rule.
At the Calcutta session of 1886, under Dadabhai Naoroji, the INC decided to avoid social questions (Hindu-Muslim, upper-lower caste, women, class) until 1907, so that it would not look pro-one-group or split. It would pick only fights where the opponent was a foreigner. In 1893 it stayed silent over the cow-killing riots, and Muslim participation fell.
→ The rule saved unity but left the leaders' own class interests untouched.

Landlords' politics.
In 1892-1905 about 20% of members were landlords, 40% lawyers and 15% traders, and the leaders were part-time politicians in a three-day annual conference. So there was no anti-Zamindar stand (they wanted PS 1793 extended), they opposed the Punjab Land Alienation Bill of 1900, and they backed Indian capital over labour (Assam tea only because the owners were European).
→ The same lens shaped their view of the factory laws.

The Lancashire game.
British textile makers in Lancashire lobbied for Indian factory rules to raise Indian costs; the Moderates replied that infant industries needed room or India would stay a raw-material supplier. The Acts were the Factories Act 1881 (Ripon 80-84; imp), the Factories Act 1891 (Lansdowne 88-94) and the Indian Mines Act 1901 (Curzon 99-05). The verdict is complex: the lobby's motive was real, but Indian workers, children included, suffered longer.
→ Whatever their reasons, their method was always the same.

Prayer, petition, protest in print.
They sent prayers and petitions, passed resolutions at annual sessions, used the press and debates, and avoided all mass action, as firm believers in the Rule of Law. The teacher's 3P is Prayer, Petitions, Protests in the press; critics, later the Extremists, called it the Strategy of Mendicancy.
→ Why did that bring no result?

A sliver with no lever.
Two problems reinforced each other: they did not represent the masses (about 90% Hindu, lawyers and landlords) and they distrusted the masses and would not mobilise them. A movement that neither represented the people nor threatened to unleash them could be ignored. The teacher's four power factors: claim, masses, demands, methods.
→ Yet it was not the end of the story.

A beginning, not the end.
Gokhale said in 1913 that without these methods the British would not have allowed the INC to function, and that the culture of direct confrontation had not yet developed. The goal itself moved on: Limited Self-Government 1885-1906, Self-Government within the empire 1906, Dominion Status 1916 and 1928, Purna Swaraj 1929.

27.spine: Because India in 1885 had no single political community, the Moderates built unity and a parliamentary habit, backed Indian capitalists, and then proved with the Drain Theory that Britain used its political control to move India's wealth away. The drain ran through plunder, tariffs, exchange rates, Council Bills and Home Charges, so the economic critique became a demand for Swaraj.
beats:
A land with no single people.
In 1885 the first INC session at Bombay declared its goal as building national unity. India was a land of regions, languages, castes and religions with no pre-existing single political community, so the Moderates decided that building one came before demanding rights from the British.
→ So how do you build a nation inside a Congress?

One versus only.
In 1886 Naoroji laid down the informal rule that the INC takes only political questions, not social or class ones, so the fight is Indians against British and not Hindu against Muslim, upper against lower caste, men against women, worker against capitalist or ryot against landlord. In 1888 the INC added a veto (no resolution if the majority of Hindu or Muslim members disagree) and in 1889 the Minority Clause, the INC's own demand for reserved seats in the ILC and PLCs.
→ Rules alone do not make leaders, so the structure had to help.

The host never presides.
Each session was held in a different part of the country and the President was never from the host region. A Marathi leader presiding in Calcutta and speaking to Bengali concerns builds an all-India leadership and inter-regional bonds, nation building by simple design.
→ Those sessions also taught India a new habit.

A parliament before a parliament.
The President functioned like a Speaker and members spoke, debated and voted on resolutions, which was new for India. Today's Lok Sabha procedures have their roots in the culture of INC sessions, so the modern political era began with the INC.
→ But a nation also needs an economy, and the Moderates had a view on that.

Why back the capitalists?
The Moderates were not anti-poor, they were pro-industrialisation: every industrialised country had risen on its capitalist class, communist industrialisation was born only in 1917 and showed results after 1929, and Indian capitalists were struggling against British imports and British firms in India.
→ Yet their sharpest weapon was an idea about wealth leaving India.

The Drain Theory.
After the disappointment with the Indian Councils Act of 1892 the Moderates built the Drain Theory: an evidence-based argument that Britain used its political control over the Indian State for its own economic benefit, so the White Man's Burden was false. Naoroji (Poverty & Un-British Rule in India, 1901), R.C. Dutt (1902 and 1904) and Ranade (father of Indian economics) made it, spread by press, speeches and books.
→ The teacher first separates rupees from wealth, then asks how the machine worked.

How British factories rebuilt India.
Before British industrialisation India was a net exporter of finished goods. Afterwards it was a raw-material source and an export market: farms grew cotton, indigo, jute and opium for British mills, handicrafts were destroyed, and artisans with no Indian factories to join were forced into an overburdened agriculture.
→ Then steam made the pump faster.

Steam, rail and the Suez shortcut.
The steam engine (1769) later brought machines, ships and railways, and the Suez Canal (1859-69) cut the sea distance by 4,500 miles. The teacher's board shows the rail-road-port loop carrying raw materials out and finished goods in, with railways built under Dalhousie 48-56 for the army, and he writes that the loot escalated.
→ Now, how exactly did the money leave?

Plunder first, policy later.
Before 1813 the drain was Dastak misuse, the Plassey plunder of 1757-65 and land revenue from 1765. After 1813 it was policy: no protective tariff until World War I, a managed exchange rate that favoured British business, and Council Bills in which the importer's forex stayed in London and the GOI paid rupees from taxpayers.
→ And then the bills were sent in the name of Britain's services.

The cafe bill and the double drain.
Home Charges are what India paid Britain for goods and services Britain said it gave, Home meaning Britain; the teacher says to think like a British nationalist, since the bill reads as services (governance and security of the territory), goods (stores), stability (War Office) and development (FDI interest). The eight heads include salaries and pensions, EIC dividends, loan and foreign-debt interest, India Office costs, stores, War Office payments and FDI interest. The army abroad is a drain but not an HC, because India gave that service. India sold more than it bought in rupees (Ex > Im) yet lost the forex it earned, a trade surplus but a wealth deficit, the double drain.
→ The British had answers, and the notes have replies.

Railways, canals and only 2 per cent.
The teacher marks this whole debate 'mmp'. The British pointed to railways (but with a guaranteed 5% in London, army purpose, 78% coverage by 1947; on his board FDI became FD: free land on a 99-year lease, buy-back, losses on the Indian taxpayer), canals (but only 25% irrigated, outside Permanent Settlement areas, water not free) and said the drain was only 2%. Naoroji replied that 2% was surplus capital that would have compounded, and the chapter closes that the critique was inseparable from the demand for Swaraj.

28.spine: The Moderates asked politely (3P) and got a shortlist, not an election: bigger councils, talk without a vote, an unchanged executive and an official majority, plus one small federal step. The hollow Act proved that petitions could not buy real power, so the Moderates raised their demand to Swaraj and the Drain Theory, and a new generation turned to the street.
beats:
Seven years of polite asking.
From 1885 to 1892 the Moderates used the 3P method (Prayer, Protest in Press, Petitions): carefully reasoned arguments for constitutional reform. The reply was the Indian Councils Act 1892, the Lord Cross Act, passed with Lord Cross as Secretary of State and Lansdowne 88-94 as Viceroy. It was a result of their struggle and proof of its failure.
→ But what did the Act actually give?

A shortlist called an election.
The most significant feature was indirectly nominated members in the ILC and the PLCs, the first time something like representative membership appeared. But the word 'election' was deliberately left out: the mechanism was nomination on the basis of recommendation. In the teacher's example, if 10 seats were to be filled, names of 50 were asked and the Viceroy or Governor chose 10.
→ So who sent the names, and to whom?

Names climb the stairs.
Tier 1: District Boards, Municipalities, Universities, Trade Associations and Zamindars sent names to the Governor, who nominated the non-official PLC members. Tier 2: the non-official PLC members and the Bengal Chamber of Commerce sent names to the Viceroy, who nominated the non-official ILC members. Gokhale and Pherozeshah Mehta were among those who served; Municipalities never recommended straight to the ILC.
→ Now, how big was the room?

A bigger room, the same majority.
The ILC's additional members rose to 10 to 16 (6 to 12 in 1861), and at least half had to be non-officials. But the VEC plus the official additional members always outnumbered the non-officials: like a board where the promoters always hold the vote, the independents may speak but cannot win.
→ And what about the inner cabinet?

The inner cabinet stays put.
The VEC did not change at all: GG + C-in-C + six Ordinary Members holding Home, Revenue/Agriculture, Law, Military, Finance (added 1861) and Public Works (added 1874). The ILC is the VEC plus the additional members: two boxes, one inside the other.
→ So what could the new members actually do?

Ask and browse, never vote.
For the first time members could ask questions (6 days' notice, no discussion, no supplementaries) and discuss the Budget (no vote, no amendment): Taxation without Representation, the 1776 slogan, with a faint echo. They could not bring resolutions or demand a vote on a government resolution, the government could legislate over them, the Viceroy could veto any Bill, and the 6-month ordinance power was unchanged.
→ Did the provinces gain anything?

One small step for the provinces.
The Governor no longer needed the Viceroy's approval to nominate non-officers to the PLC: the first relaxation of the Viceroy's grip since 1861. Rule-making powers, prior approval of certain bills, the single budget and the power to create provinces and appoint Lieutenant-Governors stayed as before.
→ Meanwhile a separate reform was happening in the services.

A reform from the same years, but not the Act.
On the Aitchison Commission's recommendations (1886-88), in Lansdowne 88-94's time, the Covenanted Civil Services became the ICS, the Uncovenanted Civil Services became the PCS, and the Statutory Civil Services were abolished. These were administrative orders, not provisions of ICA 1892: a classic exam trap.
→ So how did the Moderates do overall?

The scorecard: one yes, six no.
Indianisation of Civil Services and Military, a non-official majority, an elected majority, proper indirect election, powerful legislatures and constitutionalism were all refused. Only expansion of the ILC and PLCs scored a yes, and a dissatisfied one. The word 'election' did not make it into the text.
→ Disappointed, the Moderates changed the ask.

Raising the ceiling.
The Moderates began asking for self-government on the lines of Australia (1901) and Canada (1867): the Dominion model. Swaraj, self-government within the Empire (Home Rule), became the INC goal at Calcutta in 1906. They also developed the Drain Theory: the political demand and the economic critique became the twin pillars of their politics.
→ But the method itself was in doubt.

The soil for Extremism.
If prayers and petitions could produce only this hollow Act (a Budget talk with no vote, questions with no follow-up, no elections, no non-official majority), the method was bankrupt. Belief in British benevolence cracked; street protest and mass politics took root, with the Bengal Partition of 1905 as the catalyst.
