29.spine: The Moderates failed, so the Extremists took religion and culture to the masses; Curzon 99-05's laws and the Partition of Bengal gave them a villain and the first mass protest; the Swadeshi toolkit could not reach the poor, the Muslims or the Lower Castes, the INC split at Surat, and the tested toolkit waited for Gandhi.
beats:
The petitions that went nowhere.
The Moderates have led the INC since 1885, and their method is petition, prayer and press. By the early 1900s it has brought no self-governance, no economic relief and no political power. The Extremists read this as proof that gentle methods do not work against a colonial administration.
→ But a new generation has a different recipe.

Culture becomes a weapon.
Lal-Bal-Pal and Sri Aurobindo lead the Extremist phase: Lajpat Rai in Punjab, Tilak in Maharashtra, Pal and Aurobindo in Bengal. Tilak had already turned the Ganapati Festival (1893) and the Shivaji Festival (1896) into political platforms: culture first, then political energy. Most want Swaraj within the Raj; Aurobindo (1907, in Bande Mataram) and Pal want Purna Swaraj.
→ Then a Viceroy hands them a villain.

Curzon 99-05's three orders.
In 1899 the Calcutta Municipal Corporation Amendment Act cuts elected members; in 1904 the Indian Universities Act takes the universities under direct control, calling them factories of sedition; and in 1904 the Indian Official Secrets Amendment Act cuts press freedom. Local self-government, education and the press are all hit. The teacher: the stronger the villain, the stronger the hero.
→ And then he cuts a province in two.

The Partition of Bengal.
The Risley Papers of 1903 reveal the plan. It is announced in July 1905 and takes effect on 16 October 1905: Bengal (West Bengal, Bihar, Orissa) and East Bengal and Assam, a new Muslim-majority province. The stated reason is good governance; the Indian view is Divide and Rule, since Bengalis become a minority in Bengal and Hindus a minority in EBA. Nawab Salimullah welcomes it and the Muslim League follows in 1906.
→ Bengal answers first with the pen.

The pen, then the boycott.
From 1903 to 1905 Surendranath Bannerjea and C.R. Das run a press campaign and Tagore tries Constructive Swadeshi at Shantiniketan; Deuskar's Desher Katha (1904) uses 'Desh' for all India. After about 1.5 years of the Moderates' three Ps the Partition still comes, and on 7 August 1905 the Moderates themselves pass the Boycott Resolution at Calcutta Town Hall.
→ Now the Extremists take the movement over.

The Extremists take over.
The Extremists add Swaraj to the goal and Passive Resistance (NC + CD + CW, with violence only if the government uses repression) to the method, and carry the movement out of Bengal: Das and Pal, Tilak, Haidar Raza, Lajpat Rai and Ajit Singh, and V.O. Chidambaram Pillai. At Barisal in April 1906 the police stop a procession of Bande Mataram badges, and it becomes a big boost to the movement.
→ They need a toolkit to match.

The toolkit.
Boycott and Swadeshi (two sides of one coin), national education with the Bengal National College under Aurobindo, enterprises such as TISCO (1907) and the Swadeshi Steam Navigation Company (1906), picketing, Samitis, Jatras, religious symbols and workers' strikes. Constructive Work aims at Atmashakti, the individual and then the community.
→ But a toolkit is not yet a mass movement.

Why it fell short.
Swadeshi goods are costly, so the poor stay out; student volunteers use force and social boycott on Lower Castes and Muslims; institutions are thin; Muslims are put off by Jatras, the Muslim League and the heavy Hindu symbolism; and the Extremists spend energy trying to capture the INC. British imports are not hit.
→ And then the Congress itself breaks.

Calcutta, then Surat.
At Calcutta (1906) Naoroji presides and the Extremists pass Swaraj, Boycott, Swadeshi and National Education. Morley's 1906 Budget speech hints at council reforms, and the Moderates move the 1907 session from Poona or Nagpur to Surat. A fight over the presidency between L.L. Rai and Rash Behari Ghosh ends with shoes hurled and the Extremists expelled; in 1908 the Allahabad Convention declares loyalty to the Raj.
→ The Extremists are scattered.

Leaders scattered, guns appear.
Tilak is deported to Mandalay (1908-14), Aurobindo retires, Pal retires for a time, and Rai goes abroad (1914-20). Leaderless, the movement gives way to the Revolutionaries (1908-11). The teacher's chain: when the pen failed people came out, when people failed guns, when guns failed MG.
→ Yet the movement leaves something behind.

What was left.
Nationalism stays lit, mass politics has begun, the Drain is explained to the poor, Bande Mataram becomes the INM's anthem, and Passive Resistance, Constructive Work, Jatras and Prabhat Pheris are a toolkit Gandhi inherits in 1920. At the Delhi Durbar of December 1911 the Partition is annulled and the capital moves to Delhi; the Muslim League's birth leaves communal politics as the long shadow.

30.spine: After the Extremists fell by 1908, a small committed group chose armed struggle: repeat 1857 in the long run, heroic action now. Their secret societies and centres abroad fed a string of attacks (1907-12), the British answered with the CID and the Cellular Jail, and the phase ended repressed but not futile: it gave pride, helped bring 1911, and its Rash Behari Bose line runs to the INA.
beats:
Pen, People, Guns.
By 1908 the Swadeshi Movement was leaderless: Tilak was deported to Mandalay, Aurobindo retired, B.C. Pal retired temporarily and L.L. Rai went abroad. The politically radicalised asked what next if mass politics had failed. The teacher's chain says it all: when the Pen failed, People came out; when People failed, Guns came out; when Guns failed, MG came out (1920+).
→ So the Revolutionaries gave two answers at once.

Two answers: a long game and a quick strike.
The long-term goal was to repeat 1857: a civil rebellion and disaffection within the army. The immediate method was individual heroic action: assassinate hated officials to strike fear in British hearts, remove fear from Indians and arouse nationalism. If caught, the trial became a stage and a death sentence a supreme sacrifice.
→ Heroic action needed structure, so they built societies.

Bengal builds the Anushilan.
In 1902 Pramathanath Mitra founded the Anushilan Samiti in Calcutta for physical training and character building, with armed resistance as its inner purpose. By 1906 an impatient inner circle formed around the newspaper Jugantar of Barindra Kumar Ghosh, Bhupendranath Datta and Abinash Bhattacharya. The British replied in 1903 with the CID, after the Fraser Police Commission of 1902.
→ But Bengal was only one stream, and the two streams soon diverged.

Jolt now, drill for later.
Jugantar was a loose, decentralised confederation that believed in propaganda of the deed and assassination to show the British were not invincible. The Dacca Anushilan Samiti of Pulin Behari Das (1906) was rigidly hierarchical and built for long-term military preparation, the teacher's 'Repeat 1857'. In the west the Savarkar brothers turned Mitra Mela (1899, Nasik) into Abhinav Bharat (1904, Pune), copying Mazzini's Young Italy.
→ Now the Revolutionaries looked beyond India's borders.

Why go abroad? VOICE.
Abroad they could speak freely in newspapers, procure weapons despite the Arms Act 1878, assassinate officers at Home in England, win diplomatic pressure by highlighting colonialism and raise awareness among NRIs. Savarkar sat in London, Hardayal reached the USA, Shyamji Krishna Varma ran the IHRS and India House (1905) before moving to Paris in 1907, and Madame Cama unfurled the first Indian flag at Stuttgart in August 1907.
→ With arms and money needed, the actions began.

1908: Barrah, Muzzafarpur and the bomb that missed.
The Dacca Anushilan looted the Zamindar of Barrah to fund the revolution, since dacoity targeted collaborators. At Muzzafarpur Prafulla Chaki and Khudiram Bose bombed Magistrate Kingsford's carriage, but he was not inside and two English women died. Chaki killed himself and Khudiram, 18, was executed and became an instant martyr, the opposite of what the British intended.
→ The bomb alarmed the British into a wider crackdown.

Alipore and the Andamans.
The Alipore Case brought mass arrests, including Aurobindo from Murari Pukur Road. C.R. Das defended him and B.C. Pal refused to testify, so he could not be convicted; he fled to Pondicherry and spiritualism. Barindra Kumar Ghosh and Ullaskar Dutta were sentenced to death, commuted to transportation for life in the Cellular Jail, which broke the early Jugantar.
→ Even a newspaper could now be sedition.

Tilak, Kesari and Jinnah.
In Kesari, Tilak condemned the Muzzafarpur violence but defended Chaki and Bose on the ground that sustained oppression breeds violence, in an article titled 'Arrival of Bomb'. He was charged with sedition, sentenced to six years and sent to Mandalay, Burma, with Jinnah, a young constitutional lawyer, conducting his defence.
→ Meanwhile Abhinav Bharat struck at home and abroad.

1909: Dhingra, Nasik and Savarkar's sentence.
In London in 1909 Madan Lal Dhingra killed Lt. Col. William Curzon-Wyllie, who was not Curzon 99-05 but worked with the Secretary of State for India. In Nasik, Anant Laxman Kanhere killed District Magistrate Jackson with a pistol that Savarkar had sent from London. In 1910 Savarkar was sentenced to transportation for life in the Cellular Jail.
→ Repressed, the phase still left its mark.

Pride, reform and Delhi.
The Revolutionaries gave back pride and dignity, and many felt the Morley-Minto Reforms of 1909 were a reform offered to buy peace. In 1911 the Partition was annulled and Delhi became the capital at the Durbar of December 1911, reducing Bengal's outsized influence; in 1912 Bihar and Orissa and a full province of Assam followed. Curzon 99-05 lost the map but won the plan.
→ One more bomb fell in the new capital, and its thrower's story did not end.

Rash Behari Bose to the INA.
In 1912 Rash Behari Bose threw a bomb from a balcony at Viceroy Hardinge 10-16 on an elephant in Chandni Chowk; Hardinge was wounded but survived. He led the Ghadar Movement (1913-15), escaped to Japan in 1915 and in 1942 convened the Tokyo and Bangkok conferences forming the IIL. Under it Captain Mohan Singh organised the first INA; after Mohan Singh's arrest Rash Behari Bose took over and, for old age, handed it to Netaji in 1943.

31.spine: The Census, the religion-wise reports and low Western education made Muslims a separate, deprived group that British Divide & Rule could favour; Sir Syed gave it the qaum idea, the Simla Deputation 1906 and the League asked for separate electorates, and the ICA 1909 granted them inside a council that had no real power, so the seed of Partition was sown.
beats:
The count that made a community.
Census 1881 was the first full census of British India (the 1872 attempt was incomplete). It found Muslims roughly 20% overall, a majority in Punjab and about 50% in Bengal, and it told a Bengal weaver and a Punjab landlord that they were one community with one set of interests. Government reports on education, employment and poverty by religion then showed Muslims behind Hindus.
→ But why were Muslims behind in the new jobs?

Behind in the new jobs.
Western education was expensive and most Bengal Muslims were poor ryots. The Ulamas resisted it for fear that Western literature would erode their community control, some wished to preserve Persian, and rich landlords saw little use for middle-class jobs. So Hindus, who took to Western education more readily, gained the new professions.
→ The rulers noticed, and had a plan.

The rulers' plan: appease and divide.
The teacher's frame: the goal of imperialism is economic loot and the tool is Divide & Rule, co-opting one side to loot the other. W.W. Hunter's Indian Musalmans (1871) argued the British should appease Muslims, job reservation followed in 1897, and the 1905 Partition made East Bengal and Assam a Muslim Majority Province. All three favoured the elite.
→ Meanwhile a Muslim leader gave the plan an idea.

Sir Syed's qaums.
The Mohammadan Association (1855) was pro-British and opposed the 1857 revolts. Sir Syed Ahmed Khan (1817-98) said India was a summation of qaums and that the Muslim qaum, the former rulers, needed Western education to claim special status; he built MAO College (1875) and the Mohammadan Educational Congress (1886) as a rival to the INC. He was not a full separatist, but he drew the blueprint of the Two Nation Theory.
→ And Hindu revivalism widened the wedge.

The Hindu wave and the Muslim withdrawal.
The Arya Samaj (1875) turned aggressive after Dayanand died in 1883, and the Cow Killing Riots of 1893 followed; the INC, bound by its 1886 rule of political issues only, did not condemn them, and Muslim participation fell. The Hindi-Urdu controversy (success for Hindi in 1900) tied Hindi to Hindus and Urdu to Muslims, and the Swadeshi movement's symbols (Bande Mataram, Kali worship, Ganpati and Shivaji festivals) deepened the alienation.
→ Then the Partition of 1905 sent the elite to the Viceroy.

Simla 1906.
Elite Muslims led by the Aga Khan met Viceroy Minto 05-10 at Shimla. They asked for no annulment of the Bengal Partition, reservation proportional to population in the ILC, PLCs and jobs, and separate electorates in future council reforms. Separate electorates are the hinge: once Muslims must elect Muslims, the Two Nation Theory is institutionally accepted.
→ An organisation followed within months.

The League is born.
The All India Muslim League was set up at Dacca in December 1906 to hold the British to the Simla promises, promote Muslim interests and promote Muslim loyalty. Its Green Book was written by Mohsin-ul-Mulk and Mohammed Ali Jauhar, provincial Leagues came in 1907-09, and the London branch (1908) under Ameer Ali influenced ICA 1909. The PCCs became mass instruments only in 1920, so the League had a 13-year head start.
→ Meanwhile the Viceroy's side had a reform track.

Two tracks: repression and reform.
Swadeshi (1905-11), the Extremists and Revolutionary Activities (from 1908) made India restless, so the British ran repression and reform together; Morley, a Liberal, was open to reform. Move 1 split the INC: Morley's 1906 Budget speech hinted at council reforms, the Moderates feared Extremist agitation would kill them, and the INC split at Surat in 1907. Move 2 divided Hindus and Muslims through separate electorates.
→ What did the Act actually give?

A bigger council, not a stronger one.
ICA 1909 made the ILC 69 members (9 + 60: 27 elected, 33 nominated) but kept an official majority, 37 against 32. It used the word 'election' for the first time, with proper indirect elections, gave the PLCs a non-official majority (mostly nominated), put S.P. Sinha in the VEC, and let members vote on Budget items, ask supplementary questions and pass non-binding resolutions. Morley stated there was no intent of responsible government, only Limited Self-Government.
→ And for the Muslims?

The separate electorate.
Muslims got separate electorates in the ILC, PLCs and local bodies: 8 of 27 elected ILC seats, about 30% against a population of about 20% (the INC's own 1889 Minority Clause had asked for 20%). They also voted in the general seats, had a lower income threshold and direct elections in Muslim seats. Joint electorates give a candidate of the People; separate ones give a candidate of a Group, for a Group, by a Group.
→ So how did the story end?

Failure and the long shadow.
ICA 1909 lasted only 10 years, the shortest of the council reforms (30, 17, 10, 16, 15). The Moderates wanted real power, the INC's goal since 1906 was Swaraj, Muslims got separate electorates and the legislatures were powerless, so it was a Benevolent Despotism. Minto 05-10 became the Father of Communal Electorate, and organised communal politics, never reversed, hardened until 1947.

34.spine: Pressure from WWI and the INM forced Britain to promise gradual responsible government (1917); the Act (1919) gave elected houses and Dyarchy but kept real power: the Centre stayed irresponsible, the Governor held the key subjects, and separate rolls divided voters, so the INM called it a half-step.
beats:
The war's slogan comes home (1914-18).
WWI is fought by Britain, France and the USA under the banner of democracy and self-determination, and Indians fight and die in large numbers. At home the pressure keeps building: Swadeshi 1905-08, Revolutionaries 1907-15, Ghadar 1913-15, Home Rule Leagues 1916-18 and the Lucknow Pact of 1916. Swaraj now has moral weight.
→ So Britain has to answer: what about democracy in India?

Montagu's promise (20 August 1917).
Edwin Montagu, Secretary of State, tells the House of Commons that British policy is the gradual development of self-governing institutions towards the progressive realisation of responsible government within the Empire. Gradual means step by step; progressive means every step toward the goal, with the timeline in British hands. Swaraj is no longer seditious.
→ But a promise needs a plan.

The tour and the Report (1917-18).
Montagu personally tours Indian provinces, an unusual step, and writes a joint report with Viceroy Chelmsford 16-21: the Montagu-Chelmsford Report of 1918. It is the blueprint; the Act is the law; together they are the Montford Reforms.
→ Parliament now turns the blueprint into law.

The Centre gets two houses (1919).
The Act creates a bicameral Legislature for British India for the first time: the CLA (~145, 3 years) and the CoS (~60, 5 years), with elected majorities and direct elections in CLA, CoS and PLCs (at least 70% directly elected in a PLC). Adjournment motions are allowed; the Gaya 'End or Mend' resolution of 1922 leads the INC into the 1923 elections.
→ But who may vote, and who rules?

Who may vote.
The franchise stays tied to income and property; there is no universal adult franchise, though the Lucknow Pact asked for one as broad as possible. Women are not enfranchised directly: PLCs may remove the sex disqualification, but under the same property bar, so under 1% qualify. The husband's-property rule comes only in 1935.
→ And the voters are divided as well.

Separate rolls made watertight.
Separate electorates for Muslims continue from 1909 but become watertight: Muslims can no longer vote in unreserved seats. The principle is extended to Sikhs, Anglo-Indians and Christians. Depressed Classes get nominated seats. The British seize on the Lucknow Pact's logic for Divide and Rule.
→ Yet the Centre still answers to no one.

Powers on paper, strings in hand.
Subjects are divided between Centre and Provinces for the first time, but with no lists, so the Centre can take any back; Land Revenue goes to Provinces, Customs and Income Tax to the Centre, and provincial budgets are separated. The VEC has no cap, by convention 3 Indians of 8. The Viceroy keeps veto, approval of rejected bills, ordinance for 6 months, restoring cuts and 75% non-votable budget items.
→ Taxation without representation continues.

Services and Princes.
The ICS exam is held in India alongside England (first in 1922); Section 96C creates the Public Service Commission (1926, Ross Barker); the ICS splits into All India and Central services; 33% Indians are promised gradually. The Narendra Mandal, recommended by the Report, is constituted by Royal Proclamation in 1921 as a purely advisory body for the Princes.
→ Now the provinces: the most debated feature.

Dyarchy: dual rule in the provinces.
Provincial subjects are split into Reserved (Police, Justice, Finance, Land Revenue, Irrigation, Control over Officials) under the Governor, unaccountable to the PLC, and Transferred (health, education, local government, agriculture) under elected ministers responsible to the PLC. The board compares it with ToA 1765 and the 1784 Act: Reserved is the old authority's, Transferred the new one's.
→ But ministers hold the soft half of the bargain.

Why Dyarchy failed.
Ministers have no money (Finance is Reserved) and no control over officials; the Governor can overrule them on any matter and take over Transferred subjects on failure of constitutional machinery. When they fail they lose public trust, as the British designed, delaying the demand for full responsible government.
→ So the INM judges the Act.

The verdict of the INM.
Six grounds: the division of subjects is not federal; Dyarchy mocks federalism; there is no universal adult franchise; no responsible government at the Centre and only partial in the provinces; seats go by importance not population; there is no effective self-government. Better than 1909's limited self-government, but far from Swaraj.

35.spine: Injustice, then a method, then a mass movement, then victory: an ejection and two Natal laws (injustice) lead to petitions (Phase 1), then to Satyagraha (the method) built on a code and two training farms, then to the 1913 turn (mass), and finally to the three-demand settlement of 1914 (victory).
beats:
A barrister, a ticket and a platform (1893).
Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi arrives in South Africa as a young barrister hired for a commercial case of a Memon Muslim merchant. At Pietermaritzburg station he is ejected from a first-class compartment solely for being Indian, despite a valid ticket. The humiliation on the cold platform becomes his political catalyst.
→ So he resolves to fight, not to endure.

The community asks him to stay.
He planned a short stay, but the Indian community was leaderless and had no educated advocate who understood both law and their grievances. He was the only person who could fight within the system, so he stays: a short visit becomes twenty-two years (1893 to 1915).
→ Soon two Natal laws give him his first fight.

Two Natal laws (1894-95).
The Franchise Amendment Bill 1894 would strip Indians of the vote on racial grounds: taxation without representation, like the American colonists of 1776. The Immigration Law Amendment Bill 1895 forces an indentured labourer, after his contract, to leave, re-indenture for two more years, or pay a poll tax of £3 a year.
→ Gandhiji answers within the law.

Petitions, prayers and the press (1896-1906).
He founds the Natal Indian Congress, modelled on the INC, and the newspaper Indian Opinion. His methods are petitions, prayers and public meetings: a Moderate in South Africa, like the INC Moderates at home.
→ But the government is unmoved by petitions.

Satyagraha is born (1906).
By 1906 he concludes that constitutional methods are not enough, and that the answer must be direct but non-violent. A true Satyagrahi is truthful, non-violent, fearless, ready to accept suffering and loving to the wrongdoer. In 1904 he had already founded Phoenix Settlement near Durban, inspired by Ruskin's Unto This Last.
→ Now a law arrives that tests the method.

The Black Act and the broken promise (1906-14).
The Asiatic Law Amendment Act 1906 forces every Indian in Transvaal to carry a Registration Certificate, on pain of fine, jail and deportation. The government offers to withdraw it if Indians register; Gandhiji registers first, and the promise is broken. He leads a bonfire of RCs and Jail Bharo through the Passive Resistance Association.
→ The government now closes the borders.

Caged within provinces (1907-08).
The Transvaal Immigration Restriction Act 1907 bars movement from Cape, Natal and Orange Free State into Transvaal. Indians cross illegally, refuse bail and hawk without licence to fill the jails; Gandhiji is jailed in 1908.
→ A long struggle needs a base.

Tolstoy Farm and Gokhale (1910-12).
In 1910 Tolstoy Farm near Johannesburg becomes the residential base for Satyagrahis and their families, part ashram and part training ground: Phoenix, then Tolstoy, then the Indian ashrams. In 1912 Gokhale visits, the government promises repeal and breaks the promise, and Gokhale advises focus on two demands: abolish the Poll Tax and the RC.
→ Then a court ruling lights the fuse.

1913: the movement goes mass.
The Poll Tax Campaign brings indentured labourers in. A Supreme Court judgement recognises only Christian marriages, so Hindu and Muslim wives are legally not wives. Indians cross into Transvaal illegally, Kasturba Gandhi is arrested, 2,000 workers march, and all workers strike.
→ Pressure now comes from India as well.

Gokhale tours India; Hardinge 10-16 speaks.
Gokhale travels across India building public opinion, and Viceroy Hardinge 10-16 publicly condemns the South African government: unprecedented pressure from within the British Empire. The South African government comes to the table.
→ So the talks end in a settlement.

Victory and return (1914-15).
The government concedes all three demands: the Poll Tax is abolished, the RC requirement is dropped and Indian marriages are validated. Gandhiji returns to India in January 1915 as a leader who had won, having learned that mass civil disobedience works. The laboratories of Natal and Transvaal would be deployed at Champaran, Kheda and Dandi.

36.spine: Ideology comes first: Gandhi's cultural nationalism and moral critique of the West give him a stateless, village-based ideal, and Satyagraha (rising tempo, control, S-CW-S, an undefined Swaraj) is the method that carries ordinary people towards it.
beats:
Why start with ideology.
Modern politics has goals, plans, a programme, leadership, voice and money, and the root of all of them is ideology. Gandhi is the Father of the Nation because he brought the masses (religions, castes, genders, regions, ethnicities) into a movement to establish a Nation State, though his was the maximum contribution, not the only one.
→ So where do we read his mind? In one book.

Hind Swaraj and a cultural nationalist.
Hind Swaraj (1909) was written on a ten-day sea voyage as a dialogue between a Reader and an Editor. Gandhi stood in the tradition of Dayanand's Arya Samaj (1875), Vivekananda's Ramakrishna Mission (1897) and Bankim, but he took it further: he dressed and spoke like the masses, used Ram Rajya, Sita and Draupadi, and used religion to mobilise.
→ Was he then against everything modern?

Not anti-modern, but moral.
Gandhi criticised Western modernity, built on industrial capitalism, the profit motive and the coercive State, not reason or science. Western civilisation was Godless, and Indians enslaved themselves when doctors, lawyers and railways became instruments of an alien system looting India. He called an act immoral (adharma), not merely illegal.
→ If the State is coercive, what should replace it?

A stateless ideal.
Gandhi's end-goal, like Marx's, was a stateless society, but through Enlightened Anarchism: every individual his own master, morality in place of law. He wanted direct democracy and Village Republics, with the Gram Sabha (Article 243) as the living legacy, and he accepted parliamentary democracy with a weak State only as a transition. Ambedkar replied that a strong State with constitutional law protects the oppressed.
→ And the economy under such a polity?

The village economy.
He wanted a village-based, self-sufficient economy modelled on ancient India, rejecting the Industrial Revolution that uproots villagers into factories. Almost everyone else was pro-IR; Mao turned against it in 1958 for a different reason. Land should come by voluntary gift: Vinoba Bhave's Bhoodan (Telangana, 1951).
→ But what of capitalists?

Trustee and arbitrator.
He did not want capitalists abolished: under Trusteeship the owner holds the enterprise for the welfare of workers and community, so ownership stays and purpose changes. Disputes go to Arbitration: reveal the truth of both sides, then a middle path. The same method united Moderates and Extremists in 1920.
→ The method for politics is Satyagraha.

Satyagraha and its two principles.
Satyagraha, truth-force, is Non-Cooperation, Civil Disobedience, Constructive Work, Non-Violence and Morality, with a Satyagrahi who is truthful, fearless, non-violent, ready to suffer and morally superior. He would not gain from the evil doer's weakness (he backed Britain in both wars) and hated breach of promise (Montague 1917, Rowlatt Act 1919).
→ How did he run a movement?

Tempo, control, truce.
He began with lighter forms and escalated; he insisted on a controlled mass movement and withdrew the NCM after Chauri Chaura (22 policemen, February 1922). The truce was never idle: Constructive Work filled it, so S-T-S was really S-CW-S, a lineage from the Ramakrishna Mission to Sabarmati.
→ Why did it work?

Why it worked, and an undefined Swaraj.
Satyagraha united Moderates and Extremists (Surat 1907), let common men and women join, and made repression a propaganda disaster. Gandhi never defined Swaraj, so a peasant, worker, woman and nationalist could each find their own meaning; Jinnah and Tagore were uneasy about this.
→ Where did the ideas come from?

Five influences.
Ruskin's Unto This Last (1862) gave Sarvodaya and the Phoenix Settlement (1904); Tolstoy (1894) gave non-resistance and the Tolstoy Farm (1910); Thoreau (1849) gave civil disobedience; the Gita gave Nishkama Karma; the Sermon on the Mount gave love of the enemy. The mix made Satyagraha a universal method.
→ And the record of his life?

Fasts, writings, jails.
Nine fasts run from Ahmedabad 1918 to Delhi 1948, including the Epic Fast 1932 (Poona Pact, 71 to 147) and the 1933 temple-entry fast. His papers run from Indian Opinion 1903 and Hind Swaraj 1909 to Young India 1919 and Harijan 1933. Ten arrests run from 1906 to Quit India 1942, with the 1922 trial as the only major trial in India.

37.spine: MG built a method in three small pilots, learnt from the Rowlatt failure that a mass movement needs control, and used the Khilafat anger to make the INC a mass organisation (NCM 1920-22). When Chauri Chaura broke that movement, the INC split over council entry but stayed whole, and Constructive Work kept it alive until the Simon Commission.
beats:
The cake is cut (1915-18).
MG arrives in January 1915, tours India on Gokhale's advice and stays out of the INM during WWI because he will not use the enemy's weakness. After two years he picks three local fights: Champaran (civil disobedience against indigo planters, Tinkathia abolished, Act 1918), Ahmedabad (fast and arbitration: 50, 35, 27.5) and Kheda (first non-cooperation, law on the ryots' side, Patel joins).
→ But a pilot is not a nation: the next call is for all Indians.

The Rowlatt promise broken (1919).
In February 1919 the ILC passes the Rowlatt Act over the opposition of every Indian member: it carries the Defence of India Act 1915 into peacetime, with WWI misery and the fear of communism behind it. MG, who backed the war hoping for self-government and who hates a breach of promise (Montague Statement 1917, MC Report 1918), calls a nationwide non-violent strike.
→ But a strike without a driver runs wild.

The driverless truck (April 1919).
Leaders are arrested, violence spreads in Punjab, O'Dwyer empowers and Dyer applies martial law. On 13 April at Jallianwala Bagh Dyer's troops fire for 10 minutes: 379 dead by the official count, 1,500 by the INC's. The Hunter Committee lets Dyer off; MG withdraws the movement with two lessons: control the INC, and train people in non-violence.
→ Anger over Punjab was about to meet anger over Turkey.

Khilafat joins the cause (1919-20).
The Treaty of Sèvres (1920) strips the Khalifa, and the Ali Brothers set up the Khilafat Committee in March 1919. At Allahabad in June 1920 the movement is launched with boycott and a no-tax call. MG sees a once-in-a-hundred-years chance for Hindu-Muslim unity and brings the INC along, even C.R. Das; Tilak, B.C. Pal, Besant, Jinnah and the ML stay out or oppose.
→ So the INC meets, first in Calcutta, then in Nagpur.

Calcutta and Nagpur (September and December 1920).
At Calcutta (Lajpat Rai presiding) the INC launches the NCM with three goals: Swaraj, Punjab wrongs, Khilafat wrongs; Swaraj is promised in one year, with a CDM after. At Nagpur (C. Vijayaraghavachariar presiding) MG takes over: the method changes from the pen to Satyagraha, and a CWC of 15, linguistic PCCs, a 4-anna fee, Hindi and Princely States' members make the INC a body of the masses.
→ Now the movement has to run.

The movement runs (1920-22).
The Tilak Swaraj Fund raises Rs 1 crore; the Reading talks fail because MG refuses to be used for Divide and Rule. Peasants (Awadh Kisan Sabha), workers, tribals and new regions join, British imports halve and only 5% vote in 1920. When the Prince of Wales visits in November 1921 the strikes turn violent, and MG confines the CDM to Bardoli.
→ But the next violence he could not contain.

Chauri Chaura breaks it (February 1922).
Police fire on satyagrahis, killing 3; the crowd burns 22 policemen alive. MG withdraws the NCM, suspends the Bardoli CDM and passes the Bardoli Resolution: Constructive Work must precede any movement. 170 are sentenced to death; Malaviya defends them and 19 are hanged. The Rowlatt Act is repealed in March 1922, but Khilafat ends in 1924 when Turkey abolishes the Khalifate.
→ With no mass movement to run, the INC asks what to do next.

Mend it or boycott it (1922-24).
All agree there is no CDM yet. The Swarajists (Das, Motilal Nehru) want to end or mend the councils; the No-Changers (Patel, Rajendra Prasad, Rajaji) want boycott and Constructive Work. The Gaya resolution fails, the Swarajists form the Congress Khilafat Swaraj Party and contest the 1923 elections. MG opposes but compromises, and at Belgaum 1924 the Gandhi-Das Pact makes them the INC's parliamentary wing.
→ But the party in the councils soon came apart.

The Swarajists in the councils (1923-26).
They demand a new constitution, civil liberty and help for Indian industry, and use the adjournment motion. But they have no street support, Das dies in 1925, the ML is lost over Bengal's Muslim tenants, and the 1924 riots split off the Responsivists. The party loses heavily in 1926 and the INC leaves the councils.
→ Meanwhile the quiet work went on.

The quiet machine (1922-27).
Constructive Work keeps cadres busy, unites castes and communities, deepens the INC's rural hold, builds the masses' confidence and sets up national schools and panchayat courts. The Passive Phase is 'anything but passive'; the Simon Commission of 1927 rekindles the INM.

32.spine: Punjabi NRIs in the US and Canada were shut out by racist rules, so they turned to revolution, inspired by the Swadeshi revolutionaries. They built a press campaign abroad (Free Hindustan, Swadesh Sevak, The Ghadr) and a party in San Francisco in 1913, guided by Lala Hardayal's anarchist ideas. The Komagata Maru humiliation and the outbreak of WWI gave them the trigger and the opening, so they planned three plots with German help: a Punjab mutiny, a Pacific arms shipment, and a Christmas Day rising. British intelligence and the Defence of India Act crushed all three, but the martyrs, from Bagha Jatin to Kartar Singh Sarabha, inspired the next generation.
beats:
Doors close on Indian emigrants.
Many Punjabis went to Canada and the US for land and jobs; many were ex-soldiers of the British Empire. Canada allowed entry only after a direct journey from India (rule since 1908), and the US barred Indians from buying land. Britain feared that they would pick up ideas of liberty, democracy and a republic.
→ So anger at racism had nowhere to go but politics.

Swadeshi's revolutionaries light the way.
The revolutionary strand of the Swadeshi Movement (1905-11) inspired them, above all the Delhi Conspiracy Case 1912, which targeted Viceroy Hardinge 10-16. Revolutionary action was seen as the inspiration to copy.
→ So they began with the weapon nearest to hand: the press.

A press campaign abroad.
Tarak Nath Das wrote Free Hindustan (1907) in Vancouver; G.D. Kumar wrote Swadesh Sevak (1909) in Canada and asked Indian troops to revolt. In 1913 the Ghadar Party was set up in San Francisco with Sohan Singh Bhakna as 1st President and its HQ called Yugantar Ashram. Lala Hardayal launched the weekly The Ghadr.
→ But anger needed an idea, and Hardayal supplied one.

Bakunin and the deed.
Hardayal founded the Bakunin Institute in 1912, a monastery of anarchism. Bakunin taught that the State is an instrument of oppression and must be destroyed; propaganda of the deed says that acts ignite where words only educate. Hardayal married this to the grievances of Punjabi labourers, peasants and ex-soldiers.
→ Now a trigger was needed, and it came by sea.

Komagata Maru, 1914.
Baba Gurdit Singh chartered the Japanese ship Komagata Maru from Hong Kong to challenge Canada's direct-journey rule. 376 passengers, mostly Punjabi Sikhs, reached Vancouver in May 1914 and were refused landing. Forced out in July, the ship reached Budge Budge in September, where police firing killed about 20.
→ And just then the world went to war.

WWI opens the window.
WWI began on 28 July 1914, and Britain was stretched on many fronts with fewer British Indian Army units in India. The returning Komagata Maru passengers were treated as dangerous enemy operatives under wartime conditions.
→ So the revolutionaries went looking for guns.

The Rodda heist.
In August 1914 Bengal revolutionaries, helped by insider Shrish Chandra Mitra and Haridas Datta, diverted one of seven bullock carts of German arms from the Calcutta Customs House. The haul was 50 Mauser C96 pistols and 46,000 rounds, and not a shot was fired.
→ Now the guns met the grand plan.

Three plots of the Hindu-German Conspiracy.
Plot 1: RB Bose's Punjab mutiny set for 21 Feb 1915. Plot 2: the Pacific arms plot (Apr to Jul 1915), 30,000 rifles via the SS Maverick. Plot 3: the Christmas Day plot of Dec 1915 in Bengal under Bagha Jatin.
→ But the British were already listening.

Intelligence crushes the plots.
The Punjab mutiny was pre-empted, the arms ships were intercepted, and British intelligence cracked the Christmas plot's codes. Bagha Jatin and four comrades were cornered at Balasore in Sept 1915 and fought about 75 minutes with the Rodda Mausers until the ammunition ran out.
→ So the movement lost the fight but not the memory.

Repression and legacy.
The Defence of India Act 1915 and the First Lahore Conspiracy Case destroyed the organisation in India. Kartar Singh Sarabha was hanged at 19 in Nov 1915, and the survivors carried on in Kisan, Communist and Akali movements.

33.spine: In 1914 the national movement was dull: Extremists crushed, Moderates spent. Tilak and Annie Besant, working outside INC, built two Home Rule Leagues in 1916 to carry educative propaganda from towns to villages. Besant's arrest in 1917 backfired, united Moderates and Extremists and made her INC President, but the Leagues could not become a mass movement and faded, leaving momentum for Gandhi. Alongside, the Lucknow Pact of 1916 joined INC and the Muslim League on joint demands, after a decade of British actions had alienated Indian Muslims.
beats:
A dull phase, 1914.
Tilak came back from Mandalay in 1914 after six years in prison. Extremists and Revolutionaries had been crushed. Moderates had become irrelevant because their method had failed in 1892 and again with ICA 1909. Self-Government, INC's goal since the 1906 Calcutta Session, had not arrived.
→ So the movement needed new energy and an organisation that could carry it.

Tilak's calculated position.
Tilak wanted the Extremists back inside INC, because outside it the British could repress them easily. He declared four things: Swaraj means self-rule within the Empire, violence has hurt the INM, Indians should support the war, and he is loyal to the Crown. The British and the Moderates were pleased.
→ But a united organisation also needed an ally with a base in the South.

Besant joins and the re-entry fight.
Annie Besant, an Irish woman inspired by Home Rule in Ireland and head of the Theosophical Society at Madras, joined INC in 1914. She pushed for Extremist re-entry but Pherozshah Mehta blocked it. The 1915 Bombay Session decided to allow re-entry after Mehta died; the actual re-entry came at Lucknow 1916.
→ But INC still would not back Home Rule Leagues, fearing propaganda could slide into violence.

Two Leagues, one movement.
Tilak set up the Indian Home Rule League in April 1916, with 6 branches and headquarters at Poona. Besant set up the All India Home Rule League in September 1916, with 200 branches and headquarters at Madras. They cooperated but did not merge, to prevent friction among followers.
→ So the two spread the same message in separate zones.

The message: Swaraj and more.
Tilak's rallying cry was 'Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it'. He also demanded vernacular education, linguistic provinces and an end to untouchability. He framed the fight as a clash of national interests, not of religions, so Jinnah, Besant and Tilak could work together.
→ Now the message needed carriers: newspapers.

The press and the Commonwealth idea.
Tilak ran Kesari (Marathi) and Maharatta (English). Besant ran New India and Commonweal, from which came the word Commonwealth. She later wrote the Commonwealth of India Bill (1925) for Dominion Status.
→ But the war was straining the masses, and the British grew anxious.

The arrest that backfired, 1917.
WWI brought inflation and anger among the masses. Besant was arrested and interned in 1917. Moderates now joined the Leagues, Sir S. Subramania Iyer gave up his knighthood, and Gandhi began a signature campaign. Besant was released and made INC President at the 1917 Calcutta Session.
→ But the Montague Statement and a quarrel over Passive Resistance split the camp.

Montague and the split.
The Montague Statement of 1917 was a Divide and Rule tactic: Swaraj would come gradually. Extremists proposed Passive Resistance, meaning boycott plus deliberate law-breaking. Moderates opposed it and Besant, a constitutionalist afraid of anarchy, sided with them.
→ So the Leagues stalled while the mood outside was rising.

Fading, but not for nothing.
By 1917-18 the British had repressed the Leagues and they became defunct. They failed to build a mass movement, and Lower Castes in Madras stayed away. Yet 60,000 members joined, new regions woke up, Nehru joined, and a network was left for later phases.
→ Meanwhile a parallel deal had been struck between INC and the League.

The Lucknow Pact, 1916.
INC and ML1906 gave joint demands to the British for the first time: separate electorates, an elected majority, 50% Indians in the VEC, broad direct franchise, and early self-government. The League gave up general seats; INC accepted separate electorates and a fixed quota. GOI Act 1919 later hardened this into watertight rolls.
→ Why had the League moved so far from its loyal start?

The Decade of Alienation.
Bengal Partition annulled (1911), Italy took Libya (1911), the first Balkan War (1912) and WW1 (1914) pushed the League towards INC. Then the Balfour Declaration (1917) and the Treaty of Sevres (1920) turned the anger into the Khilafat Movement.

38.spine: After the Home Rule Leagues and the Non-Cooperation Movement taught villagers the language of rights and the tools of protest, peasants in Awadh, Malabar, Gujarat and Punjab organised around their own grievances: cesses, eviction, forced labour, rent and revenue. These movements were boosted by the INM but never owned by the INC. Those that dropped non-violence or lost their leaders (Eka, Mapilla) were crushed or derailed, while Borsad and Bardoli, run on Gandhian lines by Patel, won concrete outcomes. The Akalis fought a religious-reform battle that also politicised Punjab's peasantry.
beats:
The countryside is educated.
The Home Rule Leagues (1916-18) and NCM (1920-22) taught urban workers and rural ryots to take part in politics. Peasants learnt by doing and saw the use of satyagraha, boycott, civil disobedience and social boycott. This gave them a **vocabulary of protest** for their own fights.
→ So peasants began organising, but they had real grievances of their own.

Awadh peasants are squeezed.
Big landlords (zamindars and taluqdars) levied illegal **abwabs and nazrana**, evicted at will (**bedakhli**), and forced **hari and begar**. WWI inflation raised prices while rents and cesses did not fall.
→ So they set up their own Sabhas.

Kisan Sabha 1918 and Awadh Kisan Sabha 1920.
The **UP Kisan Sabha** was set up in Feb 1918 by Mishra and Dwivedi with Malaviya as senior patron. Malaviya was a Moderate and opposed the Non-Cooperation Movement, so **Baba Ramchandra**, with Nehru's support, founded the **Awadh Kisan Sabha** in 1920 for extra-constitutional struggle.
→ But the movement turned violent in 1921.

Repression plus a concession.
In 1921 the British used the **Seditious Meetings Act (1911)** to crush the agitation. They also passed the **Awadh Rent Amendment Act (1921)**, which met some rent grievances and took the sting out of it.
→ Meanwhile a parallel Awadh movement rose under a new leader.

Eka 1921: a lower-caste leader.
The **Eka Movement** had the same grievances plus **thikedars** (rent collectors) and the same methods. **Madari Pasi**, from the lower castes, led it. It did not hold to non-violence, so the British crushed it on law-and-order grounds by 1922.
→ But Awadh was not the only region in revolt.

Malabar 1921: Mapilla revolt.
Muslim tenants, the **Mapillas**, were part of Khilafat and angry with Hindu **Jenmies** over rents and eviction. INC joined at first, but arrests of INC leaders left the revolt without guidance. It turned violent and communal, and the British declared **martial law**.
→ Then NCM itself was withdrawn, and the next fight was fought on pure Gandhian lines.

Borsad 1922-24: dual tyranny.
After NCM was withdrawn in 1922, **Patel** led Borsad against dacoits, police collusion and an additional police tax. Villagers refused the tax non-violently and **volunteer corps** warned them of police confiscation. The Governor of Bombay ordered an inquiry and withdrew the tax.
→ Patel's organising skill was now proven, and Bardoli would test it at scale.

Bardoli 1928: the model.
Bardoli had Kaliparaj and Ujaliparaj, the Hali system and a **30% revenue rise** based on a miscalculation. Gandhi did constructive work from 1927, Patel led from 1928, Bombay legislators resigned, and Gandhi arrived. A tribunal cut the rise to **6.03%**, and the women of Bardoli called Patel **Sardar**.
→ Meanwhile in Punjab a religious fight was becoming a peasant and national one.

Punjab: Akalis versus Mahants.
Udasi **Mahants**, enriched by Ranjit Singh RS01-39's land grants, controlled Gurudwaras and backed the British. They honoured **General Dyer** after Jallianwala Bagh, and the outrage launched the **Akali Movement (1920-25)**. Nankana, the Keys Affair and Guru Ka Bagh followed.
→ The British finally gave way because they feared the Army.

Outcome and lesson.
The British passed the **Gurudwara Reform Act, 1925**, and the elected **SGPC** took all Gurudwaras. Gandhi had already withdrawn support over the Nabha issue. The chapter's lesson is that the INM gave peasants consciousness and language, and the peasants gave the INM its mass character.

39.spine: NCM was withdrawn in 1922 and released revolutionaries, disliking both council-entry and constructive work, went back to arms. This time the Russian Revolution of 1917 had given them socialism, so HRA 1924 became HSRA 1928 and a fight against class oppression joined the fight against the British. Kakori, the Lahore Conspiracy, the bomb in the CLA and Chittagong followed, ending in hangings by 1934. The movement was crushed, but it left a secular, ideological, thinking revolutionary tradition.
beats:
Crushed, then released.
In World War I the **Defence of India Act 1915** was used to jail many revolutionaries. The **1920 amnesty** let them out. They joined Gandhiji's **NCM 1920-22** with enthusiasm, leaving arms behind.
→ But NCM was suddenly withdrawn.

Chauri Chaura breaks the hope.
In **February 1922** NCM was withdrawn after Chauri Chaura. The revolutionaries were deeply disappointed. They had no interest in the **Swarajists** (Pro-Changers) or the **No-Changers'** Constructive Work.
→ So they went back to what they knew, but with new ideas.

A new idea arrives.
The **Russian Revolution of 1917** spread communist thought. They now wanted to end **class oppression** as well as colonial oppression. Mass poverty under colonial rule made **socialism** attractive, and they believed non-violence had failed.
→ So they built a new organisation.

HRA 1924 is set up.
**Ram Prasad Bismil, Ashfaqullah Khan, Jogesh Chatterjee, Chandrashekhar Azad and Sachin Sanyal** founded HRA in 1924. The goal was armed revolution for a **United States of India** with universal adult franchise.
→ But arms cost money.

Kakori 1925.
HRA looted cash from a train in the **Kakori Robbery case, 1925**. Many were arrested. **Bismil and Ashfaqullah were hanged**. Azad escaped. With its leaders gone, HRA went inactive.
→ But Azad and a young Punjab revolutionary revived it.

HSRA 1928 and the Lahore Conspiracy.
**Azad and Bhagat Singh** revived HRA as **HSRA 1928**, adding 'Socialist'. Lala Lajpat Rai died of lathi injuries in November 1928. Bhagat Singh meant to kill **James Scott** but killed **John Saunders** by mistaken identity.
→ So they turned from killing to making a statement.

Bomb in the CLA, 1929.
The CLA was discussing the **Public Safety Bill** and **Trade Disputes Bill**, aimed at the working class and communists. **Bhagat Singh and B.K. Dutt** threw a harmless bomb with leaflets to 'make the deaf hear' and courted arrest. The trial became their platform.
→ Meanwhile, in Bengal, a different story was running.

Bengal after C.R. Das.
Bengal revolutionaries backed Swarajist leader **C.R. Das**, so the British repressed Swarajists too. After Das died in **1925**, Bengal Congress split between **S.C. Bose (Yugantar)** and **J.M. Sen Gupta (Anushilan Samiti)**. **Gopinath Saha's** failed attempt on the Police Commissioner brought Bose's arrest.
→ Then East Bengal opened its own front.

Chittagong 1930-33.
During CDM 1930-34, **Surya Sen**, a school teacher, set up the **IRA** and raided the Chittagong Armory. They declared a **Provisional Revolutionary Government**, cut communications and went into the hills. Women, schoolgirls and Muslims fought and died.
→ But the state hit back hard.

The end of the phase.
Azad died at Alfred Park on **27 February 1931**. Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev and Rajguru were hanged on **23 March 1931**. The Chittagong group was crushed by **1933** and Surya Sen was hanged in **1934**. The armed phase after NCM ended, though it inspired the nation.

40.spine: In 1927 Britain sent an all-British Simon Commission to review the 1919 reforms, two years early. Indians were insulted, and Birkenhead dared them to write their own constitution. INC set up the All Party Conference and produced the Nehru Report (Aug 1928), but the Muslim League's Delhi Proposals, Calcutta Amendments and 14 Points showed that consensus had broken. Britain answered with the Butler Committee for the Princely States and Irwin's vague Diwali Declaration. INC replied with the Delhi Manifesto, which set the conditions for the Round Table Conference.
beats:
The review arrives early.
The Montague Statement of 1917 promised gradual Swaraj, and GOI Act 1919 was the first step with a review after 10 years. In 1927 the Conservative Government in Britain appointed the Simon Commission two years early. It did not want to leave a sensitive question to the next government after the coming elections.
→ But the Commission had seven members and not one of them was Indian.

Not a single Indian.
All seven were British MPs under Sir John Simon, and Clement Attlee was one of them. Swaraj includes a say for Indians in their own constitution. GOI Acts and Councils Acts were British legal instruments, so excluding Indians even from the review was an insult.
→ So INC rejected it, and Birkenhead dared Indians to do better.

Birkenhead's dare.
The Secretary of State for India, Birkenhead, challenged Indians in the British Parliament to draft a constitution themselves. He believed their internal differences would stop them from acting together. This taunt gave INC its task.
→ So the Madras session of 1927 rejected Simon and set up an All Party Conference.

Madras 1927 and the streets.
INC rejected the Commission and decided on an APC to draft the Principles of a Constitution. When Simon came again in October 1928, protests swept the country. In Lahore Lala Lajpat Rai was lathi-charged by SP James Scott and died in November 1928.
→ Meanwhile the Muslim League made its own offer before the APC could finish.

Four Delhi Proposals.
In December 1927 ML1906 sent Four Delhi Proposals to Motilal Nehru: three new Muslim Majority Provinces, one-third at the Centre, reservation in Punjab and Bengal, and joint electorates if all that was met. INC first accepted them, but the APC later rejected them.
→ So the Nehru Report had to settle the communal question itself.

The Nehru Report.
The APC under M.A. Ansari formed a Motilal Nehru committee in May 1928, and the Report came in August 1928. It asked for Dominion Status, a Union of India with the Princely States, a unitary British India, 19 Fundamental Rights and no separate electorates. It conceded some Muslim demands and refused others.
→ But ML1906 wanted more and raised its demands at Calcutta.

Calcutta, December 1928.
Jinnah proposed Three Amendments in the APC: one-third at the Centre, Punjab-Bengal reservation until UAF, and residuary powers to Provinces. All were rejected. INC then approved the Nehru Report. Bose's Purna Swaraj resolution failed, so INC set a one-year deadline for Dominion Status and passed a Constructive Work resolution.
→ So Jinnah turned the rejected demands into one master list.

The 14 Points.
In March 1929 Jinnah issued the 14 Points, a summary of every communal demand ever made by any Muslim organisation. It became the blueprint of all later ML1906 politics. Birkenhead won his challenge: Indians could not agree.
→ Meanwhile Britain was dealing with the Princely States separately.

Butler Committee and AISPC.
The Butler Committee, appointed in 1927, reported in 1929 that Paramountcy over the States was re-affirmed and that States should not be moved into a Union of India without their consent. The AISPC, set up in 1927, told it that the people, not the Princes, represent the States. This is the 1927 root of the Patel challenge of 1947.
→ Now Viceroy Irwin spoke on behalf of Britain.

Diwali Declaration.
On 31 October 1929 Irwin said Dominion Status is implicit in the Montague Statement and that the intent is to give it at a future date, with a Round Table Conference in London. It had no decision, no timeline and the wrong forum, since it proposed an RTC in London and no Constituent Assembly in India.
→ So INC answered with conditions.

Delhi Manifesto.
In November 1929 INC leaders set three conditions for joining the RTC. It must act as a Constituent Assembly for Dominion Status, a majority of Indian delegates must be from INC, and there must be amnesty in the Bomb in CLA case and the Meerut Conspiracy Case. The next chapter picks up from here.

41.spine: Irwin 26-31 turned down the Delhi Manifesto, so INC adopted Purna Swaraj at Lahore and MG offered eleven demands as a last chance. When they were refused, he broke the salt law at Dandi and the whole country followed, from Vedaranniyam to Peshawar. Violence and exhaustion forced a truce in the Delhi Pact, but the 2nd RTC deadlocked on separate electorates, the Communal Award and the Poona Pact followed, and MG turned the 2nd phase into a campaign against untouchability. CDM ended in 1934 with little to show on the street, yet INC cashed in the political capital in the 1937 elections.
beats:
Delhi Manifesto turned down.
The Manifesto asked for an RTC acting as a Constituent Assembly with dominion status, an INC majority among Indian delegates and amnesty in the Bomb in CLA and Meerut cases. Irwin 26-31 refused all of it.
→ So INC had to answer at its next session.

Lahore chooses Purna Swaraj.
At Lahore (Dec 1929, Nehru presiding) INC made complete independence its goal, fixed 26 January 1930 as the pledge day, rejected the RTC, quit the legislatures and empowered the AICC to launch CDM.
→ But MG did not launch it at once.

Why MG waited.
Muslim leaders of INC wanted an INC-ML pact like Lucknow, capitalists feared the Great Depression, ML1906 spoke of Hindu raj, other parties envied INC's popularity and CPI1925 called INC bourgeois.
→ So MG offered an olive branch first.

Eleven demands.
In January 1930 MG listed four middle-class, two peasant and five general demands, from the 1s 4d rupee to abolition of the salt tax. If the British met them, INC would not need to fight.
→ But Irwin 26-31 rejected all eleven.

Salt as the weapon.
Salt was used by everyone, was neither a Hindu nor a bourgeois issue and carried little risk of immediate repression. MG began at Dandi from Sabarmati Ashram in March 1930 and the Salt Satyagraha spread across regions.
→ Now the movement was all-India.

Regions join in.
Rajaji marched to Vedaranniyam, Kelappan to Poyannur, Inchudi became the Second Dandi, Ankola the Bardoli of Karnataka, and Andhra built Sibirams. INC's organisation since 1920 made this possible.
→ But the Frontier had its own story.

Peshawar and the Garhwalis.
Ghaffar Khan's Red Shirts met machine guns at Qissa Khwani Bazaar on 23 April 1930. The Royal Garhwal Rifles refused to fire on the unarmed Muslim crowd.
→ So the movement kept growing, and so did the state's anger.

Dharasana and arrest.
MG warned the British about the Dharasana raid and was arrested in May 1930. Naidu, Manilal and Imam Saheb led 2,500 volunteers against 400 police; Webb Miller's report shocked the world.
→ But violence at Chittagong, Peshawar and Sholapur was rising.

Truce and Karachi.
The Delhi Pact of 5 March 1931 suspended CDM and brought INC to the 2nd RTC. Bhagat Singh was hanged on 23 March, and Karachi approved the Pact amid black flags, with rights and an economic programme.
→ But London produced no settlement.

Deadlock and Award.
The 2nd RTC failed on separate electorates and MG resumed CDM. INC was banned in January 1932 and the Communal Award of August 1932 extended separate electorates to the Depressed Classes.
→ So MG fasted, and the Poona Pact followed.

Pact and Harijans.
The Poona Pact (24 Sept 1932) replaced separate electorates with reserved seats raised from 71 to 147. MG's 2nd phase turned to anti-untouchability, with the Harijan Sevak Sangh, Fund and magazine. CDM ended in 1934; INC won big in 1937.

42.spine: The British did not give GOI 1935 out of generosity. Linlithgow36-43 called it the best way to maintain control, and it grew out of pressure from below (revolutionaries, Anti-Simon, Civil Disobedience, the Great Depression) and consultations above (Simon, three Round Tables). Its federal Centre needed 50% of the Princes to sign, so it never started and the 1919 machinery kept ruling the Centre. Only the provincial half worked from 1937: dyarchy ended and Congress took 8 of 11 provinces for 28 months, which gave it experience, energised the Princely States and tested the British plan to split INC.
beats:
A candid Viceroy.
Linlithgow36-43 implemented the Act in 1937 and admitted it was the best way to maintain control over India. It runs to 321 sections. Nothing in it was a gift of self-government.
→ But why did Britain bother at all?

Pressure from below.
Revolutionaries (HRA1924, HSRA1928, Chittagong Armory Raid 1930-33), the masses (Anti-Simon 1928, Civil Disobedience 1930-34) and the Great Depression of 1929 kept Britain nervous. The board calls reform a safety valve on a pressure cooker of Indians.
→ So Britain also needed a legal route.

Consultations above.
The Simon Commission (1927, no Indian member) reported in June 1930: provincial autonomy, nothing at the Centre, more franchise, separate electorates, Burma out. Three Round Table Conferences followed (1930, 1931, 1932).
→ But Indian demands were rejected, so the Act was against self-government.

The Act of August 1935.
The Act has two halves. The Centre half proposed a Federation of British India and Princely States with dyarchy at the Centre. The provincial half proposed autonomy with a still-powerful Governor.
→ So what stopped the Centre half?

The Princes say no.
The Federation needed at least 50% of Princes to sign the Instrument of Accession (Section 6). They feared two bosses, losing financial autonomy, low representation and democracy. The threshold was never met.
→ Now the Centre stayed on the old Act.

The Centre stays on paper.
The Act of 1919 kept governing the Centre. The Federal Court was set up in 1937, but the Federal Assembly, Council of States and dyarchy at the Centre never began. The Viceroy kept 80% of the Budget non-votable.
→ But the provinces were different.

Provinces go live in 1937.
Dyarchy ended and all provincial subjects became transferred. A Premier and Council of Ministers became responsible to the Assembly. Orissa, Bihar and Sindh became provinces (1936) and Burma was separated (1937).
→ But the Governor was still powerful.

A strong Governor.
Forty percent of the provincial Budget was non-votable. The Governor could summon the Assembly, veto bills, issue ordinances, run tribal areas, protect minorities and British interests, and take over the government indefinitely.
→ Now who benefits from this design?

The British plan.
Hold the Centre, hand over provinces and keep INC busy governing. Provincial leaders would become autonomous power centres, so Divide and Rule would be applied to INC itself. INC rejected the Act and demanded a Constituent Assembly by Universal Adult Franchise.
→ So INC still decided to contest.

Congress ministries 1937-39.
INC contested for the same reason as the Pro-Changers of 1923: occupy the space and do Constructive Work, now with executive power. It won a majority in 6 provinces and formed ministries in 8 of 11. Punjab went to the Unionists and Sindh to the Sind United Party.
→ So what did 28 months change?

The impact.
Morale of cadre, peasants and workers rose, INC gained governance experience, and Praja Mandals or State People's Congresses spread in Princely States. The Chamber of Princes (1921) was the British answer from above; the ministries energised the answer from below.

43.spine: In September 1939 Britain dragged India into the war without asking, and the Congress answered by pulling its ministries out. Britain tried to buy cooperation back with the August Offer (1940) and the Cripps Mission (1942), but each offer either kept power in the Viceroy's hands or planted seeds of partition. The INC wanted Purna Swaraj and a united India; the Muslim League wanted a veto, then Pakistan; Britain wanted to prevent decolonisation. Every offer failed on one of the four questions, and the failure of Cripps pushed the INM towards Quit India.
beats:
A weak villain, a strong hero.
Teacher opens the chapter with one question: why did India become independent? The INM was the strong hero. The colonial power was the weak villain, bled by three huge economic shocks in 31 years (WWI, the Great Depression, WWII) and shaken on the military front by the INA and the Naval Mutiny.
→ So to read 1939 to 1947 properly, you need to see who is playing and what they are fighting over.

Three players, four questions.
The British, the INC and the ML1906 bargain over four things: transfer of executive power (ToP), the kind of Swaraj, who drafts the Constitution (COI), and Unity (565 Princely States, Pakistan). Britain's best case is no ToP, no Dominion, COI by Britain and a united Indian colony. INC wants ToP to one centre, Purna Swaraj, one COI by Indians. ML wants two centres and two COIs.
→ But first Britain made a move nobody asked it to make.

September 1939: India is taken to war.
Britain declared war on Germany and declared India a belligerent. Viceroy Linlithgow36-43 did not consult a single Indian leader. This act of colonial arrogance set the tone for six years.
→ So the INC had to decide what to do, and it did not speak in one voice.

Three views inside the INC.
MG: unconditional support, because Britain was the victim of Axis aggression. Bose: Britain's weakness is India's chance, start a Civil Disobedience Movement now. Nehru: no cooperation without Purna Swaraj, but no mass movement either. Most leaders privately wanted an Allied win, since the Axis were dictatorships and India might become a Japanese colony.
→ But the INC did not take any one pole; it named a price for cooperation.

The INC's price and Linlithgow36-43's no.
The INC asked for responsible government at the Centre, a post-war Constituent Assembly and a declaration of war aims. In return it would help the war effort. Linlithgow36-43 rejected all three and offered only an advisory committee.
→ So the CWC met at Wardha and the INC walked out of the government.

Wardha 1939: ministries resign.
The CWC refused to support the war and directed the Congress ministries to resign, ending the 28-month rule. Linlithgow36-43 panicked and promised Dominion Status after the war. The ML1906 spotted its opening and passed the Lahore Resolution in March 1940.
→ Now Britain needed to bring the INC back to the table.

August Offer 1940.
Advisory War Council, a bigger VEC, a post-war Constituent Assembly of mainly Indians, Dominion Status after the war, and no constitution without the consent of minorities. The last clause handed the ML a veto over the Constitution.
→ But both sides said no, for opposite reasons.

Both reject, then Individual Satyagraha.
The INC rejected Dominion Status and the backdoor partition in the veto. The ML feared a Hindu-majority Centre would ignore its veto, leaving it with neither power nor Pakistan. MG, pressed to launch a mass movement, chose a limited Individual Satyagraha in October 1940: Bhave, Nehru, Brahma Dutt arrested in that order.
→ Then the war itself turned against Britain.

1941: the war turns.
In 1941 the VEC was expanded to 8 Indians out of 12, but Defence, Home and Finance stayed out of Indian hands. Germany attacked the USSR in June, Japan hit Pearl Harbour in December, and the INC offered support for Purna Swaraj after the war plus immediate ToP.
→ So when Rangoon fell, Britain had to send someone to Delhi.

Cripps 1942: the post-dated cheque.
Japan took Rangoon in March 1942. Under US and USSR pressure, Churchill sent Sir Stafford Cripps. The offer: Dominion Status plus foreign policy, a solely Indian CA, a right to secede (565 + 11 = 576 entities) and Defence with the Viceroy during the war. The talks broke on that last point. MG called it a post-dated cheque.

44.spine: By 1942 the Cripps Mission had failed, war inflation was biting and Britain had run away from Burma and Malaya, so Gandhi drafted a Quit India resolution that the INC passed in Bombay on 8 August 1942. Within hours the top leadership was jailed, so the movement ran leaderless at the top but rooted below: the mass phase was angry and crushed in six weeks, then it went underground and later threw up parallel governments at Ballia, Midnapore and Satara. Gandhi's 1943 fast carried the cause abroad, and by June 1945 the leaders were freed for the Simla Conference. The movement won no instant freedom, but it proved India ungovernable by force and made the British know they could not stay.
beats:
The last door shuts.
The **Cripps Mission (1942)** offered only vague post-war promises and nothing on real transfer of power during the war. It showed that Britain meant to rule on its own terms whatever Indians thought. The last hope of a negotiated settlement was gone.
→ But anger was already rising outside the talks.

Prices and fear.
War **inflation** squeezed ordinary people while British policy ignored the rising cost of living. Britain had also abandoned its colonial subjects in **Burma and Malaya** when Japan invaded, and Indians feared the same fate.
→ So Gandhi asked how a frightened people could resist an invader.

Gandhi's logic.
The INC did not want Indians to meet a Japanese invasion in low morale and passive helplessness. **MG's idea:** a high-spirited, nationalist people would resist far better than a demoralised one. He drafted a resolution demanding Quit India and non-cooperation against Japan if it invaded.
→ Now the party had to authorise him.

Wardha and Bombay.
The **CWC accepted the idea at Wardha in July 1942**. On **8 August 1942** the INC held a special session in Bombay and passed the QIM resolution demanding immediate **Purna Swaraj**. The same evening at **Gowalia Tank (Azad Maidan)** Gandhi gave his **"Do or Die"** speech.
→ But the government struck that same night.

The night of 9 August.
The entire top INC leadership was arrested. The detailed resolution could not be made public, so the public knew only what MG said in the speech. Everything not in the speech, such as the land-revenue plan, stayed a private strategy.
→ So the crowds acted on what they understood.

Six angry weeks.
The **mass struggle** was not non-violent: crowds pulled up railway tracks, blew up bridges, cut telegraph wires and attacked stations, police stations, courts and post offices. Provincial leaders led, villagers joined, and **peasants were the soul** of the movement.
→ But Britain had prepared its weapons.

The harshest repression.
Under the **Revolutionary Movement Ordinance** and **Defence of India Rules** the press was gagged, aircraft carried machine guns, villages were fined and burnt, and **60,000** were arrested by the end of 1942. The mass phase was crushed in **six weeks**.
→ Yet the movement refused to die.

Underground.
The **Congress Socialist Party** leaders ran an underground network: Achyut Patwardhan, Lohia, Aruna Asaf Ali, JP and others. Bombs, arms, couriers, leaked raid plans and rich donors kept it alive, and **Usha Mehta** ran the Congress Radio.
→ Meanwhile Gandhi gave the cause a moral boost from jail.

The fast.
Held at **Aga Khan Palace, Pune**, Gandhi refused to condemn the movement's violence and began a **21-day fast (1943)** against British violence. Indian members of the Viceroy's Executive Council resigned and world media took notice. He lost **Mahadev Desai (15 Aug 1942)** and **Kasturba (22 Feb 1944)** in the same palace.
→ And in places British authority collapsed outright.

People's governments.
**Ballia (Aug 1942, Chittu Pandey)** was the first. **Jatiya Sarkar** at Midnapore (Dec 1942 to Sep 1944) had courts, school grants, rice, cyclone relief and the Vidyut Vahini. The **Patri Sarkar** of Satara (mid-1943 to 1945) was the most successful.
→ Then the war ended and the jails opened.

The end and the verdict.
Gandhi was released in **May 1944** on health grounds and turned to constructive work. In **June 1945** all INC leaders were freed for the **Simla Conference**, which formally ended QIM. India had proved ungovernable by force; after 1942 the British knew they could not stay.

45.spine: In 1943 Bengal starved while food was sent to feed the army: a man-made famine that turned Indian opinion, and British opinion, against the Raj. Japan's sweep through Malaya, Singapore and Burma gave Indian PoWs and expatriates a chance: Mohan Singh built the INA, R.B. Bose held it, and Netaji gave it money, regiments and a Provisional Government. The INA failed at Imphal, but its soldiers, tried at the Red Fort in November 1945, became national heroes and produced the greatest unity of the freedom movement. That sympathy reached the Royal Indian Navy in February 1946; once sailors and airmen defied the Raj, the British saw that the army could no longer be trusted and that transfer of power could not wait.
beats:
A famine with no shortage.
In 1943 roughly 5 million Indians died in Bengal although crops had not failed. Food from India was sent to feed British soldiers and Europeans, Burma's imports stopped after Japan took it in March 1942, logistics were run badly, and war speculation made prices unaffordable.
→ So Indians felt their lives ranked below European lives, but the inquiry that followed did not fix the blame.

The inquiry and the economist.
The Famine Inquiry Commission (1945) under Sir John Woodhead blamed natural factors and supply disruption and let the administration off. Decades later Amartya Sen showed it was a failure of entitlement: wages collapsed, prices soared, procurement drained rural markets.
→ But the famine was only one wound; the same war was cracking British power in South-East Asia.

Japan topples the British in Asia.
Japan took Malaya in January 1942, Singapore in February and Burma in March. Territories held for decades fell in weeks, and thousands of Indian soldiers were now Prisoners of War.
→ So Captain Mohan Singh saw a chance to turn the PoWs into an Indian army.

Mohan Singh builds the INA.
After Singapore fell, Mohan Singh persuaded the Japanese to hand over Indian PoWs; 40,000 in Singapore joined and the First Division was formed in September 1942. In June 1942 expatriates had set up the Indian Independence League at Bangkok as the political wing. In December 1942 Mohan Singh was arrested for demanding real autonomy.
→ But the army needed a leader, and the old Ghadar revolutionary Rash Behari Bose took it over in early 1943.

Netaji's long road.
Bose broke with the Gandhian leadership, formed the Forward Bloc (May 1939) and left the Congress after Tripuri. Arrested in July 1940, he fled house arrest in January 1941 via Afghanistan and the USSR to Germany by March 1941, where he ran Azad Hind Radio and raised the Free Indian Legion from Indian PoWs.
→ Yet Hitler saw Indians as an inferior race, so Bose left Germany in February 1943 for Japan's side of the war.

Netaji takes over the INA.
He crossed the Indian Ocean from a German to a Japanese submarine and reached Singapore in July 1943, where he took over the IIL and the INA from Rash Behari Bose. He raised money from NRIs, formed the Rani Jhansi, Gandhi and Nehru regiments and got Tojo's assurance that Japan would not annex India.
→ With funds and an assurance in hand, he declared a government.

A Provisional Government and the Andamans.
On 21 October 1943 Netaji set up the Provisional Government of Free India with INA headquarters in Rangoon and Singapore. The INA liberated the Andaman and Nicobar Islands; Bose raised the flag there on 29-31 December 1943 and renamed them Shaheed Dweep and Swaraj Dweep.
→ But a flag is not a campaign; the test was the Indian border.

Imphal fails, Japan surrenders.
In 1944 the INA and Japan attacked towards Kohima and Imphal and failed; INA soldiers were even short-changed on weapons and supplies. Japan surrendered on 15 August 1945 and a reported plane crash at Taihoku on 18 August 1945 is said to have killed Netaji.
→ The soldiers were now prisoners, and the British decided to try them.

The Red Fort trials backfire.
In November 1945 Shah Nawaz Khan, Prem Sehgal and Gurbaksh Singh Dhillon were tried at the Red Fort. The British had miscalculated: the country rose, spontaneously and across communities, and even officials gave money. The Congress made the INA a campaign issue, defended the accused under Bhulabhai Desai and ran an INA Relief Committee.
→ That sympathy was strongest inside the forces, and in February 1946 the navy moved.

HMIS Talwar and the Naval Mutiny.
In February 1946 ratings on HMIS Talwar struck over fear of unemployment, poor conditions and racial pay, and INA inspiration. They raised the tricolour with INA, Congress and League flags, wrote 'Quit India' on ships and toured Bombay with Netaji's pictures. The CPI backed them, Bombay's workers struck, and Aruna Asaf Ali led them against Gandhi's and the Congress's advice.
→ Congress and League withdrew support and Patel and Jinnah calmed the ratings, but the damage to British confidence was done.

The signal that ended the Raj's confidence.
With RIAF strikes too, the 'martial races' myth broke and the British saw that the armed forces, the last reliable instrument, were cracking. The Cabinet Mission arrived the very day the mutiny began in Bombay, and this was one of the key factors that made transfer of power impossible to postpone.
